20306-europe-after-8-15:
Europe After 8:15, from 1914, is a bright travel book overtaken by world war. Innsbruck shows checkerboard parks and Christmas garden villas to the writer. An Austrian battalion drills in the Exerzierplatz below his view. It looks like an army of grey ants, barely visible from above.

Somewhere left, past the Hungerberg, the night train labors toward Venice. Such gay travel writing met the guns of August that same year. The title plays on trains and timetables across a continent at peace. Readers get a poignant tour of Europe on the edge of the abyss.
22300-the-menorah-journal-volume-1-1915:
Volume one of The Menorah Journal came out in 1915. The journal served the Menorah movement and its growing Menorah Societies across the country. Its opening pages say the journal must be far more than an official organ for those societies.

Inside, the volume works to carry forward the aims and hopes of the movement. That role grew more pressing as the societies multiplied in number and influence. Readers get a record of an organized Jewish cultural effort taking shape in print. It speaks to its members and to a wider public at the same time.
adventures-of-huckleberry-finn-chapters-: Huck and Jim's raft drifts on through fog, feud, and trickery in these middle chapters of Twain's masterpiece. The Grangerford-Shepherdson feud and the wrecked steamboat show the river's beauty and menace. Huck's education in human nature continues apace. Through fog and feud Huck learns the river's lessons, and Twain's humor never once flags.
arthashastra-shamasastry-1915:
R. Shamasastry published the first English translation of Kautilya's Arthashastra in 1915. Kautilya was chief minister to Chandragupta Maurya, founder of an Indian empire. His treatise on statecraft dates to around the fourth century BCE.

The Arthashastra is a cold-eyed manual of rule in fifteen books. Taxes, spies, diplomacy, war, and law enforcement all receive exact treatment. Kautilya advises kings on testing ministers and trapping enemies without sentiment. Shamasastry had discovered the lost Sanskrit text only years before translating it. His version first showed the work to the modern world. Readers often compare Kautilya to Machiavelli, who wrote eighteen centuries later.
arxiv-2512-00015:
Jack Furby, Dan Cunnington, Dave Braines, and Alun Preece study how concept explanations change human-machine teamwork. Deep networks are often black boxes, so concept models were built to predict human-defined concepts first. That intermediate step makes the final prediction easier to inspect and question.

The authors test how such explanations, and direct interventions on the concepts, affect collaboration. A user who can correct a concept may steer the model better than one who only sees scores. The work informs design of AI tools that people can genuinely supervise.
arxiv-2512-00215:
Large language models can predict what a program will print, but their reasoning on the way there is murky. Mohammad Abdollahi and co-authors study errors inside those reasoning traces in 2025, focusing on code execution simulation. They examine how intermediate states and control flow lead to final results.

Earlier studies mostly compared output accuracy and treated reasoning as a black box. Understanding a program's runtime behavior is essential for reliable code generation, debugging, and automated reasoning. By demystifying where traces go wrong, the study helps developers judge when a model's confident answer rests on broken steps. Code execution is a strict test, because one wrong intermediate value usually ruins the answer.
arxiv-2512-00315:
Dengue fever follows the mosquito, but it may also follow the street network. Marcílio Ferreira dos Santos and co-authors study dengue incidence in Recife, Brazil, across a decade, in a 2025 study. They ask whether the structural connectivity of urban roads helps explain where cases concentrate.

For each neighborhood, the team computes communicability curvature, a graph measure of how strongly a place can influence others through many network paths. A Bayesian spatial analysis then links that structure to recorded incidence from 2015 to 2024. If road structure drives spread, city planners gain a new lever for targeting mosquito control. Bayesian methods let the team state uncertainty neighborhood by neighborhood.
arxiv-2512-00515:
Sentiment analysis reads opinion from text, and doing it well in Turkish raises challenges English tools never face. A doctoral thesis summarized in 2025 develops a comprehensive framework for sentiment analysis that accounts for its many aspects, mainly for Turkish. Several approaches specific to English are also proposed.

The work reports five major and three minor contributions. Its novel feature set combines unsupervised, semi-supervised, and supervised metrics for stronger classification. Turkish is rich in suffixes and flexible in word order, so features built for English transfer poorly. A dedicated framework helps Turkish media, commerce, and research. Feature design is where the thesis stakes its main claim to novelty.
arxiv-2512-00615:
Group theory studies how the structure of a group constrains the values its commutator words can take. Martina Capasso, Liliana Lancellotti, and Pavel Shumyatsky study Chernikov-by-nilpotent groups in 2025. They focus on the lower central word and the subgroup it generates.

For each level, the authors consider the set of word values and the corresponding term of the lower central series. Chernikov groups are built from finite and quasicyclic pieces, giving the class a rich but tractable structure. Results here feed the broader program of understanding how verbal subgroups behave in restricted classes of infinite groups. Lower central series measure how far a group is from being abelian.
arxiv-2512-00915:
Junwoo Chang and five coauthors blend symmetry into robot learning in a 2025 paper. Reinforcement learning teaches agents by reward, and many tasks have group symmetries, motions that leave the task unchanged. Respecting those symmetries helps an agent generalize, since it can reuse lessons across symmetric states and actions.

Real settings, though, almost never keep symmetries perfectly. Dynamics, actuator limits, and reward design break them, often only in places. The team's partially equivariant method keeps symmetry where it holds and relaxes it where it breaks. That balance could make robot policies both data-efficient and honest about real-world messiness.
arxiv-2512-01115:
Tao Zhang and Yevgeniy Vorobeychik extend a privacy framework in a 2025 paper. Pufferfish privacy is a family of definitions that state exactly which secrets a data release must protect. Its Rényi version gives strong guarantees, but two practical gaps remain: calibrating noise needs high-dimensional optimal transport, and iterative learning lacks a general composition rule.

Their sliced version replaces high-dimensional comparisons with directional ones over a set of unit vectors. That makes guarantees geometry-aware and tractable to compute. They also apply it to private learning with gradient clipping. Practical accounting rules decide whether privacy methods leave the lab.
arxiv-2512-01615:
Sergiy Mankovsky and co-authors compute electric polarization driven by spin alignment. In type II multiferroics, slanted spins create electric polarization. That link lets magnetic order switch electric traits. First-principles methods can predict the effect.

Their approach parametrizes polarization with terms from a Green function method. The cell polarization is split into three-site terms. Those terms show which spin triples drive the signal. Such insight helps design materials where magnetism controls electric response for sensors and memory. Three-site terms show that pairs alone understate the effect, a lesson for model builders who truncate spin interactions too early.
arxiv-2512-02115:
Mapping the Milky Way's gravity reveals where its ordinary and dark matter sit, but star surveys see the galaxy through dust and uneven coverage. Taavet Kalda and Gregory Green present in 2025 a new variant of the Deep Potential method that infers the gravitational potential without modeling those selection effects.

The method learns from a snapshot of stellar positions and velocities, the raw material of galactic dynamics. Selection functions, the corrections for what a survey missed, normally complicate such inference and can bias it. Skipping that modeling makes the potential estimate cleaner and more direct. A trustworthy gravity map is a foundation for weighing the galaxy's dark matter halo.
arxiv-2512-02315:
Protein engineers often have only a handful of measurements for a new protein, far too few to train a predictor. Felix Teufel and co-authors introduce PRIMO in 2025, a transformer framework that predicts protein fitness from few examples by learning in context and continuing to train at test time.

In-context learning lets the model adapt to a new protein and assay from the examples in front of it, without a large task-specific dataset. Test-time training squeezes more from those few examples before predicting. Reliable few-shot fitness prediction would speed protein engineering, where every experimental measurement is slow and costly.
arxiv-2512-02515:
Lixing He and three co-authors work on clearer speech from earbuds and headsets used in noisy places. Tiny devices leave little room for microphones, yet calls and voice assistants must still hear the user well. A single all direction microphone struggles when other voices crowd the same space.

VibOmni adds bone conduction sensing, picking up voice through vibrations in the head itself. Those vibrations carry the wearer's speech while mostly ignoring outside noise. Blending both signals aims for clean voice pickup that scales across earables, a growing class of small devices people wear all day. Clear voice pickup is a must for calls made on a busy street or a loud train.
arxiv-2512-02615:
Nicolai-Leonid Bathen and nine co-authors measure the twist between two stacked sheets of tungsten diselenide. Twisted bilayers form moiré patterns, regular superlattices that reshape how electrons and light behave. The physics depends sharply on the exact twist angle, which disorder and rebuilding can shift.

Small angle errors change the energy landscape and the electron correlations researchers want to study. The team reads the angle from optical moiré phonons, vibrations tied to the pattern itself. A precise, light based ruler for twist angle helps labs build samples whose behavior they can trust and repeat. Light based checks are fast and do no harm to the flake, which keeps the best flakes in play.
arxiv-2512-02715:
Peirong Zhang and eight co-authors help AI find tiny objects in satellite images from text queries. Visual grounding links words to the image region they describe. Remote sensing makes this hard: targets can be specks in scenes kilometers wide, and queries often use relative positions.

GeoViS adds geospatially rewarded visual search to multimodal language models for this task. Rewards favor answers that respect spatial relations and context across distant objects. Better grounding speeds map making, disaster checks, and land monitoring, where analysts now hunt small features by eye for hours. Search that knows the land can cut hours of eye work for teams that map floods, fires, and crop loss.
arxiv-2512-02915:
Paweł Nosal studies very short sums of a classic number theory symbol over prime ranges. Character sums measure how evenly a sequence, here the Legendre symbol, spreads its signs. A central limit theorem describes the whole distribution of such sums, not just their average size.

Nosal proves that behavior for almost all primes, with the starting point chosen at random in a growing range. The interval length may grow slower than any power of the prime. Distributional results like this sharpen our sense of how random arithmetic sequences truly behave. Short sums are the wild west of this field. Mean based rules fail there, and full spread laws are the ones worth their ink in print.
arxiv-2512-03015:
Waves on a line of points follow rules worth knowing well. Carsten Peterson builds up the basic theory of the discrete wave equation in this 2025 work. His aim is to support study of waves on affine buildings, a newer topic in math.

Peterson works on the integers, the whole numbers in a line. From there he explains known results about waves on regular graphs, where each point has the same number of links. Clear basics help others tackle scattering and quantum chaos. The work gives a firm base for more advanced wave studies. Graph wave results then rest on a firm base built step by step from the line case.
arxiv-2512-03315:
Simulating turbulent flow needs filters that adapt to the flow. Mohammadmahdi Ranjbar, Ali Mostafavi, and Farzad Mashayek present a self-tuning filter in this 2025 work. It builds on their earlier dynamic modal filter for large-eddy simulation.

The new filter tunes its own parameters from local flow features. It also extends how modal values are found, beyond Chebyshev grids to general points and polynomial bases. Adaptive filters can cut cost while keeping accuracy in jet, wing, and engine simulations. That balance is key for practical engineering design. Local tuning avoids hand-set filters that fail when flow conditions change mid-flight.
arxiv-2512-03515:
Chaotic systems still show strong statistical patterns. David Burguet, Chiyi Luo, and Dawei Yang prove an effective form of such a pattern in this 2025 work. They study ergodic measures with large entropy for surface maps and three-dimensional flows.

They prove such measures give uniformly large weight to points with long stable and unstable manifolds. As a consequence, they establish an effective SPR property for smooth surface diffeomorphisms. Effective versions turn qualitative theory into usable bounds. That helps in dynamics, where explicit rates are often missing. Uniform bounds are the prize, since pointwise results can hide bad behavior on small sets that matter for long-term prediction.
arxiv-2512-03815:
Software teams argue endlessly about keeping code in one giant repository or splitting it into many small ones. Shayan Ghasemnezhad, Samarth KaPatel, and Sofia Nikiforova propose a middle path in a 2025 software preprint. Single repositories give consistency but strain tooling as they grow, while many small ones ease the split into parts yet complicate coordination and shared dependencies.

Their Causify Dev system is built around the runnable directory, a self-contained unit that carries its own development, testing, and deployment life cycle. A thin shared environment, common helper utilities, and container-based workflows keep setups consistent across units while the links stay isolated. Continuous integration and delivery then run efficiently per unit. The authors present the approach as a practical compromise for large, complex codebases. It aims to keep the reliability of a monorepo and the independence of separate ones at the same time.
arxiv-2512-03915:
Mixture-of-experts models save computing by sending each token to only a few specialist subnetworks, but the routing can overload some experts and idle others. X. Y. Han and Yuan Zhong supply theory for a popular fix in a 2025 optimisation preprint. The method under study is the auxiliary-loss-free load balancing procedure introduced by DeepSeek researchers, which skips the usual extra penalty term.

Han and Zhong recast the procedure as a primal-dual method solving an assignment problem, with one quick update per training step. In a simplified deterministic setting, they prove the objective improves monotonically and that tokens migrate from overloaded to underloaded experts, ending near balance. In the messier online setting of real training, they derive a logarithmic expected regret bound. Experiments on a billion-parameter DeepSeekMoE model accompany the theory. Together, the results give the heuristic a principled foundation.
arxiv-2512-04015:
To edit an image in a controlled way, say rotating only the object, a model must know which parts of its internal representation a transformation touches. Farhana Hossain Swarnali, Miaomiao Zhang, and Tonmoy Hossain automate that discovery in a 2025 computer vision preprint. Earlier latent-space methods forced researchers to split the representation into changing and fixed parts by hand.

Their framework learns group actions directly on latent image manifolds. Learnable binary masks, trained with a straight-through estimator, partition the representation into transformation-sensitive and invariant components without manual labels. Disentanglement and the transformation mappings are learned jointly in one optimisation, and the method wraps around any standard encoder-decoder. Tests on five image datasets show the system finding the right factors alone. Downstream classification confirmed the representations stay useful, and code is publicly available.
arxiv-2512-04115:
What Finnish teenagers fear about artificial intelligence depends, it turns out, on how competent they feel using it. Ville Heilala and colleagues survey upper secondary students in a 2025 preprint on computers and society. About one hundred sixty students rated their own AI competence and their concerns about AI across personal, institutional, and systemic domains, and the team mapped how answers co-occurred.

Students with lower self-rated competence dwelled on personal risks: shrinking creativity, weaker critical thinking, and misuse. Students who felt more competent looked upward instead, worrying about bias, inaccuracy, and cheating. The same technology thus reads as a threat to one's own learning or as a threat to institutions, depending on the reader. The authors argue schools should respond with AI literacy in the curriculum and guided teacher support. One-size teaching will miss risks that students actually perceive.
arxiv-2512-04215:
The Yang-Baxter equation, born in mathematical physics, has a set-theoretic shadow whose solutions are built from algebraic structures called racks and braces. Marzia Mazzotta, Paola Stefanelli, and Magdalena Wiertel open a systematic study of the 'quasi' versions of those solutions in a 2025 algebra preprint. Their motivation comes from dual weak braces, whose solutions land in these looser classes.

The authors introduce and examine quasi racks and the derived solution construction, extending the classical definitions. One family of such solutions, the quasi left non-degenerate ones, is built from quasi racks and g-twists, paralleling the well-understood non-degenerate case. They also completely characterise one class of quasi racks: those that are Plonka sums of racks. The paper sets up foundations rather than applications, giving the quasi theory the same careful scaffolding the classical theory already enjoys.
arxiv-2601-07215:
Gabriel Silva wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on the spike trains sent by nerve cells. A nerve cell fires by means of an action potential, a sharp pulse of voltage. The pulse acts like a digital blip in the cell's signal line. A spike train is the set of times when one cell fires. Silva works in the field of bioengineering and brain science.

The full pulse has a shape that plays out over time. That shape is tied to the voltage across the wall of the cell. To treat spikes as bare points in time is to drop that shape. Silva argues that the two views are far apart in strict math terms. He sets out a frame that treats a spike train as a spread-out object, in the sense of functional analysis. The frame may change how teams read and weigh spike data from the brain.
arxiv-2601-07715:
Hugo Matias and Daniel Silvestre keep a moving agent safe among obstacles whose motion is uncertain. Their 2026 preprint presents a sampled-data framework for safe navigation. The obstacles follow linear dynamics with uncertainty. Collision-free motion comes from two parts working together. One part filters control commands for safety. The other estimates the obstacles' states as sets.

Safety filtering uses control barrier functions, which block commands that would breach a safety margin. State estimation uses constrained convex generators, a way to represent sets of possible obstacle states. Together they handle both control and perception uncertainty. Robots, vehicles, and drones all face moving obstacles with imperfect tracking. The paper speaks to control engineers who need guarantees, not just good average behavior. It aims for safety that survives the stated uncertainty.
arxiv-2601-07815:
Erhan Bayraktar and Jiamin Jian study how large-population control problems settle as the horizon grows. They investigate convergence and turnpike properties for linear-quadratic mean field control with common noise. The framework unifies three problems: a finite-horizon social optimization, its mean field limit, and the matching ergodic problem. Mean field control models crowds where each agent reacts to the average behavior. Common noise shakes the whole population at once.

Turnpike properties say optimal paths spend most time near a steady state, whatever the endpoints. Proving convergence links the finite and infinite versions of the problem. Such results justify using the simpler ergodic problem for long horizons. The paper serves scholars in stochastic control and mean field games. Applications range from energy systems to large fleets of devices. It supplies theory for a widely used approximation.
arxiv-2601-08015:
Abhishek Kumar presents a decoder that generates three-dimensional structures ready to print. The framework decodes latent representations into geometrically valid, printable objects. It respects manufacturing constraints such as overhang angles, wall thickness, and structural integrity. Many generative models produce shapes that look fine but cannot be built. His 2026 preprint builds manufacturability into the generation itself. The decoder is the core of the deep learning framework.

Additive manufacturing fails when designs overhang too far or walls run too thin. Checking after generation wastes most candidate designs. Generating within the constraints yields usable objects directly. That shift matters for automated design tools and rapid prototyping. The paper serves scholars in generative design and manufacturing. It argues the printer's limits belong inside the model, not in a cleanup step.
arxiv-2601-08215: Seng Pei Liew, Kenta Shinzato, and Yuyang Dong seek principled design rules for mixture-of-experts language models. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that modern designs rest on two factors: total parameters and active parameters. Total size sets the memory footprint, while active size sets inference cost. The authors find these two factors alone cannot describe an optimal architecture. Memory and inference limits shape real deployments, so missing factors can mislead builders. The paper aims at design rules that reflect how such models are actually run and stored.
arxiv-2601-08315: Qi Yao, Jun Zhang, Wenxian Zhang, and Chaohong Lee extend qubit coherence with a hybrid decoupling method. Their 2026 arXiv paper addresses decoherence from a qubit's coupling to its environment. Dynamical decoupling and bath engineering are two parallel defenses against that coupling. The hybrid approach joins pulsed decoupling with bath spin polarization. Tests run within the central spin model, a standard testbed for this problem. Longer coherence times would let quantum processors run deeper circuits before noise erases the computation.
arxiv-2601-08415:
Brittany Davidson, Kate Muir, Florian Burnat, and Adam Joinson compare the terms of service of major language model providers. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that these models now sit inside academic research pipelines. The rules governing their use remain under-examined, though.

The team analyzes terms from Anthropic, DeepSeek, Google, OpenAI, and xAI, collected in November 2025. Gray areas in such terms can leave researchers unsure what uses are allowed. Data handling, publication rights, and liability often hide in fine print. For universities and labs, a clear comparison helps set policy before a project depends on a model whose terms may shift.
arxiv-2601-08615:
Kansei Inamura and Shuhei Ohyama build lattice models of a class of guarded states of matter. Such states hold their traits in the bulk, not just at the edge. Their models have a rare type of rule that can not be flipped like a plain switch. The team calls these states by the name cluster states, in a broad sense.

They build the models by fixing part of a plain rule group in place. They then study the traits with grid nets that stand for the states. Work covers walls where two states meet, and whole sets of states that shift by a knob. A reader in this field gets new model cases. They help map how non flip rules guard a state of matter.
arxiv-2601-08815:
Qing Ye and Jing Tan set rules for AI agents that must work with firm caps. An agent here is a program that acts on its own for a set time. Old group rules let agents pass tasks by deal, but they set no cap on cost or time. A runaway agent could burn cash or run far too long.

Their frame is called Agent Contracts. A deal states what the agent may use, how long it may run, and when it must stop. The rules are formal, so a host can check them by machine. A reader who lets agents act gets a guard rail. It lets agents work free, but only in a box that both sides agreed.
arxiv-2601-09815:
John Joseph M. Carrasco and four co-authors derive the full four-graviton effective theory from a duality. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds on the Bern-Carrasco-Johansson double copy. That construction reveals a deep structural link between gauge theory and gravity.

At its heart, the double copy rests on a duality between color algebra and kinematic algebra. The authors generalize the principle beyond the Lie algebra structure of tree-level Yang-Mills theory. From it, they obtain the entire four-graviton effective field theory. The result extends a calculational trick into a statement about how gravity is built.
arxiv-2601-09915:
Andrei Kulikovsky and Tatyana Reshetenko model water inside fuel cell membranes and test the model against spectra. Their 2026 arXiv paper joins a water transport model with an impedance model for PEM fuel cells. Good water management is essential for these cells to perform at their best.

The impedance model covers liquid water moving through the membrane. It is coupled to a two-phase model for the cathode side. The full model was fitted to measured spectra at three humidity pairings, from 32 to 100 percent. Currents ranged from 100 to 1000 milliamps per square centimeter. Fits like these turn impedance spectra into a diagnostic for what limits a working cell.
arxiv-2601-10415:
R. M. F. Andersen and co authors test how cloud traits are read from burst shots of cold atoms. A Bose Einstein cloud is a gas cooled till its parts act as one. Warm clouds mix a dense core with a loose halo. A shot is taken as the cloud bursts free.

From the burst shape, labs read heat, atom count, and the dense share. The team ask how the push twixt core and halo warps that read. The core and halo shove each other as they grow. That shove can bias the halo shape. The work maps the bias so reads can be set right.
arxiv-2601-10915:
Yangshuo He, Guanding Yu, and Jingge Zhu analyze how wireless channels degrade edge inference. In edge inference, a neural network is split across nearby devices. The parts must talk over wireless links while they compute. Standard networks are trained in noiseless settings. Live channels are noisy, so a mismatch opens between training and deployment.

The authors use PAC-Bayesian analysis, a framework that bounds how much performance can drop. Their bounds tie channel noise to inference loss in a principled way. Such bounds can guide where to split a network and how much redundancy to add. The work serves designers of phone, camera, and vehicle systems that must think over the air.
arxiv-2601-11515:
Callum Donnan and six coauthors confirm a galaxy at redshift 13.53. Their 2026 preprint reports JWST spectroscopy of the source. The galaxy was a robust candidate near redshift 14. It was picked from pure-parallel NIRCam imaging data.

NIRSpec PRISM observations then gave the team a spectrum. Modeling of the Lyman-alpha break fixed the distance. The confirmed value is 13.53, with small error bars. The galaxy is large and luminous for its era. Its emission lines are weak, an odd trait so early. Such finds test how fast the first galaxies grew. Weak lines may hint at young stars and low metal content.
arxiv-2601-11715:
Nicolas Mazziotti, Michael G. Jones, Donghyeon J. Khim, David J. Sand, and Paul Bennet report a search for faint, spread out galaxies in the Fornax group. The search was done by citizen science, with the public helping to spot weak shapes in sky images. Such faint galaxies are hard for code alone to find.

Their list holds 643 diffuse galaxies in the group. They judge that about one in five has a bright core, based on counts they give in the text. They note this is the first crowd based count of this kind at the scale of a whole group. The list gives a base for later work on how such faint systems form.
arxiv-2601-12215:
Megha Thukral, Cyrus Tanade, Simon A. Lee, and a large team build foundation models for PPG signals that heed their wave structure. PPG tracks blood flow from light on skin, as in wrist wearables. Such models could learn traits that move across health tasks.

Most past training skips the spectral form of PPG, where body rhythms sit in split frequency bands. Their wavelet-driven masked method rebuilds hidden parts across scales. That should bake rhythm form into the traits. Good PPG traits aid heart and sleep tools from wearables.  Rhythm bands are the cue past models missed most.
arxiv-2601-12315:
A MAGPI survey team with Bodo Ziegler measure dark matter in star-forming disk galaxies at redshifts from about 0.1 to 0.85. They use spatially resolved kinematic data from the MAGPI survey, which uses integral field spectroscopy. Their sample holds 266 rotation-supported, main-sequence galaxies.

They analyse how dark matter content links to galaxy structure. Such links test how baryons and dark matter co-evolve. Disk galaxies at those distances show the universe at a younger age. The work gives a large, uniform sample for that test.  The sample is large for this kind of disk study.
arxiv-2601-12615:
Robert Prater and ten co authors measure the electronic band structure of a compound called CeCoGe3. They use angle resolved photoemission spectroscopy, a method that maps electron energies across a crystal. Their study covers the entire Brillouin zone, the full cell of momenta in the crystal. They work in the non magnetic regime of the compound.

The measured structure agrees in large part with first principles calculations. That agreement includes predicted topological nodal lines in the band structure. Nodal lines are features where bands cross in a protected way. Confirming them by direct measurement grounds the theory of this material. The work serves studies of topological metals and cerium based compounds.
arxiv-2601-12915:
Francesco Salerno proves a sharp lower bound for Monge Ampere torsion on convex sets. The torsion functional measures how a convex set responds to a classic equation of geometry. The deficit compares the value on a given set with the value on a matching ball. That ball shares the same quermassintegral, a mixed volume measure.

A lower bound on the deficit says how far a set must fall short of the ball. Sharp means the bound is the best possible of its kind. Results of this shape are isoperimetric in spirit: balls win, and others pay a quantifiable price. The setting covers open, bounded convex sets with smooth boundary. The work serves convex geometry and partial differential equations.
arxiv-2601-13015:
Nowfel Mashnoor, Mohammad Akyash, Hadi Kamali, and Kimia Azar work on code for chips. Large language models can now draft register transfer level code, the form that tells chip tools what gates to build. The snag is that drafts for hard designs often fail on syntax or on logic.

Their fix is called MeltRTL. It blends the skill of many expert parts inside the model. It also steps in while the model writes, to steer the draft. No fresh train of the base model is needed. The authors say this lifts the share of drafts that are both well formed and right in what they do. Chip teams may find the route a cheap way to get more from models they already run.
arxiv-2601-13315:
Rakesh Kumar SivaKumar and a co-author ask why dark matter and plain matter come in near matched sums. In the Randall-Sundrum set up, space has a spare dim with two walls, called branes. Our world sits on the low energy wall, the IR brane. The team puts both dark and plain fields on that wall.

The two talk just through the graviton and the radion, the field that sets the wall gap. Dark bits are made by freeze in, a slow leak from the hot bath, not a freeze out. The team shows the count seen by the Planck craft can be met for a wide span of reheat heats. They test scalar, fermion, and heavy vector forms of the dark bit.
arxiv-2601-13515:
Huah Yong Chan and co-authors tune a Kubernetes auto scaler to both serve load and block attacks. The scaler is the HPA, which sets how many pods run an app. In their test, HTTP status codes serve as the custom mark the scaler reads. Attack floods can fool a plain scaler into waste or crash.

A random forest judge reads the codes to call if a surge is an attack. It then shifts the top pod cap the scaler may use. A true surge can still grow. An attack surge is held in check. For cloud teams, a scaler that can tell load from attack saves both cost and uptime.
arxiv-2601-13615:
Lifu Ding, Chunhui Hou, Yutong Li, and Qinmin Yang study control of small local power grids in 2026. These microgrids mix two kinds of inverters, grid-following and grid-forming units. Long-term cost plans pull one way, while split-second balance needs pull an other. Each unit also has its own hard limits, and cyber attacks add more risk.

The team sets out a layered control plan called RHPC. The plan tries to join cost aims and fast balance in one frame. It is built to stay firm when attacks or faults hit the grid. Such control could help small grids run clean power with less waste and fewer blackouts.
arxiv-2601-14015:
Jason Douglas Todd and Ismar Volić build a voting method that borrows from web search ranking in 2026. BallotRank is a ranked preference aggregation method derived from PageRank. PageRank ranks web pages by the links that point to them. BallotRank adapts that idea to ballots, without a damping factor.

The method is Condorcet-consistent, meaning it honors a candidate who beats each rival head-to-head. They tested it on nearly two thousand ranked choice elections. Over twenty thousand internet polls were also examined. At conventional damping values, BallotRank always identified the Condorcet winner.
arxiv-2601-14215:
Arianna Nigioni and co-authors build a global formation model for planets in binary systems in 2026. Roughly half of Sun-like stars have at least one stellar companion. Most known exoplanets are assumed to orbit single stars, largely from observational biases. New surveys are steadily increasing the count of confirmed exoplanets in binaries.

Astrometric surveys, direct imaging, and speckle interferometry drive that growth. Their PAIRS project models planet formation in binaries at a global scale. A global model can predict where planets form around two suns. Those predictions guide observers to the most promising pairs.
arxiv-2601-14915:
Xiao-En Huang, Shan Cheng, and De-Liang Yao study how certain charm mesons decay. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with D and Ds mesons that decay into an eta meson, a charged lepton, and a neutrino. Fresh precise data from the BESIII detector prompts the work.

The team reworks the decay form factors with QCD light-cone sum rules. They add high-twist terms and known next-order QCD fixes. Their study confirms a chiral boost that comes from twist-3 terms. It also shows that the expansion behind the method settles down fast and cleanly.
arxiv-2601-15015:
Jannis Becktepe, Aleksandra Franz, Nils Thuerey, and Sebastian Peitz build a fair test track for learning-based flow control. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with active flow control, where actuators steer a fluid flow. Reinforcement learning has shown promise in this field.

Progress is hard to judge, though. Past studies used unlike sensors, actuators, setups, and scoring rules. Existing test suites lean on outside fluid solvers and lack full 3D or multi-agent support. The authors offer a plug-and-play benchmark to fix that. One setup lets rival methods be compared head to head.
arxiv-2601-15215:
Nicolas Gilliers and David Jekel mix the five classic forms of independence into one notion. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with non-commutative probability, where random quantities need not commute. They define joint independence for several algebras at once.

The pairwise relations between the algebras are coded by a bigraph. A bigraph is a graph with two sets of edges. Depending on the edges, each pair follows one of the five types: tensor, free, monotone, anti-monotone, or Boolean. The frame thus holds all five classic types in a single unified combinatorial structure.
arxiv-2601-15715:
Zhitao He, Zongwei Lyu, and Yi R. Fung study academic rebuttal as a persuasion game in a 2026 arXiv paper. AI now helps at many stages of research. Rebuttal, the reply to reviewers, remains underexplored. It is not a plain technical debate. Authors must persuade under severe information asymmetry. They do not know exactly what each reviewer thinks or values.

The title frames their approach: strategic persuasion via theory of mind. Theory of mind means modeling the other side's beliefs. A good rebuttal guesses what worries a reviewer and answers that. The paper's title, Dancing in Chains, hints at the constraints authors feel. For researchers, rebuttal skill can decide a paper's fate. A formal account of that skill could help both humans and AI assistants.
arxiv-2601-15915:
Chen Xu proposes a first-order method for hard optimization in a 2026 arXiv paper. The problem class is nonconvex optimization. The objective averages a function over data drawn from a distribution. Such problems sit under most machine learning training. Nonconvex landscapes have many traps: local minima and saddle points. First-order methods use only gradients, so they scale well. His method is Progressive Power Homotopy, or Prog-PowerHP.

Homotopy methods solve a hard problem by morphing an easy one into it. The progressive power idea shapes that morphing. A well-built path can steer gradients past traps. Training large models is a costly search through such terrain. Any first-order method with better navigation earns attention from practitioners and theorists alike.
arxiv-2601-16515:
Tongcheng Fang and coauthors make sparse gaze fast for video spread coders. Their 2026 preprint, named SALAD, deals with video build by spread steps. Coders for video use gaze to join frames in time. Full gaze costs much and slows each build step. Sparse gaze cuts cost but can drop grade if set by hand.

The team tunes straight gaze to act as sparse gaze with skill. Tune steps keep the grade of full gaze at low cost. Fast video builds then fit more gear and more use. Gains count for long clips and high res builds. The work joins gaze tricks in one tune path.
arxiv-2601-16615:
Xiang Chen sets out a fast edge vision model named AuroraEdge-V-2B. His 2026 preprint deals with models that join pics and words. Plants now seek such models for use on the shop floor. Shop gear needs fast, strong models that run on site kit. Big cloud models oft fail that need on speed and cost.

AuroraEdge aims to be both fast and strong on edge kit. Its size sits at the two B scale in the name. Tests check grade and speed on plant like tasks. A strong edge model could spread shop AI wide. The work frames edge use as the main design goal.
arxiv-2601-16715:
Adrick Tench and Thomas Demeester help health teams find cause links in data. True cause maps make health calls clear and sound. They let teams gauge what a drug or act will do. But dozens of cause-hunt tools crowd the field. No tool wins on all data types. Their 2026 preprint blends tools with expert help.

Their blend shifts weight among tools as proof comes in. A guide tool steers which tool to trust when. The mix aims to beat any lone tool's map. Sound cause maps shape care, trials, and health spend. This blend may spare teams the trap of a poor lone pick.
arxiv-2601-16815:
Shaoqing Wang and a team of six co-authors sharpen how apps pick what to show you. Shops and feeds must pick top picks from vast pools fast. Old picks lean on item-to-item links or twin tower nets. Those tools miss fine user-item sparks. They also cut lists in blunt, same-for-all ways. Their 2026 preprint builds a pick frame tuned to each user.

Their frame weighs item links with a user's own past acts. It aims to keep the picks apt at low cost. Sharp picks lift sales and user trust in apps. The work was shared at a top web meet in Dubai.
arxiv-2601-17315:
Xiaoyang Li and Runni Zhou present ClinNet, a tool to grade knee osteoarthritis from X-ray images. Grading is hard for three reasons. Grades differ by small signs. Human labels carry real doubt. And the grades form an order, from mild to severe. Most past tools treat the task as plain class choice. That misses the order and the doubt.

ClinNet uses evidential ordinal regression to keep both. It adds a check on left-right asymmetry in the knees. It also keeps a prototype memory of past cases. The mix aims for grades a clinician can trust. Better grading guides care for a joint disease that affects many older adults.
arxiv-2601-17515:
Rudraksh Sharma studies quantum phase transitions in the transverse-field Ising model. The model is a line of spins with two rival forces. One force aligns spins with each other. The other pulls them with a cross field. Their clash drives a quantum phase change. Sharma compares three ways to study the ground state and critical dynamics.

The ways are exact diagonalisation, variational quantum eigensolver runs, and quantum hardware runs. Each has known strengths and flaws. A side-by-side test shows where cheap methods hold up. It also shows where hardware noise breaks the picture. Such benchmarks guide quantum simulation at large. They tell labs what today's machines can prove.
arxiv-2601-17615:
Rahul Bera and co-authors present Athena, a system that joins two ways to hide memory delay. Prefetching loads data before it is needed. Off-chip prediction guesses if a load will miss the cache. Both fight the same delay from unlike angles. Athena synergizes them with online reinforcement learning. The learner adapts choices as the program runs.

A joint policy can beat each trick used alone. Online learning fits shifting program phases. Faster memory means faster chips at the same clock rate. The work targets high-performance processors. It comes from teams at ETH Zürich and NTNU. Their design treats latency as a control problem, learned live.
arxiv-2601-18115:
Guyang Cao, Shuyao Li, Sushrut Karmalkar, and Jelena Diakonikolas study learning one neuron under harsh conditions. Their 2026 preprint uses squared loss, the standard score for fit. The data may carry arbitrary label noise, so some labels are simply wrong. Groups in the data may also shift in share, which can wreck a model tuned to one mix. The goal is a best-fit neuron that still does well under the worst reweighting of the groups.

That worst-case goal is the group DRO view: no group should be sacrificed. A single neuron is the smallest unit of a neural network, so clean results here anchor bigger theory. The work covers a broad family of input distributions.
arxiv-2601-18215:
Yan-Wei Li, Rui Ding, and Wen-Hao Ma separate the energy and entropy shares in a two-dimensional melting step. Their 2026 preprint studies the hexatic-liquid transition in repulsive systems. Decades of work show this transition can be first-order or continuous. The kind depends on the potential and on system details in ways that stayed unclear. The thermodynamic roots of that sensitivity are the paper's target.

By splitting energy from entropy, the team can say which force drives the switch. That split may explain why similar systems melt in different ways. Two-dimensional melting is a model for films, colloids, and surface layers. A clear cause helps predict behavior in new materials.
arxiv-2601-18415:
Ivan Bondarenko and five colleagues built Pisets, a speech to text tool made for lectures and for long talks with guests. Such sound files are key for lab staff and news staff, but a wrong word in a quote or a claim can do real harm. One well known tool, Whisper, can add words that were never said.

Pisets cuts that risk with three parts that check each other. A first part turns sound to text in a strict way. A second part weeds out false hits by a check on the sound form. A last part runs Whisper for a clean final text. The chain aims for text that staff can trust when they write up a talk or print a quote from a guest.
arxiv-2601-18815:
Juan Madrigal-Cianci, Camilo Monsalve Maya, and Lachlan Breakey treat the price path of a bet market as a clue to be read back-wards. In such a market, folk bet on an event, and the price sums up what they know. But the path from lone facts to the price is noisy. Folk are un-like, some bet by plan, and the trade it-self bends the price. The team ask what the full path of price and trade size can tell us of the event.

They frame the ask as a back-wards task in the school of Bayes. The hid truth is the event's end state. The seen facts are the price and size path. From them they work out how much can be known, and how much gain each new trade gives. Such maths could help grade how much a market truly knows.
arxiv-2601-19715:
Poulami Paul and Chanchal Kundu work on building investment portfolios under risk. Picking stocks means balancing expected return against the danger of loss. Investors differ in how they feel about risk, and a good model should respect that. The authors build decision models around a fractional-order entropy measure proposed by Ubriaco.

Entropy here measures uncertainty in returns. The fractional version can capture different attitudes toward risk. The team normalises the measure and uses it inside portfolio choice models. Their earlier work introduced the entropy for this purpose; this paper develops the decision framework around it. Such models aim to give investors portfolios that match both the numbers and their own tolerance for risk.
arxiv-2601-19915:
Paul Tarau reimagines the architecture of language models through the lens of logic. Standard models encode word order by adding position signals to token vectors and mixing them with attention. Tarau instead reads next-token prediction as intuitionistic implication, a constructive form of logical deduction. The prefix of a sentence becomes a chain of implications.

His Arrow Language Model encodes that chain directly. Each token implies the next in a left-nested structure. Order is preserved by non-commutative composition, meaning the chain cannot be shuffled without changing meaning. The design tests whether logical structure can replace attention's mixing. It is a conceptual probe as much as a practical model. Such probes clarify what mainstream architectures actually rely on.
arxiv-2601-20015:
Amani Agrawal, Tianxin Wang, and Dennis Shasha release a test suite for database tuning. Database systems expose many tuning options, layered across storage and query settings. Knowing which options pay off under which loads is mostly folklore. Their suite, DBTuneSuite, runs experiments on four widely deployed free database systems.

The suite varies query and upsert loads and flips tuning options in combination. It ships scripts to generate data, install systems, and run the tests, so others can extend it. The authors draw out which systems suit which query types. They also present quantitative evidence on widely used tuning practices. Practitioners get measurements instead of rules of thumb. The suite is built to grow with new systems and tests.
arxiv-2601-20115:
Emanuele Del Sozzo, Martin Fleming, Kenneth Flamm, and Neil Thompson track how much NVIDIA datacenter graphics processors have improved over time. These chips now drive graphics, supercomputing, and most large AI training. Knowing the real pace of their progress helps labs plan what science they can attempt.

The authors measure past and current gains across chip generations. Their aim is to show where progress is fast, where it slows, and what limits may come next. Such a record matters because research plans, budgets, and energy use all hinge on how much compute each new chip truly adds.
arxiv-2601-20215:
Na Li and eleven colleagues work on a gap in short-video recommendation. Systems rank videos by clicks and watch time, but those signals only proxy what users truly feel. Noise and bias creep in, so a video can rank high while leaving viewers unsatisfied. The authors aim to align ranking with user satisfaction itself.

Their route uses questionnaires to measure satisfaction directly, and to tie that measure into the ranking goal end to end. Honest satisfaction signals could reduce the push toward mere engagement. For platforms with huge user bases, even small gains in real satisfaction matter for trust and long-term use.
arxiv-2601-20915:
Deepthy Bhaskar, Minimol B, and Binu V P defend federated learning against clients who cheat. Their 2026 paper concerns collaborative training across distributed clients. In federated learning, raw data stays on local devices. Only model updates travel. That design protects privacy, but it opens a door to abuse. Malicious or unreliable clients can send misleading updates. Those updates can harm the shared model's performance and reliability.

The authors propose detection based on loss trend deviation. Honest training shows a steady loss pattern over rounds. A client whose loss trend strays in odd ways stands out. Flagging such clients protects the global model without reading their data. The method serves hospitals, banks, and phone networks that train together. It adds a guard where trust cannot be assumed.
arxiv-2601-21115:
Mingzhi Zhu and five co-authors compare two recipes for building small, versatile code models. Their 2026 paper concerns multi-task code LLMs. Recent work favors deploying smaller, specialized code models in agentic frameworks beside frontier models. That sparks interest in efficient multi-task learning. Such learning must balance performance, constraints, and costs. The authors compare data mixing against model merging.

In data mixing, tasks train together on a blended dataset. In model merging, separately trained models are fused into one. Each route has fans and trade-offs. The paper tests which serves small multi-task code models better. The answer guides teams that cannot afford a giant model per task. It is a practical study for the age of agent teams.
arxiv-2601-21215:
Mehmet Ergezer benchmarks brain decoding on movies, not lab flashes. The 2026 paper studies naturalistic EEG decoding. It asks how model architecture and temporal context interact. The data come from the HBN movie-watching dataset. Five architectures enter the test: a CNN, an LSTM, a stabilized transformer, S4, and S5. The task has four classes. Segment lengths run from eight seconds to one hundred twenty-eight.

Accuracy improves with longer context, the study finds. At sixty-four seconds, the S5 model reaches the top score reported. Longer windows let models use the story a viewer is following. Naturalistic decoding matters for brain-computer interfaces in real life. People watch films; they do not stare at flashing grids. The benchmark shows which designs exploit real temporal context. It sets a reference point for future EEG work.
arxiv-2601-21315:
Seonghwi Kim, Sung Ho Jo, Wooseok Ha, and Minwoo Chae study learning when training data and test data come from different worlds. Labels exist only for the source world, while the target world gives unlabeled examples. The task is to sort target items well despite the shift.

The authors build a classifier that stays robust across several source domains at once. Their approach plans for the worst plausible shift rather than the average one. That stance suits settings like hospitals, where each site scans patients a bit differently. Robust sorting across sites is a step toward models that travel well.
arxiv-2601-21515:
L. Ts. Adzhemyan, M. V. Kompaniets, and A. V. Trenogin analyze a field theory model with two kinds of self-interaction. The model mixes a fourth-power term and a sixth-power term in one field. Its couplings shift with two control parameters, like temperature and pressure.

A special point where the parameters meet governs the model's critical behavior. The authors apply the renormalization group method with a small-parameter expansion carried to six loops. Six loops is deep enough to give sharp estimates of the critical exponents. Such models describe real phase changes, so precise exponents help match theory to lab results.
arxiv-2601-21615:
Jiaxin Zhang, Yiqi Wang, and six co-authors adapt graph networks to new data at test time without retraining the weights. Graph models often sag badly when test graphs differ from training ones. Test-time training helps, but tuning all parameters on the fly can erase what the model learned.

Their framework refines the inner representations instead of the parameters. Leaving the weights fixed protects the original knowledge from being overwritten. The shift targets the part of the model that actually meets the new data. It suits live settings like fraud or traffic graphs, where the stream drifts daily.
arxiv-2601-21815:
Seongchan Park and co-authors study how moral anger in news media shapes what audiences do. In the attention economy, channels compete for views, and moral-emotional framing is a powerful lever. The team examines mainstream news channels on YouTube in two countries, South Korea and the United States.

YouTube speaks through pictures as well as words. So the authors build a classifier for moral emotion. It reads both thumbnail images and video titles. They build it by fine-tuning a vision and language model. With it, they can track how outrage framing relates to user behavior that goes beyond mere attention, such as lasting commitments. The work speaks to debates about whether platforms reward outrage, and what that does to public life in different cultures.
arxiv-2601-22115:
Léna Parc and co-authors weigh small planets around two red dwarf stars. Measuring the masses, radii, and compositions of small planets around M dwarfs is key to understanding how they form. Such planets are also the best targets for later atmosphere studies with telescopes like the James Webb Space Telescope.

The team characterizes two planetary systems, around the stars TOI-4336 A and TOI-4342, using observations from the ESPRESSO spectrograph. From those data they derive the planets' densities, the clue that separates rocky worlds from puffy ones wrapped in gas. Their 2026 preprint adds two more measured systems to the small census of small planets with known makeup.
arxiv-2601-22215:
Marcus Högås and Edvard Mörtsell argue that a famous cosmic disagreement partly reflects the assumptions fed into it. Measurements of the Hubble constant from the local distance ladder clash with values inferred from the early universe. The dispute is usually blamed on new physics or hidden systematic errors.

Far less attention has gone to the priors, the assumptions about parameter values that the ladder analysis builds in from the start. The authors show that physically motivated priors significantly reduce the tension. Their 2026 preprint does not claim the dispute is over. It shows that part of the gap lives in modeling choices, which reframes what new telescopes need to prove.
arxiv-2601-22315:
Xin Jennifer Chen and Yunjin Tong pair a costly truth source with a cheap guess source to tune hard choices. Past runs give both past truths and past guesses to learn from. Their 2026 preprint uses Gaussian process bandits, a method that learns while it tests, guided by model forecasts.

The setting fits cases like human grades or lab tests, where truth is dear and guesses are cheap. A smart plan spends truth calls only where guesses stay unsure. Their work also aims at a bold use: forming new hunches for science. The method shows how to learn more per costly call.
arxiv-2601-22415:
Sadaf Syed, Wolfgang Utschick, and Michael Joham settle a hard fair-share puzzle for group broadcasts. Multicasting sends one stream to many users at once. Their 2026 preprint tackles the max-min fair form: lift the worst-off user's rate as high as it can go. The puzzle is known to be NP-hard.

The team derive the true best answer in closed form. They show that a rate-balancing route reaches that best under set conditions. From that insight they build a light method for real use. Fair streams matter for live events and group calls. The work turns a hard puzzle into a usable rule.
arxiv-2601-22515:
Forged images and video now look so real that hunting surface flaws no longer works well. A 2026 preprint argues that the skill to spot fakes may already sit inside pre-trained models. If so, no heavy retraining of a black-box base is needed. The work proposes a way to draw that hidden skill out.

Drawing out what a model already knows would save vast compute. It would also keep the base model as it is, which aids checks. The method is called discriminative neural anchors. It digs from coarse to fine to surface that hidden skill. The claim is bold and needs care.
arxiv-2601-22815:
A large survey team led by M. Ould-Elhkim reports on the SPIRou Legacy Survey of small, cool stars. These stars, called M dwarfs, are prime targets in the hunt for planets. They are common, and their small size makes planet signals easier to spot by the radial velocity method.

The survey watches these stars in near-infrared light, where the method gains precision and star activity adds less noise. Long, careful surveys like this one build the planet census around our nearest neighbors. They also show which small stars are calm enough for deeper study.
arxiv-2601-23115:
Riccardo Adami and three co-authors study a nonlinear wave equation on graphs with a magnetic field. Their setting is a noncompact metric graph, a network of lines joined at nodes. They ask when the magnetic Schrödinger equation has ground states, its lowest-energy standing waves.

They prove the magnetic system matches a non-magnetic one plus extra repulsive terms on the graph's cycles. Those terms are fixed by the magnetic flux through each loop. The result links quantum waves on networks with classic electromagnetic effects. Ground states are the target solutions, the lowest-energy configurations whose existence on noncompact graphs is not guaranteed.
arxiv-2603-01515:
Building a 3D mesh one point at a time makes long lists that cost a lot to generate. Hanxiao Wang, Yuan-Chen Guo, Ying-Tian Liu, and colleagues rethink that order in this 2026 work. They argue the flaw is the unit: a mesh is made of faces, not lone points.

Their system, FACE, treats each triangle face as a single token for the generator. That one choice cuts the list length by a factor of nine and beats prior compression by half. A strong encoder reads point clouds into a compact code that the face decoder then expands. Tests show top rebuild quality on standard sets, and a diffusion model on the same code turns one image into a detailed mesh. The result lowers the cost of quality 3D content.
arxiv-2603-02015:
Amir Asiaee, Zhuohui Liang, and Chao Yan wrap synthetic data generators with causal rules they cannot break. Their 2026 work notes that generators match observed patterns well, yet warp the causal structure beneath them. Causal uses like treatment effects and policy tests need that structure preserved above raw fit.

Their wrapper, CausalWrap, takes partial causal knowledge as trusted edges, banned edges, and monotonic rules. It needs no access inside the base generator, whether that base is adversarial, variational, or diffusion based. A light correction map, trained with causal penalties, adjusts samples after generation. Tests span simulated causal models, semi-synthetic benchmarks, and a real intensive care cohort. Treatment effect errors fall sharply while ordinary utility largely holds, which makes synthetic data safer for causal work.
arxiv-2603-02115:
Anthony Liang, Yigit Korkmaz, Jiahui Zhang, and colleagues address robot training in this 2026 paper. Robots learn faster when a reward model grades each step of a task. Grading single frames from expert demos works, but real data holds many failed tries with no clear grades. Their system, Robometer, learns from both kinds of data.

Robometer mixes two lessons: frame grades on expert runs, and whole-run rankings across runs. Ranking tells the model which full try was better, even for failed ones. Training used a new set of over one million runs from many robots and tasks. In tests, its rewards held up better than prior methods. Downstream robot learning improved across many tasks as well.
arxiv-2603-02215:
Ran Li, Shimin Di, Haowei Li, and colleagues train a small chemistry model in this 2026 paper. Predicting how chemicals react helps plan new drugs and syntheses. Large models chase scale, yet they often miss basic chemical sense. The core gap, the authors argue, is chemical insight, not size.

Their model, RxnNano, has only half a billion parameters, far fewer than rivals. Training moves in stages, from basic syntax up to deeper chemical thought. A new goal keeps reactions reversible and physically sound as points move in a latent space. A further rule forces the model to learn atom links that stay fixed under relabeling. On strict tests, RxnNano beat models ten times its size by a clear margin.
