First Lieutenant Gerald Francis Kinsman is the subject of a CIA record dated February 2, 1971. The title notes that a first document in the file also mentions the execution of two men. Kinsman's own case stands at the head of the record.

Inside, the file concerns the lieutenant and the grave matter mentioned beside his name. Records that join a named officer to an execution report are among the hardest in the set. The file preserves what was known and reported at the time. Later readers must weigh a case that mixes one man's fate with a report of killings in the same pages.
cia-0000044015:
Possible FMLN links to the priests' murder were suggested, in a CIA record dated January 2, 1990. The title ties the suggestion to the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. The suggestion ran against the charge most voices laid on the army.

Inside, the counter-claim is preserved as it was put forward. Blaming the rebels served the government's friends at a hard moment. Few outside that circle credited the idea for long. The file keeps the attempt on record anyway, since the struggle over blame was itself part of the case's history from its earliest days onward.
cia-0000044415:
The foreign minister accused the FMLN of killing the priests, in a CIA record dated October 4, 1989 in the catalog. This file stands beside a companion record with a nearly matching title. Two filings of one charge show how widely it was pushed.

Inside, the accusation is recorded again, for a further audience. Repetition was the method: say it in every capital that would listen. The government's friends abroad needed the counter-story in hand. The file preserves that effort's second trace, and with it the shape of a campaign to move blame before any court had heard a word of evidence.
cia-0000045215:
Officials hoped the kidnapping situation would become more clear in 24 hours, in a CIA record dated September 2, 1985. A one-day promise is a hostage to fortune in any crisis. The kidnappers, not the officials, held the real timetable that week.

Inside, the short-lived optimism of that forecast is preserved. Deadlines in kidnapping cases are set to calm the public. They are just as often missed, to the government's cost. The file holds one such promise at its making, a small and human record of hope spoken aloud in a crisis that refused to follow anyone's schedule.
cia-0000047315:
Studies in Intelligence was the CIA's own professional journal, written by officers for officers, and this entry holds its winter 1974 issue, volume 18, number 4. The issue's named piece treats General de Gaulle in action. De Gaulle, France's wartime leader and later president, dealt with American intelligence across three decades.

Inside, the journal's pages carry the trade talking to itself: methods, history, and lessons drawn from past operations. A study of de Gaulle fit that mission, since few foreign leaders had tested American spies so often. Declassified long after printing, the issue now shows readers how the agency studied its craft from within.
cia-0000049315: Briefing Senator Leahy on Panama and El Salvador is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049315, dated January 1, 1990. The record concerns a briefing given to Senator Leahy covering two countries, Panama and El Salvador. It survives as a short declassified note of the session, useful mainly as evidence that the briefing took place and what ground it covered.
cia-0000049415: El Salvador requests extradition of Hans Christ is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049415, dated May 3, 1981, filed under an international terrorism weekly heading. The item records a formal request naming Christ. It survives as a short declassified notice of that request, useful for the named person and the legal step stated in its title.
cia-0000096715: The Spread of Lawlessness in Communist China is the title of declassified CIA document 0000096715, dated June 5, 1968. The heading describes a condition spreading across the country. The brief file is a declassified paper on that breakdown as its subject, broader in scope than the single-province unrest reports filed around the same dates.
cia-0000098315: Problem of expose of CIA clandestine youth and student activities, with date estimated, is declassified CIA document 0000098315, dated February 3, 1967. The heading flags its own dating as estimated. Readers get a short declassified item on the risk of exposure for youth and student work, its concern stated in the title as a problem.
cia-0000107415: Dated January 5, 1962, declassified CIA document 0000107415 carries Chiang Kai-shek's views on whether GRC action was advisable. Its heading marks one word deleted and breaks off at the word The. GRC shortens Government of the Republic of China in the title itself. No target is named in the surviving heading. The brief record preserves the deletion mark and the broken ending as released.
cia-0000124315: An August 1951 CIA document covers American prisoners of war in Shanghai and Canton. The two great coastal cities served as way stations in the movement of captured men. The paper records the agency's picture of both places in that system during the Korean War. Two-city papers let analysts cross-check movement reports against each other, building the chain of custody that families and negotiators both needed for any name to count.
cia-0000132515:
Thirteen days before the Bay of Pigs landing, on April 4, 1961, the CIA briefed on Cuba one more time. Exile forces were in their final preparations for the invasion of Castro's Cuba. The operation would collapse within days of the landing.

Final-phase briefings like this one carried the agency's last picture of the island to the officials who had approved the plan. Its calm place in a routine series contrasts with what followed: a failed landing and a lasting scar on the Kennedy presidency. The declassified paper, released years later, preserves the eve-of-invasion view.
cia-0000132615: A Cuban Communist Party congress drawing strong foreign delegations fills item 13 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated July 2, 1960. The headline breaks off at the word del, short for delegations. The congress would make the party's growing power inside the revolution more formal. The short item previews the gathering and its expected guests.
cia-0000135815: Filed on 1 May 1954, this CIA planning paper concerns the K Program and a talk about travel to Guatemala, with the other name deleted in the heading. The record comes from the run-up to the June 1954 coup that removed President Arbenz, the goal of the CIA plan called PBSUCCESS. Students of the 1954 coup use such records to check later accounts against what was written at the time.
cia-0000135915: One CIA cable dated about January 1954 handles a cable from Lincoln asking for broad authority, a freer hand with fewer checks from headquarters. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Read on its own terms, the record shows the operation at work in its own words, with some names still blacked out.
cia-0000136015: On 5 February 1954, the agency filed a cable, now declassified, on tasking information for DTFROGS, the heading spelling the sending verb with a typo, profiding. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136115: Cable in the declassified files, dated 4 April 1954, covers an investigation into the possibility of sabotage, asked for with two typos in the heading. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Students of the 1954 coup use such records to check later accounts against what was written at the time.
cia-0000136215: One declassified cable from the CIA files, dated 1 May 1954, covers Instructions 2 about Monday's broadcast, the radio station's script guidance for Langevin. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. The paper trail here is small but direct, a single piece of the huge file the operation left behind.
cia-0000136315: A current strategic analysis for CADICK fills this late June 1954 cable. His big offensive in the HANK complex could hurt the enemy's main force badly. His edge lies in movement with air support. The enemy is strongest when sitting still. So his tactics must stay dynamic. A Jalapa asset could help cut the enemy off from ADAM. Both roads, north and south, could be closed. Diplomatic interruption may come in five or six days. A decisive blow should land soon.
cia-0000136615: Dated 6 January 1961, this Spanish text comes from the declassified papers of Brigade 2506, the exile force preparing to invade Cuba. The brigade's paperwork ran in Spanish, and this item is part of the early-January run. The catalog gives it no subject heading. Kept in Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, the document is a dated primary source from the brigade's final season of training.
cia-0000136915: Sabotage is the subject of this April 1954 cable to LINCOLN. The sample kept here is mostly routing headers. The working paragraphs do not survive in readable form. So little can be said with confidence. The cable belongs to the sabotage planning traffic of spring 1954. A companion cable weighs sabotage against arms shipments. Its own targets and orders cannot be recovered from this copy. The file itself is the record of that gap.
cia-0000137315: A government shakeup is the latest move in Cuba's rapid trend left, the CIA briefing for the 425th National Security Council meeting of 1 December 1959 reports. The 26 November shakeup brings pro-communist Che Guevara even more to the fore as new head of the National Bank. Guevara is described as a 31-year-old Argentine soldier-of-fortune. The file also includes a paper prepared for the briefer by J. C. King, the agency's Western Hemisphere chief who had run the Guatemala operation five years earlier.
cia-03162015: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1955/03/29, a CIA publication. The March briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cia-06157015: PHOTOGRAPH OF A B-41 (PG-7) ANTITANK GRENADE FOR DISPENSING CHEMICAL AGENTS, a CIA document. The weapon photo. This file preserves that declassified paper. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
cia-06767515: REPORT OF INSPECTION OF MKULTRA, a CIA document. The mind-control program's inspection. The archive keeps it. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
congress-of-vienna-final-act-1815:
After Napoleon's defeat, the great powers of Europe met at Vienna to redraw the continent's map. Their Final Act, signed in June 1815, gathered the whole settlement into one long document with many added treaties. Austria's Prince Metternich was the leading hand in the design, working beside the rulers of Russia, Prussia, and Britain.

The settlement moved borders, restored kings, and built a balance of power meant to stop any one nation from ruling Europe again. Smaller states were traded and merged with little regard for the wishes of their peoples. Even so, the Vienna order kept a general peace in Europe for decades and shaped diplomacy for a century.
conrad-victory-1915:
Joseph Conrad set Victory among the islands of the Dutch East Indies, where he had sailed as a young officer. The novel was published in 1915, during the First World War. It became one of his most popular books with general readers.

Axel Heyst, a Swede who has withdrawn from life, runs a failed coal station on a remote island. He rescues a young English musician, Lena, from a traveling orchestra and brings her to live with him. Rumors of hidden treasure then draw three sinister visitors to the island. Heyst's lifelong detachment fails him just when action matters most, with tragic results.
conrad-within-tides-1915:
Within the Tides, published in 1915, gathers four of Conrad's late stories, written as his powers and the Europe he knew both darkened. Three of the tales turn to the sea and the eastern ports of his youth.

'The Planter of Malata' follows a planter undone by obsessive love on his island. 'The Partner' is a grim tale of insurance fraud and a wrecked ship. 'The Inn of the Two Witches' moves to Spain for a story of murder and superstition, and 'Because of the Dollars' returns to eastern seas. The collection shows a master in his late, somber manner.
constitution-bulgaria-2015: Bulgaria's 1991 Constitution, amended through 2015, frames its republic. It guards rights. The Tower library holds the full text. It buried communism. Party fell. People voted. Europe beckoned. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-colombia-2015: Colombia's 1991 Constitution, amended through 2015, rebuilt its republic. It sought peace. The Tower library holds the full text. It faced cartels. Guns roared. Law answered. Peace came. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-congo-2015: Congo's 2015 Constitution, passed by referendum, frames its republic. It reset term counts. The Tower library holds the full text. It restarted the clock. Votes passed. Terms reset. Rule stayed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-estonia-2015: Estonia's 1992 Constitution, amended through 2015, frames its digital republic. It guards rights. The Tower library holds the full text. It wired a nation. Soviets left. Bytes ruled. Freedom clicked. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-mexico-2015: Mexico's 1917 Constitution, amended through 2015, is a revolutionary charter. It grants social rights. The Tower library holds the full text. It crowned a revolution. Dictator fell. Land reformed. Rights bloomed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-myanmar-2015: Myanmar's 2008 Constitution, amended through 2015, reserves army power. Soldiers keep veto. The Tower library holds the full text. It guarded barracks rule. Generals wrote. Civilians voted some. Guns stayed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-rwanda-2015: Rwanda's 2003 Constitution, amended 2015, frames its republic. It healed genocide. The Tower library holds the full text. It buried horror. Killers tried. Women rose. Peace grew. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
croce-hegel-living-dead-1915:
What Is Living and What Is Dead of the Philosophy of Hegel, published in English in 1915, is Croce's critical rescue of the German master. Croce had passed through Hegelianism himself; this book sorts what survives the system from what must be left behind.

Living, he finds, is Hegel's sense of thought as concrete and historical, his doctrine of opposites driving development. Dead is the system-building vanity: nature and history forced into triads by formula. The sorting is brisk, learned, and unsentimental. The book shaped how the twentieth century read Hegel, in Italy and far beyond it.
dawson-woodward-piltdown-bone-implement-:
The third Piltdown paper, read in late 1914 and published in 1915, presents a worked bone. Dawson and Woodward described it as a tool from the Piltdown gravel. A shaped bone implement seemed to give their dawn man a culture.

The object, carved from fossil elephant bone, later became central to the fraud case. Its cut surfaces helped investigators prove deliberate fabrication in the 1950s. At the time, it simply extended the growing pile of supporting finds. The short note survives as a footnote to the most embarrassing episode in British paleoanthropology.
dostoevsky-the-idiot-martin-1915:
Fyodor Dostoevsky wrote The Idiot in Russian, and Eva Martin made it English in 1915. Martin's version, for J. M. Dent, was an early Everyman-era English Idiot. The novel tells of Prince Myshkin, a good man in a grasping world of money.

Myshkin returns to Russia after years in a Swiss clinic for his epilepsy. His candor and kindness baffle a society built on rank, cash, and intrigue. He loves two women, the proud Nastasya and the pure Aglaya, and fails both. Rogozhin's dark passion for Nastasya ends in murder and shared night-long vigil. Dostoevsky asks if true goodness can live in the modern world at all.
dreiser-genius-1915:
Theodore Dreiser published The 'Genius' in 1915, his most autobiographical novel. Its hero is an artist rather than a financier, but the driving appetites are pure Dreiser. The book was attacked as obscene and effectively suppressed for years, with Dreiser's publisher too frightened to fight for it.

Eugene Witla climbs from a small Illinois town to New York success as an illustrator and painter. Fame and money feed a restless erotic life that wrecks his marriage and, at last, his art. Dreiser writes his own hungers into Witla with unusual nakedness, in long brooding passages on beauty and desire. The suppression fight made the novel a famous case for free expression. It remains his most personal work.
durkheim-elementary-forms-swain-1915:
Emile Durkheim's The Elementary Forms of the Religious Life appears in Joseph Ward Swain's translation of 1915. Durkheim studies totemism among Aboriginal peoples of Australia as religion's simplest form. He argues that the sacred is society worshipping itself. When the clan gathers, its shared energy creates gods, rites, and moral rules.

Collective effervescence is his term for that charged group feeling. The categories of thought itself, he claims, are born in religion. The book founded the sociology of religion as a field. Its theory shapes anthropology and religious studies still. Swain's version was the standard English text for decades. Few works match its ambition.
elliot-smith-migrations-of-early-culture:
G. Elliot Smith gave talks in 1915 that came out as The Migrations of Early Culture. Smith was a brain man and a dig man of high rank in London. He held that one source fed the great traits of the old world. That source, he said, was Egypt of the pharaohs.

Stone tombs, the art of the mummy, and sun cults form his proof. He tracks these traits from the Nile to the far isles of the Pacific. Most dig men of the next age turned from his grand claim. The talks are the first full plea for the spread of one culture.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-15: The fifteenth volume collects essays from Montaigne's mature years. He studies habit, custom, and the education of children with care. Practical wisdom shines brightly on every page. A guide to living from a master observer of men.
europmc-pmc10320115:
Blin and a wide team presented antiSMASH 7.0 in 2023, a tool that mines microbe DNA. Many microbes make small active compounds that can kill germs or cancer cells. Genes for each compound sit in a cluster, a group of genes side by side. The tool finds those clusters in bacteria, fungi, and archaea.

Version 7 can now spot 81 types of cluster, up from 71 before. Blin improved how the tool predicts the shape of each compound. It also draws the step by step build of a compound more clearly. A further gain is a better read on how cells switch each cluster on or off.
europmc-pmc10427715:
Wang and co-authors reviewed in 2023 how cells clear out worn power units, and what goes wrong in disease. The clearing process is called mitophagy. It removes extra or broken mitochondria, the parts of the cell that make energy. A healthy stock of these units keeps the cell in balance.

Cells keep several routes to start this cleanup on time. Wang lays out the gene signals that drive each route. When cleanup fails, harm can build in the brain, heart, lungs, liver, and kidneys. The review maps which diseases link to which faults in the process. It also lists drugs that tune the cleanup and their stage in trials.
europmc-pmc1079815:
Jensen, Bohonak, and Kelley built a free web tool for population geneticists in this 2005 paper. Their field studies how gene variants spread through groups of plants or animals. One common pattern is isolation by distance, where groups far apart in space grow less alike in their genes. Few easy tools existed to test for that pattern, the authors note.

Their site lets users run strong tests and get results back fast. It offers Mantel tests, a method that checks if two sets of distances track each other, plus regression fits and pair-wise gene difference scores. It also returns basic summaries and print-ready charts that users can download. The code was shared openly so others could inspect and reuse it. The authors aim to lower the barrier for routine tests of spatial gene patterns.
europmc-pmc11006615:
Zepeda-Rivera and a large team pinpoint which strain of a mouth germ truly fills bowel tumours in this 2024 study. Fusobacterium nucleatum normally lives in the mouth and is rare in the healthy lower gut. It is enriched in colorectal cancer tumours, and heavy loads track with relapse and spread. Which genetic branch of the germ drives this was unknown.

The team built full genomes for 135 strains from mouths and tumours. A branch long treated as one subspecies split into two clades, meaning family branches. Only one branch, called Fna C2, dominated the tumour niche, they found. It carried 195 extra genes tied to gut survival and fuel use. Mice given that branch grew more gut growths. Tests on tumours from 116 patients confirmed its enrichment.
europmc-pmc11063215:
Mai, Lin, Lin, Zhao, and Cui review how the stiffness of tissue scaffolding shapes cancer therapy in this 2024 paper. The extracellular matrix is the protein mesh that holds cells in place. In tumours it can stiffen as scar-like cells switch on and mesh proteins pile up and crosslink. That stiffness changes how tumour and immune cells behave.

Stiff mesh can blunt four therapy types, the review finds: checkpoint blockade, cell therapy, virus therapy, and cancer vaccines. Checkpoint blockade frees immune cells from brakes that tumours exploit. The authors detail how stiffness drives each failure mode. They also flag the hard step of moving lab findings into the clinic. Better lab materials that copy real mesh are needed, they argue, alongside drugs that soften the mesh.
europmc-pmc11408715:
Zheng and colleagues review the receptor behind a blockbuster class of diabetes and weight drugs in this 2024 paper. The GLP-1 receptor sits on many cell types and binds GLP-1, a gut hormone that steers blood sugar and fat metabolism. Drugs that activate the receptor have drawn intense interest for their treatment effects. The authors trace the drug class from discovery to clinic.

Successive drug versions differ in how long they act and how they are given, the review details. Their pharmacology, meaning how the body handles them, is compared drug by drug. Beyond diabetes, the authors explore uses in brain protection, infection control, inflammation reduction, and cardiovascular support. Efficacy and safety are assessed in depth for each area. The paper closes with the development prospects of the class.
europmc-pmc11683415:
Kumar and colleagues introduce version 12 of the MEGA software for studying evolution in this 2024 paper. MEGA builds family trees of species from DNA and protein sequences. Version 12 cuts the computing time of maximum likelihood methods, a standard but slow way to fit trees. New heuristics, meaning shortcut rules, skip work that is likely needless.

Tests on real and simulated datasets show substantial time savings with no loss of accuracy, the authors report. The gains cover picking the best model of sequence change and bootstrap tests, which resample data to judge how firm a tree branch is. A linked method flags fragile clades, tree branches with weak support, and the sequences behind them. Finer parallel processing, support for high-resolution screens, and an enhanced Tree Explorer round out the release.
europmc-pmc11694015:
GBD 2021 US Obesity Forecasting Collaborators estimate US overweight and obesity from 1990 to 2021 and forecast to 2050 in this 2024 study. The epidemic has imposed a significant health and economic burden over past decades. National and state trends are crucial for judging interventions and shaping policy. The team estimated prevalence for ages 5 to 24 and for adults of 25 and over.

Data came from 134 unique sources, including all major national surveillance surveys. Adjustments corrected for self-reporting bias, since people understate weight. For adults, overweight was defined as a body mass index of 25 to under 30, and obesity as 30 or higher. State-specific estimates cover older adolescents and adults in all 50 states plus Washington, DC. Forecasts extend every series to 2050.
europmc-pmc1241915:
Kojima and co-authors screened 200 pesticides for hormone activity in 2004. Tests used hamster ovary cells carrying human hormone receptors. Two estrogen receptor types and one androgen receptor were covered. Compounds included isomers and breakdown products at low doses.

Forty-seven pesticides activated the first estrogen receptor type. Thirty-three activated the second type, and 29 hit both. Two older insecticide forms favored the second receptor type. A few pesticides weakly blocked estrogen receptors instead. None activated the androgen receptor. Kojima shows hormone screening can sort a large chemical library fast. All tests ran at doses under a set low cap. The cells were hamster ovary cells grown in lab dishes for the tests.
europmc-pmc1769515:
Trehalose, a stress sugar, is made by life across all kingdoms. Avonce and co-authors traced its biosynthesis in 2006. The sugar piles up under heat, cold, and salt stress, and was once thought limited to extremophiles and dormant organisms.

Bacteria hold five routes to make it. Fungi, plants, and animals share just one, the TPS/TPP route. In bacteria the two enzyme genes sit side by side; in eukaryotes they are fused into one protein. Vertebrates cannot make trehalose but can break it down. Avonce shows the two enzyme domains evolved largely in parallel, with duplications and sideways transfers.
europmc-pmc1779515:
Pilch and Mann carried out in 2006 a large protein census of human seminal plasma, the fluid part of semen. The fluid protects sperm and feeds them on their path to the egg. Knowing its full protein list could aid work on male infertility and prostate cancer.

Using high-confidence protein identification methods, the pair found 923 distinct proteins in the fluid. That count far exceeded what earlier smaller surveys had listed. The mix draws on fluids from the prostate, seminal vesicles, and other male glands. Because the fluid is easy to collect and rich in protein, the catalog gives a base for hunting disease markers. It also lists proteins that may play direct roles in fertilization itself.
europmc-pmc1971715:
Bass, Field and co-authors compared in 2007 six lab tests for the mutations that let malaria mosquitoes survive insecticide sprays. Knockdown resistance, or kdr, comes from changes in the sodium channel that pyrethroid sprays target. It is tracked in Anopheles gambiae, Africa's main malaria vector, to guide spray programs.

The team developed two new high-throughput tests, one based on TaqMan probes and one on high resolution melt analysis of DNA. Four established methods were optimized alongside: two PCR variants, a ligation assay, and an enzyme-linked probe assay. All six were then run blind on 96 single mosquitoes covering varied resistance genotypes and related African species. Comparing sensitivity and specificity head to head tells control programs which assay to trust when samples pour in.
europmc-pmc2124815: A medical paper on the cell changes in amaurotic family idiocy. The inherited blindness. This article preserves that neurology research. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2125015: A medical paper on the growth of chicken bone marrow in vitro and its bearing on hematogenesis. The chicken marrow. This article preserves that hematology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2125115: A medical paper with studies upon experimental pneumonia in rabbits. The rabbit lungs. This article preserves that research. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it. The archive guards it with care for all readers.
europmc-pmc2125315: A medical paper on the influence of epinephrin upon the coronary circulation of the monkey. The monkey's heart vessels. This article preserves that cardiology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2126315: A medical paper on blood volume in wounded soldiers and related blood changes. The battlefield blood. This article preserves that military medicine. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2128615: A medical paper on the effect of heat on flagellar and somatic agglutination. The heated clumping. This article preserves that serology. It waits for future eyes. History keeps its place secure. Kept for study. Scholars will consult it.
europmc-pmc2131115: A medical paper with epidemiological studies on rabbit respiratory infections, carriers. The rabbit carriers. This article preserves that epidemiology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2131215: A medical paper on the production of purpura by derivatives of pneumococcus, further studies. The purple spots again. This article preserves that pathology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2131515: Proving fowl paralysis was contagious took deliberate transmission trials, which this second study carried out. The investigators moved the disease between birds and watched it take hold. The spreading paralysis, confirmed. The article preserves that veterinary research for future readers.
europmc-pmc2441615:
Berghöfer and colleagues reviewed obesity rates across Europe in 2008. They searched studies from 1990 to 2008 and kept only surveys that actually measured people's height and weight and represented whole national populations. That filter matters, since self-reported sizes usually understate obesity.

Across the continent, obesity, defined as a body mass index of 30 or more, varied enormously. Rates in men ran from 4.0% to 28.3% depending on the country, and in women from 6.2% to 36.5% in the same comparison. A clear map emerged: Central, Eastern, and Southern Europe carried heavier burdens than Western and Northern Europe. The authors concluded obesity has reached epidemic proportions in Europe. They said the patchwork of rates underlines the need for prevention and treatment strategies fitted to each region.
europmc-pmc2574415:
Engler, Kandzia, and Marillonnet introduced a cloning method in 2008 that moves DNA fragments into expression vectors in a single five-minute step, leaving no scars. Standard recombination cloning is efficient. But it leaves leftover sequences. Those tack 8 to 13 extra amino acids onto the protein produced. Their method, called Golden Gate cloning, exploits restriction enzymes of type IIs, which cut outside the sequence they recognise.

With cleavage sites designed to match, two cut fragments join into a product that no longer carries the enzyme's recognition site. Running cutting and joining together in one tube yields close to 100 percent correct plasmids after five minutes. The authors present it as matching the speed of recombination methods while giving clean, precise constructs for high-throughput work.
europmc-pmc2575615:
Pauley and colleagues measured small regulatory RNAs in the blood cells of rheumatoid arthritis patients in this 2008 study. MicroRNAs fine-tune gene activity, and disturbed levels had been reported in the inflamed joint tissue of these patients. The team used sensitive PCR tests on immune cells from patients' blood, comparing five chosen microRNAs with healthy and disease controls.

Four microRNAs ran high in patients' cells, from 1.8-fold up to 2.6-fold above healthy levels, matching the pattern seen in joint tissue. The standout, miR-146a, normally damps production of the inflammatory signal TNF-alpha by repressing two helper proteins. Oddly, those helpers were not reduced in patients. In cell tests, repressing them cut TNF-alpha output by up to 86 percent. The authors suggest miR-146a is raised but failing to work, letting inflammation run long.
europmc-pmc2585615:
Zimyanin and colleagues filmed a key developmental signal moving inside living fruit fly egg cells in 2008. The signal is oskar messenger RNA, whose position at the egg's rear end decides where the embryo's abdomen and germ cells form. How it gets there was contested: active transport, diffusion with trapping, and exclusion from the front were all proposed.

Tracking single particles showed the RNA rides molecular motors called kinesin along microtubule tracks in every direction, with a slight bias toward the rear. That small bias is enough to accumulate the RNA at the back, a biased random walk rather than a one-way trip. Mutations in three genes, mago, barentsz, and Tropomyosin II, reversed the bias and misdirected the RNA forward. Each part of the RNA's protein escort did a distinct job in transport.
europmc-pmc2592715:
Zhang and colleagues introduced a computer method called MACS in 2008 for finding protein binding sites from ChIP-Seq data. ChIP-Seq pulls down DNA bound by a protein. Short-read machines then sequence the fragments. The result is millions of tags whose pileups mark binding sites. Calling those peaks reliably from noisy counts was the problem the method solves.

MACS exploits the two-sided pattern of tags around a true binding site to estimate how far each tag should be shifted toward the site. It then models tag counts with a Poisson distribution, a standard model for random counts. It uses a local background rate. It also reports an empirical false discovery rate, found by swapping sample and control. Tested on FoxA1, NRSF, and CTCF data sets, MACS beat other published peak finders and sharpened resolution enough to centre peaks on the binding motif.
europmc-pmc2621215:
Valdés and colleagues sequenced in 2008 the genome of Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans, the bacterium that anchors industrial copper recovery by bioleaching. This microbe eats iron and sulfur minerals for energy, thrives in acid as strong as pH 1 to 2, and pulls both carbon and nitrogen from the air. Earlier metabolic models mixed data from different strains, so the team sequenced the type strain, ATCC 23270.

The annotated genome confirmed and extended models of biofilm formation, nutrient uptake, and iron and sulfur oxidation. New draft models cover carbon use and oxygen-free metabolism, including nitrogen fixation. They also cover stress responses and DNA repair. Because the species lacks easy genetic tools, the genome map becomes the platform for predicting gene function. The authors say it explains the bacterium's double life in mines and acidic ecosystems.
europmc-pmc2661915:
Rundle and colleagues asked in 2009 whether the shops and streets around a New York City home predict a resident's weight. They studied 13,102 adults and mapped the half-mile around each home. Two features were measured: how many healthy food shops stood nearby, and how easy the area was to walk.

People with the most healthy food shops nearby, such as supermarkets and produce markets, weighed less on average. Their body mass index ran about 0.80 units lower than that of people with almost none, and obesity was less common. The link survived after walking conditions were counted. Denser streets and mixed land use also tied to lower obesity on their own. Junk food shop density, by contrast, showed no clear tie to weight. The results support the idea that neighborhood design shapes health.
europmc-pmc2694415:
Ambros and an international committee reported in 2009 a worldwide consensus on which gene tests should guide treatment of neuroblastoma, a childhood cancer of the nerve tissue. Doctors already used tumor genetics to match children to gentle or aggressive therapy. But countries ran different tests with different rules, so the same marker could mean different things in different hospitals.

The committee reviewed a shared database of 8,800 patients and compared each lab group's procedures in detail. Three markers earned a place in the new global risk system. They are the status of the MYCN gene, loss of a piece of chromosome 11, and the tumor's DNA content per cell. Standard procedures for measuring each were adopted, along with shared naming rules. Wider genome-wide panels are expected to join later. Uniform tests, the authors argue, make risk groups mean the same thing everywhere.
europmc-pmc2705515:
Brückner and co-authors reviewed in 2009 the yeast two-hybrid method, a genetic test for whether two proteins bind each other inside a cell. Protein binding builds the networks that run cell shape, energy use, and signals. Mapping those networks is a core task for systems biology, the study of the cell as a whole system.

Their review covers newer forms that can catch fleeting binding and binding at cell membranes or in cell fluid, places the classic form misses. They weigh strengths and flaws against the main rival method, which purifies protein groups and weighs them. Practical checks for confirming a hit before trusting it close the review.
europmc-pmc2738515:
Haydon, Cleaveland, Taylor, and Laurenson argued in 2002 that reservoirs of infection are often loosely defined and rarely proven. A reservoir is a host or place that keeps a pathogen alive and passes it to a target group. Most human and livestock pathogens infect several host species, so suspected reservoirs are common. Control programs sometimes attack a suspected reservoir at great cost without firm proof.

They define a reservoir only in relation to a defined target population. It must be a set of linked populations or environments where the pathogen persists for good. Infection must pass from there to the target. A reservoir is confirmed when target infection cannot sustain itself once cross-transmission is cut. When control inside the target alone suffices, detailed reservoir knowledge may not be needed.
europmc-pmc2787015:
Miller, Sorensen, Ojemann, and den Nijs reported in 2009 power-law scaling in the electric potential at the surface of the human brain. Using subdural electrode recordings from cortex, they studied broadband signals, activity spread across many frequencies rather than locked to one rhythm. The power spectrum of the signal followed a power-law shape from eighty to five hundred hertz.

The scaling exponent stayed the same across subjects, cortical areas, and activity levels. When local activity rose, the shape held while the overall amplitude grew. A knee in the spectra pointed to a characteristic time scale in the signal. Simulations of simple neuron models reproduced the pattern. The authors read this as scale-free, non-oscillatory change tied to average firing rates across a population. It complements the classic rhythm-based view of brain signals rather than replacing it.
europmc-pmc2822815:
Heiberg and co-authors presented Segment in 2010, a free software package for analyzing heart and vessel images from medical scanners. Programs sold for this work often cost much, do little, and lack careful accuracy checks. Their earlier freeware version could not be extended by other researchers, which limited its growth.

Segment reads standard scan files from all major scanner makers and works across MRI, CT, and nuclear medicine images. It outlines the heart's main pumping chamber on its own, measures blood flow, and supports manual marking and motion analysis. The team describes how each function was validated and how an automatic test script keeps future versions honest. Source code was released for research use.
europmc-pmc2831915:
Satarug, Garrett, Sens, and Sens updated the health evidence in 2010 on cadmium, a toxic metal that slips into most foods from soil. Diet is the main source for nonsmokers, and the body absorbs cadmium by borrowing the transport routes meant for calcium, iron, zinc, and manganese. Reviewed studies ran from 2004 to 2009.

Cadmium builds up in kidneys, eyes, and other organs, and kidney and bone harm appeared in the general public more often than safety models predicted. Harm showed up at urine levels far below the threshold behind the current weekly intake limit. Evidence also linked cadmium to diseases beyond kidney and bone, which leads the authors to question the safe limit itself.
europmc-pmc2835915:
Pandey and Rizvi surveyed plant polyphenols in 2009, the plant defense compounds that flood fruits, vegetables, tea, and red wine. Plants make them against sun damage and germs, and a typical glass of wine or cup of tea carries about one hundred milligrams. More than eight thousand types are known.

Population studies and pooled analyses link diets rich in these compounds with lower rates of cancer, heart disease, diabetes, bone thinning, and brain decline, the review reports. The compounds act mainly as antioxidants, soaking up damaging free radicals. The authors sort them into classes, from phenolic acids to the large flavonoid family, and weigh what each does inside the body.
europmc-pmc2847715:
Kandasamy, Pandey, and a large consortium launched NetPath in 2010, a public database of human signaling pathways checked by human curators. Signaling pathways are chains of molecular messages that steer growth, movement, and cell death. The raw facts sit scattered across thousands of papers, and no computer can assemble them reliably on its own.

NetPath's first release curated ten immune pathways, including T cell and B cell receptor routes and several interleukin chains. Curators recorded protein interactions, enzyme reactions, movements inside the cell, and genes switched on, using a companion tool called PathBuilder. Data export follows shared standards so other software can reuse it. The team aimed the resource at researchers modeling how drug candidates might disturb whole pathways.
europmc-pmc2869315:
Bergstrom and colleagues showed in 2010 that the gut's main mucus protein can be the difference between life and death in a bowel infection. The protein, Muc2, is made by goblet cells and forms the mucus blanket over the colon wall. They infected mice lacking Muc2 with a rodent germ related to E. coli strains that cause human diarrhea.

Mice without Muc2 lost weight fast and up to nine in ten died, while normal mice recovered. The germ grew ten to one hundred times more thickly in the unprotected colons, much of it clinging loosely to the wall, and ulcers formed amid bacterial colonies. Normal mice answered infection by pouring out far more mucus, which suggests the blanket works by holding germs away from the wall.
europmc-pmc2948515:
Carroll and colleagues built a rapid scoring scale for cerebral malaria in mice in a 2010 study, aiming to track the disease without waiting for death as the endpoint. Brain malaria can kill even after the parasites are cleared, and no add-on therapy exists.

Their scale rates ten behavioural and physical signs, letting one observer score a mouse within three minutes. Scores followed the worsening syndrome and matched the amount of bleeding found inside the brain. Because sick animals can be flagged early and graded, trials of new add-on treatments can start at a defined stage and compare severity fairly.
europmc-pmc3008715:
Singh and a large team searched for honey bee RNA viruses in other pollinators and in pollen in a 2010 field study across three states. Pollinator numbers were falling, and bee viruses were suspects in colony collapse, with hints they had reached bumble bees.

Testing bees, their pollen loads, and other flower visitors, they found three bee viruses in pollen pellets carried by apparently healthy foragers, the first such molecular proof. Stored pollen and honey in hives stayed infectious: a queen fed on them caught the virus and laid infected eggs. Pollen thus looks like a highway between species.
europmc-pmc3036615:
Siaut and colleagues measured in 2011 how the model green alga Chlamydomonas stores oil when starved of nitrogen. This single celled alga is a favorite test bed for efforts to make biofuel from microbes. One popular idea was that blocking starch storage would force more carbon into oil, raising yields.

Starved cells built oil droplets rich in common fatty acids, peaking within a few days as membrane fats were recycled. Common lab strains differed sharply, with the best storing several times more oil than the weakest. Surprisingly, mutants unable to make starch stored no extra oil, and oil and starch levels did not track each other across twenty strains. Salt stress, by contrast, raised oil strongly. The authors urge careful strain choice and matched controls in future work.
europmc-pmc3114815:
Hui-Ming Gao and colleagues built a mouse model of Parkinson disease for a 2011 paper in Environmental Health Perspectives. Human disease advances slowly over decades, and most animal models fail to copy that slow course. The team combined two hits: a faulty human gene for a brain protein, plus a single injection that triggers body-wide inflammation.

Both normal and gene-carrying mice showed brief brain inflammation after the injection, but only the gene-carrying mice kept it. Those mice slowly lost dopamine nerve cells, built up clumped and damaged protein, and formed round deposits like those in human disease. Blocking two enzymes that make harmful oxygen chemicals in immune brain cells prevented the damage. The model shows gene and environment faults feeding each other.
europmc-pmc3132215:
Zhonghao Yu and colleagues compared two blood preparations used in health studies in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Plasma and serum look alike, but serum comes from clotted blood, and clotting can change chemical levels. The team measured well over a hundred small chemicals in matched samples from several hundred fasting adults.

Most chemicals measured higher in serum, sometimes by a fifth or more, while repeat testing proved slightly steadier in plasma. Despite the level gap, the two preparations mostly rose and fell together across people. When comparing diabetics with others, serum flagged more differing chemicals, making it the more sensitive choice for hunting disease markers. The authors advise simply staying consistent within any one study.
europmc-pmc3145015:
Xiaoming Liu, Xueqiu Jian, and Eric Boerwinkle built a combined database for judging human gene variants in a 2011 paper in Human Mutation. Sequencing the protein-coding part of the genome turns up thousands of single-letter changes per patient, and sorting harmful from harmless ones is the bottleneck. Different prediction programs disagree, since each uses different clues.

Their database gathers scores from four leading prediction programs plus an evolution-based score for every possible protein-changing variant in the human genome, tens of millions in total. Related gene information rides along in one lightweight file. Instead of querying many websites one variant at a time, analysts can now screen a whole patient list at once. The database is free to download.
europmc-pmc3163615:
Evelyn Bromet and colleagues compared major depression across eighteen countries in a 2011 paper in BMC Medicine. Depression ranks among the top causes of disability worldwide, but comparable data were missing for many poorer countries. Face-to-face diagnostic interviews with nearly ninety thousand adults in representative national samples filled the gap.

About one adult in seven in rich countries and one in nine in poorer countries reported a depressive episode in their lifetime. Yearly rates sat near one in eighteen in both groups. Episodes began in the mid twenties on average, struck women about twice as often as men, and impaired recent sufferers most. In rich countries the young were hit hardest, while several poorer countries showed the opposite age pattern. Separation, divorce, and widowhood were the strongest social correlates.
europmc-pmc3204615:
Elaine Scallan and colleagues at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimated foodborne illness from unspecified agents in the United States in this 2011 paper. A companion study counted illnesses from thirty-one known pathogens. This one tackles everything else: agents too poorly understood to count individually, agents not yet recognized as foodborne, and agents still undiscovered.

Their estimate is large: roughly thirty-eight million episodes of illness in the United States each year, with tens of thousands of hospitalizations and well over a thousand deaths. The authors walk through why the unknown category is so big, from outbreaks where no cause is ever found to microbes recognized as foodborne only recently. The work sets the scale of the uncounted burden of foodborne disease.
europmc-pmc3260315:
Daniel Russel and colleagues presented a software platform for determining the structures of large molecular machines, in this 2012 paper in PLoS Biology. Big assemblies of proteins and nucleic acids resist single experimental techniques. Their platform takes an integrative approach, combining whatever information is available into one modeling exercise.

The method treats model building as a computational optimization problem. Everything known about the assembly, from experiments and prior data, is encoded into a scoring function that grades candidate arrangements. The software then searches for arrangements that score well, and the platform covers distributing the resulting models as well. The authors offer the toolset as shared infrastructure for a field where structures increasingly come from many partial clues rather than one decisive measurement.
europmc-pmc3261815:
Yangling Mu and Fred Gage reviewed adult neurogenesis in the hippocampus and its connection to Alzheimer's disease in this 2011 article in Molecular Neurodegeneration. The hippocampus, vital for learning and memory, is among the first areas damaged in the disease. New neurons are born there throughout adult life, and evidence suggests that process goes wrong early in Alzheimer's.

Key molecules in the disease's machinery can push new neuron production up or down, though cause and effect are not yet proven. Because new neurons help maintain the hippocampal network, failing production could deepen neurons' vulnerability and worsen memory loss, while a boost might be the brain's attempt at self-repair. The authors discuss using the neurogenesis connection for diagnosis and for therapies that restore the birth of neurons.
europmc-pmc3291415:
Bell and fellow members of a World Health Organization writing group reviewed drug free measures against pandemic flu in 2006. Their article, the second of two, covers steps taken within countries and communities rather than at borders. The guidance rests mostly on past observations rather than controlled trials, and the authors are open about that thin evidence base.

Measures discussed include keeping sick people apart, tracing and watching their contacts, and closing gathering places in some settings. Experience from 1918 showed that forced isolation often failed once cases were widespread, while voluntary staying home worked better. The authors tie each measure to the phase and severity of a pandemic, noting that delaying illness can buy time until a matched vaccine arrives.
europmc-pmc3292515:
Sørensen and colleagues took stock of the term health literacy in a 2012 systematic review. The phrase covers the knowledge and skills people need to handle health demands in daily life. Its importance was widely accepted, but researchers defined it in many conflicting ways, which made measuring and comparing it hard.

Searching the literature, the team collected seventeen definitions and twelve models of the concept. From those, they built one combined model with twelve dimensions. It covers finding, understanding, judging, and using health information across three settings: medical care, disease prevention, and health promotion. The authors offer the model as a base for programs that raise health literacy and for tools that measure it fairly.
europmc-pmc3329715:
Allison and colleagues combined published results to ask whether outcomes for a bone cancer of the young have kept improving, in a 2012 analysis. The cancer, osteosarcoma, was nearly always fatal until tailored drug combinations arrived in the nineteen sixties and seventies. Those regimens lifted survival dramatically into the nineteen eighties, turning a death sentence into a disease most patients survive.

Pooling the modern literature, the team found survival gains stalled after the nineteen eighties and on some measures slipped. Relapse rates likewise fell in the nineteen seventies and then flattened. One bright trend continued: surgeons have saved the affected limb ever more often, decade after decade, instead of amputating. The authors say the plateau proves systemic treatment needs a fresh strategy, since the cancer remains highly lethal when it spreads.
europmc-pmc3406015:
Kutter and co-workers charted in 2012 how fast long noncoding RNAs come and go in rodent evolution. Mammal genomes are copied into many long RNAs that never become proteins, and few have known jobs. The team catalogued liver transcripts in two mouse lineages and the rat, pairing RNA data with gene-switch marks.

Compared with protein-coding genes, the noncoding transcripts showed far more gain and loss between species. Nearly half the noncoding sites had appeared or vanished since mouse and rat last shared an ancestor. Sites whose copying survived also carried the most guarded DNA spelling. Newborn noncoding RNAs slightly boosted neighboring protein genes, hinting they help tune local expression.
europmc-pmc3422615:
Khuong-Quang led a team that tested forty-two childhood brainstem tumors in 2012 for mutations in the histone H3.3 gene. These tumors, called diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas, are devastating and lack any effective therapy. The team compared mutated and normal tumors for other gene flaws, chromosome changes, and patient outcomes.

A single mutation, nicknamed K27M, appeared in the large majority of tumors, alongside very frequent TP53 mutations. Tumors carrying it showed their own pattern of chromosome gains, including extra copies of growth-related genes. Every long-term survivor lacked the mutation, and patients without it lived longer overall. The authors urge testing for the mutation at diagnosis, since it splits the disease into distinct groups that trials should treat separately.
europmc-pmc3446315:
Davies and a large team charted DNA methylation across human brain regions and blood in 2012, asking how much of the pattern is tissue-specific. These chemical tags help lock in each cell type's identity, yet normal differences between brain areas were barely mapped. Tissue came from several donors and several functionally distinct regions.

Clear tissue-specific patterns emerged, clustering near genes that switch activity between regions and near pathways for nerve development. Differences between tissues dwarfed differences between people. Still, some personal variation echoed across brain and blood alike, a hopeful sign for studies that can only sample blood. The authors offer the maps as a resource for brain epigenetics.
europmc-pmc3477315:
Dickens and co-authors rebuilt the model of how a death signal switches on inside cells, in a 2012 Molecular Cell paper. Certain receptors on a cell surface can order the cell to kill itself, a process called apoptosis. They gather a complex of proteins that wakes a cutting enzyme, caspase-8. Textbook models assumed the parts sat in the complex in equal numbers.

Careful measurement showed that assumption was wrong: the complex held far more caspase-8 than the adaptor protein meant to recruit it. Dickens's team proposes that caspase-8 molecules link head to tail in a chain, each waking the next. Blocking chain joints in cells stopped the death signal cold. The chain model explains how a small trigger can fire a full death response.
