gao-gaoreports-gao-08-715: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at financial Audit: Congressional Award Foundation's Fiscal Years 2007 and 2006 Financial Statements. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-915: The Government Accountability Office dug into export-Import Bank: Performance Standards for Small Business Assistance Are in Place but Ex-Im Is in the Early Stages of Measuring Their Effectiveness in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gilman-herland-1915:
Charlotte Perkins Gilman published Herland in 1915, in her own magazine, The Forerunner. The novel imagines a country cut off from the world for two thousand years, where no men live. Gilman was a leading feminist thinker, and fiction let her test her ideas in story form.

Three male explorers, a rich playboy, a doctor, and a sociologist narrator, stumble into the hidden land. They find a peaceful, prosperous society of women who reproduce without men and raise children as a shared duty. The visitors' assumptions about women collapse one by one. Herland founded feminist speculative fiction and still reads as a bold thought experiment about gender and power.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-12-1915:
Volume 12 of the third edition of The Golden Bough appeared in 1915. James George Frazer's twelve-volume study of magic and religion ends not with a new theory but with its tools: a full bibliography and a general index. After eleven volumes of evidence, the twelfth lets readers find and check it.

The bibliography lists the travelers, missionaries, and scholars whose reports Frazer used, a map of his sources in itself. The index sorts gods, rites, peoples, and customs across the whole set. Students of religion still use such apparatus to trace a custom through the work. The volume completes the landmark edition of a founding work of comparative religion.
govdocs-archive_org-ufo2_20240815: UFO made public docs 2: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers and readers.
haslmayr-sendtschreiben-1615:
Adam Haslmayr answers the Rosicrucian manifestos in his Sendtschreiben, printed in German in 1615. The Tyrolean physician writes back to the unknown Brotherhood of the Rosy Cross with open joy. His letter, the first printed reply to the mysterious Fama, set all learned Europe buzzing with hope, doubt, and wild surmise.

Haslmayr begs the brethren to reveal themselves to a waiting world. He had already suffered prison for his alchemical faith and hopes. Enthusiasm, not irony, marks every line of his simple address. The pamphlet launched the strangest learned craze of the seventeenth century, the Rosicrucian furor, whose echoes ran for a hundred years.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum: Volume fifteen: the soldiers' king, sharing his men's hardships in the field. Carlyle celebrates the bond between Frederick and his army with moving power. The human heart of the great biography. No king ever shared more of his soldiers' dangers.
hoffmann-devils-elixir-vol1-1815:
E. T. A. Hoffmann published The Devil's Elixir in German in 1815, and R. P. Gillies translated it into English in 1824. Volume one follows Brother Medardus, a Capuchin monk tempted by a relic said to be an elixir of the Devil. One taste breaks his vows and starts his ruin.

Medardus flees the monastery into crime, disguise, and a haunting double who shares his face. Love, murder, and madness crowd the road as his past hunts him down. Hoffmann mixes Gothic horror with sharp irony about faith and desire. The novel became a founding study of the double in modern fiction. Its wild plot still grips readers who like their tales dark.
hoffmann-devils-elixir-vol2-1815:
Volume two of The Devil's Elixir brings Hoffmann's monk novel to its close, in R. P. Gillies's translation of 1824. Medardus, worn by crime and pursuit, faces the full truth of his family's curse. The double who has dogged him steps out of rumor into plain sight.

Confession, trial, and penance take the place of flight and disguise. Hoffmann untangles the knot of births, sins, and mistaken selves that drove the tale. The ending weighs guilt against grace in a haunted, Catholic frame. Read with volume one, the novel stands complete: a Gothic landmark on the divided self. Its fevered method later fed Poe, Stevenson, and many more.
homer-iliad-pope-1715:
Homer's Iliad came to Georgian England in Alexander Pope's version of 1715 to 1720. Pope's was the great Augustan Iliad, and the most famous English Homer of its age. He worked in heroic couplets and grew rich from the book's subscription sales alone.

Achilles' wrath drives the war tale, from quarrel to Hector's fall at Troy's walls. Gods scheme above while men bleed below, in Pope's polished and balanced verse lines throughout. His notes and essays frame Homer as the supreme poet of nature and fire. Purists charged Pope with making Homer a London wit, but readers loved the sheen. The version ruled English taste until the next century's plainer fashions arrived at last.
homer-odyssey-chapman-1615:
Homer's Odyssey came to England in full in George Chapman's version of 1615. Chapman's was the first complete English Odyssey, companion to his famed Iliad of that era. He used a broad, rolling ten-syllable couplet full of sea wind and strange compounds throughout.

Odysseus, after Troy's fall, wanders ten years toward home and his wife Penelope in Ithaca. Cyclops, Circe, sirens, and the dead test his craft on the long road home. At Ithaca he finds suitors eating his wealth and slays them in his own hall. Chapman's verse is rougher than Pope's but wilder, and many still prize its force. Keats linked both Chapman Homers in the sonnet that made his early name.
indrajalavidyasangraha-1915-1915: Indrajalavidyasangraha, 1915. The Sanskrit magic collection. This book preserves that text. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-15:
Volume 15, from 1898, follows the Hurons through 1638 and 1639. A strange pattern fills the reports that Thwaites prints here. Converts grow in number even while the plague years still cast a shadow.

The fathers' hope stays stubborn in the face of grim facts. Their letters home ring with trust that the mission will thrive. Modern readers know that hope is doomed, which sharpens each page. Baptisms, feasts, and new chapels mark a brief, bright season. The great chronicle keeps a steady beat as the storm builds offshore. Hope and dread share every report in this book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lyons-jacques-j:
Jacques Judah Lyons, an American minister, receives a biographical entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Surinam, Dutch Guiana, on August 25, 1814, he served its Spanish and Portuguese congregation for five years. In 1837 he left for Richmond, Virginia, where he ministered for two years. He died in New York in 1877.

The article follows his thirty-eight years at Shearith Israel in New York. There he resisted every move to change the congregation's form of worship. Beyond his pulpit he helped found the Jews' Hospital, now Mount Sinai. He also backed the Jewish Board of Delegates and the Hebrew Free Schools. He ran the Polonies Talmud Torah School and built a fine library, now held by the Jewish Theological Seminary. With Abraham De Sola he published a fifty-year Hebrew calendar in 1857. The entry portrays a traditional minister who built lasting institutions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-makower-hermann:
Hermann Makower, a German jurist, is profiled at length in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Santomischel, Posen, on March 8, 1830, he was sent to Berlin at nine, nearly penniless. There he sang as a synagogue chorister and found schooling. He died at Berlin on April 1, 1898.

The article follows a rise built on commercial law. Makower reached a judgeship at the Berlin city court, a post no Jew had held before. He left the bench for a richer practice. His commentary on the German commercial code, written with Siegmund Meyer, reached an eleventh edition by 1893. Famous clients followed, including the historian Mommsen, whom he defended against a slander charge by Bismarck. Mommsen was acquitted in 1883. Makower also backed Berlin's Jewish seminary and lectured for its benefit. The entry joins legal fame to communal loyalty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mariamne-10415:
Mariamne, Herod's Hasmonean queen, is portrayed in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The hosted text opens on her unhappy marriage. Herod loved her passionately, the article says. She could not forget that he had murdered her family and taken their throne. Her pride toward the upstart king stung his mother and his sister Salome.

The article follows the court's deadly intrigues. Mariamne's mother pressed Herod to make her young brother Aristobulus high priest. He yielded in 35, meaning to kill the youth when he could. Before facing Antony over that killing, Herod left orders that Mariamne die if he did not return. His brother-in-law Joseph, set to guard her, told her the secret as proof of Herod's love. Salome then accused the two of adultery. Herod executed Joseph at once and jailed Mariamne's mother. The entry shows a queen destroyed by one king's love and suspicion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mayer-henry-105:
Cyrus Adler and Edgar Mels profile Henry Mayer, an American caricaturist, in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Worms on July 18, 1868, the son of a Jewish merchant of London, and was educated in his birthplace. He went to Mexico in 1885, then on to Texas. There, the entry says, he discovered that he could draw, and he taught himself the craft with no master. Cincinnati and then Chicago gave him his start as a caricaturist and illustrator.

His picture books came quickly. “The Autobiography of a Monkey” came in 1898. “In Laughland” and “Fantasies in Ha! Ha!” came in 1899, and toyland and doll adventures came after those. His drawings appeared in comic papers in Munich, London, New York, and Paris. His cartoons on the Dreyfus affair, printed in English periodicals, drew wide attention on both sides of the Atlantic.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-memorial-servic:
Memorial Service, the prayer for the dead, is treated by Cyrus Adler and Kaufmann Kohler in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Prayer for the dead appears already in the Second Book of Maccabees. Reading the Torah chapter on death on the Day of Atonement seems to have suggested a special remembrance that day. Later the custom spread to other festivals.

Its real subject is the Reform remaking of the rite. Reform Judaism rebuilt the old liturgy. It rested on the immortality of the soul and on comfort for mourners. In time it became a most solemn feature of the Day of Atonement. The entry sets out the common order. First come verses on life's brevity and the twenty-third Psalm. Then come medieval poems by Ibn Gabirol, Judah ha-Levi, and Bahya, in translation. Next comes the prayer naming the martyrs. Many congregations also read the year's death-roll.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meshullam-ben-j:
Meshullam ben Jonah is the subject of a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, written by Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach. He was a physician and translator who lived in southern France in the thirteenth century. The entry presents him as a scholar of medicine rather than a working doctor.

According to the article, Meshullam studied medicine but seems never to have practised it. At the request of a friend named Ḥafeẓ, or Shalem, he translated Zahrawi's medical work Kitab al-Taẓrif into Hebrew, opening his version with a Hebrew poem in his friend's honor. A brief bibliography points readers to Steinschneider and to Neubauer's catalogue of Hebrew manuscripts at the Bodleian Library.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-miedzyboz-medzh:
Miedzyboz, a town in Russian Podolia, held 3,400 Jews among its 5,100 people when Herman Rosenthal and S. Janovsky wrote its Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. More than a thousand of its Jews were artisans, and its charities aided some 300 families with fuel and Passover help in 1898. A Jewish community there reaches back to the sixteenth century.

That community was destroyed in the Chmielnicki uprising, rebuilt to a few tax-favored houses by 1661, and struck again by the sword in 1664. The town's lasting fame came about 1740, when Israel ben Eliezer, the Baal Shem-Tov, settled at Miedzyboz. From there he began spreading the teachings that became Hasidism, making the small town a place of pilgrimage in Jewish memory.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moghilef-mohile:
Moghilef, or Mohilev, on the Dnieper, gets a documentary town history in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its authors are Herman Rosenthal, J. G. Lipman, and S. Janovsky. The surviving narrative turns on friction with the Christian merchants. Their complaints about Jewish competition reached the king. Their pressure produced a royal edict that redrew where Jews could live.

On July 23, 1626, Sigismund III ordered every Jew owning a house on the market-place to move. They were to go to the street of the prayer-house, with equivalent ground assigned there. Ladislaus IV confirmed the order in 1633. He also banned Jewish baths and breweries inside the city. The article then tells of a 1639 scare. A Christian servant's death was laid at a Jewish household's door. Inquiry showed she had drunk herself senseless at the monastery.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morgenstern-kar:
Karl Morgenstern was a German landscape-painter born at Frankfurt-on-the-Main on October 25, 1812. He receives a brief Jewish Encyclopedia notice in 1906. He trained at the Munich Academy of Arts. In 1834 he made the young painter's classic trip through the Bavarian highlands and into Italy. Italy stayed his subject for good.

The entry names three canvases. They are a view of Naples, the Bay of Baiae, and the gulf of Villefranche near Nice. The last was painted in 1843. By then it was hanging in the Städel Museum at Frankfurt. He died in his native city in 1893. Singer's artists' lexicon is the sole source. He is a painter preserved by his Italian views and one museum wall.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-of-kiev-1:
Moses of Kiev was a Russian Talmudist of the first half of the twelfth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Louis Ginzberg wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He seems to have reached western Europe after the Jews were expelled from Kiev in 1124. He may have been a pupil of Jacob Tam, the great French tosafist.

From Russia, Moses corresponded with Samuel ben Ali, head of the Babylonian academy. Through Moses, western scholars learned of an important legal decision of the Geonim that Samuel had sent him. Another responsum from Samuel to Moses survives in a manuscript. Whether he is also the Rabbi Moses the Russian of the Sefer ha-Shoham, the entry leaves doubtful.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-munden-11215:
Münden, a town in the Prussian province of Hanover, first mentions Jews in the sixteenth century. Gotthard Deutsch and Abraham Lewinsky wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on it. When Duke Heinrich drove the Jews from Brunswick in 1557, those of Münden were allowed to stay. The Thirty Years' War then swelled their numbers.

The article is a string of grievances and odd dues. Citizens petitioned General Tilly in 1626 to restrain the Jews, and the town charged burial fees by age. Jews also had to give a silver spoon each year as the marksmen's prize, a duty kept into the eighteen hundreds. The synagogue of 1834 burned and was rebuilt, and by 1903 the community counted one hundred ten souls.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naphtali-hirsch: Naphtali Hirsch ben Menahem was president of the Lemberg community in the sixteenth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia gives him a very short notice by its editorial committee and S. Mannheimer. He wrote Perush ha-Millot, explanations of difficult words in the Midrash Rabbah. The book was printed at Cracow in 1569.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-negeb-dry-land-:
The Negeb is the dry tract of southern Judah. Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The word often means simply the south. The Authorized Version renders it that way throughout. Yet the Negeb is also one named region. It forms a plateau of moderate height.

Water was scarce there, but pasture was rich. Moses' spies found Amalekites living in the Negeb. Joshua gave its twenty-nine cities to Judah. Part later passed to the tribe of Simeon. Five districts bore the names of their peoples. Judah, Jerahmeelites, Kenites, Cherethites, and Caleb each held one. Its grape cluster needed two men and a pole. Prophets later promised its ruined cities a return.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nezhin-nyezhin-:
Nezhin was a Russian town in the tobacco trade. Herman Rosenthal and S. Janovsky wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It lay in the government of Chernigov. In 1648 Cossacks took it and slew its Jews. Poles of the town died at their side.

In July 1881 an anti-Jewish riot raged three days. Most Jewish houses in Nezhin were destroyed then. Troops fired twice on the mob, killing ten rioters. New tobacco duties then crushed the small Jewish workshops. Great manufacturers absorbed the trade instead of them. The census of 1897 counted 32,108 people there. About one third of them were Jews. Jewish artisans alone numbered 980 in that count. Schools and a loan association served the community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-novy-israel-116:
Novy Israel, or New Israel, was a short-lived sect. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It arose at Odessa at the end of 1881. Jacob Prelooker, a schoolteacher, founded the movement. It leaned from Judaism toward Christianity in tone.

His stated aim was a reformed synagogue for Jews. He preached softening the split with Christians too. Brotherhood in religion was his public watchword. In secret he hoped to join Russian dissenters. Molokans and Stundists were the allies he sought. Learning and depth, the entry judges, he lacked. Few adherents ever rallied to his flag. Press and government favored it briefly, then saw through it. All trace vanished before he left for England.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-opatow-samuel-b: Samuel ben Eleazar Opatow was a rabbi in Moravia. The board and Alexander Kisch wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Bohemia, part of the Czech lands. He served as rabbi at Prossnitz in the fifteen hundreds. He wrote a book of new notes and replies on the law. Its theme was the marriage laws of the Talmud, in the tracts Ketubot and Kiddushin. The book came out at Prossnitz in 1602 or 1618.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ottolenghi-emil:
Emilio Ottolenghi was an Italian giver of aid from Acqui. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Acqui on November 5, 1830. Since 1848 he had lived at Alessandria, in Piedmont. King Humbert the First made him Count of Vallepiana.

That high title came to Emilio on February 22, 1883. In 1882 he was first named to the town board. He was named to that board for years in a row. He sat on the board of the home for beggars. He founded homes and asylums for the poor and sick. He was a chief of the Bank of Italy there. He led the aid group for his whole province. The crown gave him rank three times in his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-parnas-colloqui:
A parnas is the chief or trustee of a Jewish flock. Cyrus Adler and Gotthard Deutsch wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The word is a new Hebrew word for that post. It is found in the Targum for words that mean steward. It is met with oft in the books of the Talmud.

Men have sought the source of the word in Greek. One source may be a Greek word for one who provides. In some tongues of today it stands as a term of law. In Bavaria it came as barnos in a decree of 1813. In Dutch law it stands as parnassijns, in set form. In the Middle Ages the title was not in wide use. The piece goes on to trace the post through those ages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pera-12015:
Peræa was the part of Palestine east of the Jordan. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Josephus set its bounds from Macherus to Pella. In fact the region stretched much farther north and south.

The land is a rough plateau above the river. It drops steeply west and slopes gently east. Its rivers include the Jabbok and the Arnon. The region mattered little until the Maccabees came. Judas first brought it under firm Jewish rule. Rome's general Vespasian took it back in 67.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phillips-samuel:
Samuel Phillips was an English journalist and critic in London. He was born there in 1815 and died at Brighton in 1854. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. At fifteen he acted at Covent Garden.

Phillips then studied at Cambridge and at Göttingen. In 1841 he turned to letters and the press. His novel Caleb Stukeley won notice in Blackwood's. As the Times critic he struck at Dickens and Carlyle. His bold reviews became the talk of the town. He later directed letters for the Crystal Palace.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-plungian-plungi:
Mordecai Plungian was a Russian Hebraist caught between two camps. Herman Rosenthal and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Plungian in 1814. He died at Wilna in 1883, poor and embattled.

Young Plungian won fame as a Talmudist early. An unhappy marriage drove him from his town. At Troki his freer ideas angered the strict. At Wilna he lectured and taught for bread. The seminary made him instructor in Talmud in 1867. When it closed, he corrected proofs at Romm's press. Orthodox called him heretic; liberals called him backward.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-potchi-moses-12: Moses Potchi was a Karaite scholar who lived at Constantinople. Kaufmann Kohler and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the second half of the sixteenth century. He belonged to the Maruli family. His son Joseph took the family name as his own. One work is ascribed to Potchi but stayed in handwriting. It treats the making of the world and the being of God. A poem of his praises a book printed in 1581.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabinowitz-hirs:
Hirsch Zebi Rabinowitz was a Russian man of science and public writer. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Linkovo near Poneviezh in 1832. He died at St. Petersburg in 1889. His father, the town rabbi, was his chief teacher. Talmud and kindred lore filled his first years of study.

Yet the boy leaned toward science from a young age. He was glad when his father let a friend teach him. That friend taught him the first steps of mathematics. At twenty his life took its new turn in full. The entry follows his path from study house to science. It lists the works that made his public name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-recanati-12615:
Recanati is an Italian family named for the city of Recanati. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The city lay in the former Papal States. The article opens with a family tree.

The entry then profiles the family's leading members. Amadeo translated Maimonides into Italian in 1583. Elijah wrote a confession in rimed prose about 1660. Emanuele practiced medicine at Verona and wrote Hebrew grammars. He also made Hebrew dictionaries in both directions. Jacob Hayyim served as rabbi in many Italian towns. He wrote on Jewish law, arithmetic, and doctrine. The entry traces one family across three centuries of learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-revere-giuseppe:
Giuseppe Revere was an Italian dramatist and humorist born at Triest in 1812. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died on November 22, 1889. His parents meant him for a career in commerce.

The article says he left commerce for study at Milan. He pursued literature, philosophy, German, Greek, and Hebrew. His plays treat Italian historical figures and places. Lorenzino de' Medici appeared in 1839. In 1848 he joined a Mazzini plot at Venice. Banishment followed, and he later defended Rome. He was banished again on suspicion of republican plotting. His many poems fill the entry's later list. He also edited an official bulletin at Rome. The entry joins stage work with patriotic action.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-romberg-moritz-:
Moritz Heinrich Romberg was a German physician born on November 11, 1795. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Meiningen in Saxony. He died in Berlin on June 16, 1873.

The article says he graduated from Berlin University in 1817. He settled in the capital after a stay in Vienna. He served as physician to the poor from 1820. During cholera epidemics he ran a Berlin hospital. He rose to a full professorship in 1845. He retired in 1867 after his doctor's jubilee. His specialty was neuropathy, or nervous disease. His textbook gave the first systematic review of nervous maladies. It appeared from 1840 to 1846. He also translated Bell and others into German.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-roussillon-1291:
Roussillon is a province of ancient France, now the department of Pyrénées-Orientales. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Jews settled there early in the thirteenth century, forming many congregations.

Congregations stood at Perpignan, Collioure, Céret, Elne, and a dozen smaller towns. At Villefranche was born Levi ben Abraham, a figure in the fight over philosophy study. In 1228 King James I barred Jews from public office there. He also capped the interest Jews could charge on loans. Later kings eased some rules, such as the badge while traveling.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salamanca-13015:
Salamanca is a Spanish city, capital of its province and famed for its university. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Its Jews served King Ferdinand II of Leon well in war in 1169.

In return the king granted them equal rights with Christians in 1170. The town council must protect and even defend them, for a yearly tax. They were not spared, though, in the persecutions of 1391. In 1412 Vicente Ferrer preached there to convert the Jews by sermon. The great synagogue then became a church named Vera Cruz.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-jose:
Samuel ben Joseph Joske was a Polish Talmudist of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, born at Lublin. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was the first known rabbi of Jung-Bunzlau in Bohemia.

Joske's Lehem Rab, printed at Prague in 1609, supplements the Shulhan Aruk. It follows the Orah Hayyim section and keeps that code's own order throughout. Judah Löw ben Bezaleel, the famed Maharal of Prague, approved the work himself. A supplement so endorsed helped rabbis apply the code in practice. The entry is short, but it fixes Joske's place in that chain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sason-joseph-be:
M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Joseph ben Jacob Sason, an editor and perhaps an author. He lived in the sixteenth century. Sason edited the Maḥazor Sefardi, the Sephardic prayer book. It was printed at Venice in 1584. He also paid for a Jewish calendar covering 1585 to 1639.

The author of Shemen Sason may be this same Joseph Sason. That work treats the Masorah, the notes guarding the Bible's exact text. It quotes the ancient works on that subject. Later scholars cite it in their own books on the Masorah. Lonsano quotes it in Or Torah. Norzi quotes it in Minḥat Shai. The entry leaves his authorship open, as the evidence does.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schreiner-abrah:
Abraham Schreiner, an Austrian who discovered petroleum, is profiled by Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman in this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Schreiner was born in Galicia early in the nineteenth century. He died sometime after 1870. He traded at Boryslaw, where he owned land. A greasy, tarry ooze seeped from a hollow on that land.

Local farmers had long used the stuff as a cure-all. Schreiner rolled it into a ball, stuck in a wick, and lit it. It burned with a red flame. His first try at distilling ended with an exploding pot. He bought proper gear from an apothecary. In 1853 he produced petroleum and sold it to druggists. The Austrian Northern Railway tested his refined oil for lamps in 1854. Fire twice gutted his works. After the 1866 blaze he was ruined. American oil then flooded the market.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-semitic-languag:
Semitic languages are the tongues spoken by the Semitic peoples of the ancient Near East. Crawford Howell Toy and George A. Barton wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on them. The group includes Babylonian, Assyrian, Aramaic, Hebrew, Canaanite, and Phoenician speech. Arabic and Abyssinian tongues belong to the family as well.

The entry compares this family with the Aryan, or Indo-European, languages. Both build words by bending stems, yet their deep differences suggest separate roots. The authors then turn to the traits that mark Semitic speech itself. For readers, the piece maps a language family that shaped scripture, trade, and empire.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sheba-queen-of-:
Sheba's queen was a south Arabian monarch who visited King Solomon at Jerusalem. Joseph Jacobs and Ludwig Blau wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on her. She had heard of Solomon's wisdom and wealth from afar. She came with a brilliant retinue to test that fame.

At Jerusalem she found the truth greater than the reports. The two rulers exchanged costly presents before she went home. Josephus instead made her queen of Egypt and Ethiopia. He credited her with bringing balsam plants to the Holy Land. Scholars place her realm at Saba in southern Arabia. Yet no Sabean inscription found yet names any such queen, and one rabbi read the word as a kingdom, not a queen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-ben-samu:
Simeon ben Samuel of Joinville was a French tosafist and Bible commentator of the thirteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He is once wrongly called Samson ben Samuel by copyists. Elsewhere he appears under the name Shemaiah in error.

Simeon learned from Isaac ben Samuel the Elder in France. He in turn taught Eliezer ben Joel ha-Levi. As a tosafist he is quoted as Simeon of Joinville. Sometimes the sources cite him simply as Simeon alone. As a Bible commentator, Isaac ben Judah quotes him. That citation comes in Isaac's work Pa'neah Raza. The entry untangles a scholar hidden behind three similar names in the old books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-song-of-moses-1:
The Song of Moses is a poem found in Deuteronomy chapter thirty-two. Emil G Hirsch and George A Barton wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Moses is said to have spoken its words to all Israel. The poem shows a scale of prophetic thought found nowhere else. Its form is praised as striking and original throughout.

Heaven and earth are called to hear the opening words. The theme is God's faithfulness toward a faithless people. Next comes God's care in the wilderness and gift of land. Then Israel's lapse into idolatry is described in full. God threatens disaster, then resolves to save and vindicate them. Critics hold that Mosaic authorship is impossible on its terms.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steinhardt-mend:
Mendel Steinhardt was a German rabbi who held the rabbinate of Minden. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He lived across the late 1700s and early 1800s. In 1807 the Westphalia consistory chose him as a counselor. He became known as a defender of early Reform Judaism.

Steinhardt defended Israel Jacobson's push for reform among Westphalian Jews. His 1804 book holds ninety responsa on rabbinical subjects. An index arranges them by Talmudic tractate for easy use. A second work, printed in 1812, defended the Cassel consistory reforms. It argued the changes fit Talmudic principles. The entry shows a rabbi making the legal case for reform.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-triesch-friedri:
Friedrich Gustav Triesch was an Austrian dramatist born at Vienna in 1845. Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied sculpture briefly at the Vienna academy. Lack of money pushed him into business for a time. His farce Lachende Erben succeeded in 1867.

That success let him write plays full time. The Hofburgtheater honored his comedy Im XIX. Jahrhundert in 1868. Two more plays won similar honors in 1877. His comedy Neue Verträge took Munich's first prize in 1879. His drama Ottilie beat 383 rivals for first prize in 1892. He wrote under three pen names as well. Poems and short stories round out his output.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vital-david-b-s:
David ben Solomon Vital, called ha Rofe, was a Spanish scholar. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He left Spain early in the fifteen hundreds. He settled at Patras, in Greece. When that city fell in 1532, he lost almost his whole library. He spent his last years at Arta.

His main work is Keter Torah, printed at Constantinople in 1536. It lists the 613 commandments in verse form. It also covers rules for Hanukkah and the Sabbath. Another book gives rules for examining slaughtered oxen. His Mikhtam le Dawid versifies Maimonides' thirteen articles of faith. He wrote many liturgical poems as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wiga-judah-1491:
Judah Wiga was a Polish preacher of Lublin. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked in the late fifteen and early sixteen hundreds. Sources disagree even on his name. Sternberg calls him Wiga, from Polish records. Basnage calls him Judah Vega instead.

Basnage says Vega published sermons under King Sigismund. Wolf links him to a book called Derashot. He may be the Judah ben Moses of another record. That man wrote Malke Yehudah at Lublin in 1616. It holds fifteen sermons in one collection. The entry lays out the tangled evidence honestly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ze-enah-u-re-en:
Ze'enah u-Re'enah is a Yiddish gloss on the Hebrew Bible tales. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jacob ben Isaac of Janow made the work in his day. He lived in the 1500s and the 1600s in Poland.

The work treats the Pentateuch, the Haftorah, and the Five Scrolls. It is rich in tales drawn from the Midrash books. It draws from gloss books of tales in like measure. Each week part oft starts with a verse from Proverbs. That verse is then fleshed out with tale and gloss. The book was meant most of all for the use of women. Its name comes from a motto on its first title page. That motto is a verse from the Song of Songs.
jordanes-getica-mierow-1915:
Jordanes, a sixth-century writer, told the Goths' story in his Getica, here in Charles Mierow's 1915 English version. Origins, migrations, and kings fill his brisk Latin history. Attila's Huns, the Visigoths, and Rome's fall all pass through its pages.

Nearly all we know of early Gothic history flows through this one book. Jordanes drew on lost works, above all Cassiodorus's great history. His tale mixes legend, pride, and hard fact in equal parts. Mierow's version opened the text to English readers in clear form. It remains the most important barbarian history to survive from the age of migrations.
journal-of-discourses-vol-15:
Panic on Wall Street shapes Volume Fifteen of the Journal, from 1873. Young answers hard times with the United Order, his boldest scheme. Saints are called to pool property and labor for the common good.

Cooperation rises, in his preaching, to the rank of God's own law. Towns across Utah try shared farms, shops, and herds under the plan. Sermons praise the order as Zion's shield against greed and want. A godly economy takes shape, for a time, in the desert. The volume shows faith turned into a full plan for daily life and work for all.
kafka-die-verwandlung-1915:
Die Verwandlung, published in 1915, is Kafka's novella in the original German: The Metamorphosis. Gregor Samsa, a traveling salesman, wakes one morning to find himself changed into a huge insect, and his family's horror becomes the story.

Told in calm, exact prose, the tale follows Gregor's shrinking place in the flat, his sister's turn from care to disgust, and his quiet death. Kafka never explains the change, which is the point: the absurd is treated as fact. This Kurt Wolff era text is the founding work of the literature of alienation, read here in the language Kafka wrote.
kathavatthu-points-of-controversy-1915:
Shwe Zan Aung and C. A. F. Rhys Davids translated the Kathavatthu in 1915. Their English version bears the title Points of Controversy. The Kathavatthu is the fifth book of the Abhidhamma Pitaka.

Tradition says a council in the third century BCE composed the work. It knocks down more than two hundred disputed doctrines, point by point. Questions about the soul, the Buddhas, and time receive disciplined refutation. The method proceeds by questions that corner each opponent logically. Shwe Zan Aung, a Burmese scholar, worked from deep commentarial knowledge. The translation opens ancient Buddhism's great debate book. Philosophy as careful argument fills these pages, two thousand years old.
lawrence-rainbow-1915:
D. H. Lawrence published The Rainbow in 1915, his most ambitious novel of three Brangwen generations in the Midlands. The tale follows the Brangwens seeking fulfillment across the industrial Midlands as canals, mines, and railways remake England. Police suppressed the book for obscenity within weeks, and copies were burned by court order in 1915.

Tom Brangwen weds a Polish widow, Lydia, and their marriage of strangers opens the family saga in Marsh Farm. Anna, her daughter, weds Will Brangwen, and their struggle of wills fills the stormy, fertile middle of the book. Ursula, the granddaughter, becomes a teacher, loves and leaves Skrebensky, and seeks a self beyond marriage and chapel. A rainbow over the colliery at the close promises renewal for a world Lawrence found mechanized and spiritually starved. The novel's biblical cadence and frank desire made it a landmark of modernism.
legge-forerunners-and-rivals-vol-1-1915:
Francis Legge published the first volume of Forerunners and Rivals of Christianity in 1915. His subject is the crowded religious world around the early church, from 330 B.C. to A.D. 330. He asked what faiths came before Christianity, which ones competed with it, and how they shaped the ground it grew in.

Legge starts with the conquests of Alexander and the gods of Alexandria, where Greek and Egyptian beliefs mixed. He then traces the roots of Gnosticism and the Gnostic teachers who taught before Christ. The volume gives readers the pagan and mystery faiths that later Gnostic systems, covered in volume two, built upon.
legge-forerunners-and-rivals-vol-2-1915:
Religions competed with early Christianity across the Roman world, and Francis Legge spent two volumes mapping the rivals. Forerunners and Rivals of Christianity, Volume Two, published in 1915, takes up the story from the year 330 backward and forward through the great systems. The Gnostic schools receive the deepest treatment here.

Valentinians, Basilideans, and Marcionites appear as serious religious thinkers rather than cartoon villains. Legge's sympathy for these so-called heretics set his history apart in its day. He traces how their ideas about creation, evil, and salvation challenged the young Church. Readers gain a fair hearing for voices mostly known through their enemies. The volume remains a humane guide to a tangled religious landscape.
letters-of-a-soldier-1914-1915:
Eugène Emmanuel Lemercier's Letters of a Soldier cover August 1914 to April 1915. Constable published this authorized translation in London in 1917. André Chevrillon wrote the preface, and A. Clutton-Brock the introduction.

Lemercier writes most often to his very dear mother. His first letter calls these his first days of life at war. One line became the book's motto: you do not know the things taught by him who falls. He adds simply, I do know. The letters carry a French soldier's faith, fear, and tenderness home. Lemercier was an artist as well as a soldier. His eye for light and place sharpens even trench scenes.
lidzbarski-johannesbuch-1915:
Mark Lidzbarski, a German scholar of Semitic languages, published Das Johannesbuch der Mandaer in 1915. The book gives his German translation of the Mandaean Book of John, a scripture of the small baptist community of southern Iraq and Iran. It was the first Western rendering of the text.

The Mandaeans revere John the Baptist and practice repeated baptism in running water as their central rite. Their book tells of John's life, of light-world beings, and of the soul's ascent after death. Lidzbarski's edition, with the Mandaic text and notes, opened a living Gnostic tradition to European scholarship.
machen-bowmen-1915:
A short tale of Machen's made the most famed legend of the Great War in 1915. The Bowmen, in The Angels of Mons collection, tells of saintly archers who cover a British retreat. Readers took the fiction for fact and would not let it go.

Machen said plainly that he had made the tale up, and the legend grew all the same. The other pieces in the book are legends of the war in the same vein. The volume shows a story walking out of its author's hands into history. It is a case study in how myths are born.
magna-carta-1215:
Magna Carta, the Great Charter, was sealed by King John of England at Runnymede in June 1215. England's barons had rebelled against his taxes and abuses, and forced the charter on him at sword point. The English text here comes from Yale Law School's Avalon Project.

Most of its 63 clauses deal with feudal dues, inheritance, and the church's freedom. Two clauses outlived the rest: no free man may be punished without lawful judgment, and justice may not be sold or delayed. Later ages read those lines as the seed of liberty under law. The charter became a symbol far beyond its feudal start.
masters-spoon-river-1915:
Edgar Lee Masters published Spoon River Anthology in 1915, his groundbreaking portrait of small-town America in free verse. The dead of Spoon River speak their own epitaphs in this corrosive book of linked monologues from the hill. Masters, an Illinois lawyer, drew his town from Lewistown and Petersburg and their courthouse gossip.

Some two hundred and forty speakers confess adultery, murder, greed, faith, and thwarted love from beyond the grave. Judges, teachers, drunkards, and saints correct the town's official pieties with what they hid in life from neighbors. The Trainor the druggist, Lucinda Matlock, and Fiddler Jones stand out in a chorus of plain American voices. Masters's method, the graveyard chorus, reshaped American poetry and theatre for the century that followed his book in 1915. Its bite and pity still sting readers who think small towns simple.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-15: Volume fifteen is etext 3565 in Gutenberg's Napoleon series. Its head note, like its neighbours, pairs the title with 1815. Louis Antoine Fauvelet de Bourrienne is the author named in that head. What follows in the sample is boilerplate alone: rights, gifts, and posting dates. No page of the secretary's memoir is preserved in the held portion. Only the facts in this note can be verified from that sample.
meyrink-der-golem-1915:
Gustav Meyrink dreams a clay giant to life in Der Golem, his famed novel of 1915, in German. In the old Jewish ward of Prague, a gem cutter takes up a strange scroll and lives the life of a man from years past. The Golem, the clay shape said to prowl the ward in times of dread, stalks his dreams and steps at last in flesh through the fog bound lanes.

The prose is dense, weird, and full of occult lore. Meyrink was a sage of such lore in his own life. The book is the chief tale of the Golem.
michels-political-parties-paul-1915:
Robert Michels's Political Parties appears in Eden and Cedar Paul's translation of 1915. Michels, who had studied socialist parties from inside, states his iron law of oligarchy. Who says organization, says oligarchy is his grim summary. Even parties devoted to democracy, he argues, fall under the rule of a few leaders.

Leaders gain skills, files, salaries, and a taste for power that members cannot match. Michels draws his evidence from German socialism, the most democratic movement of its day. The book became a classic of political sociology. Its law is still quoted whenever movements harden into machines. The Pauls' translation carried it across the English world.
miller-piltdown-jaw-1915:
Gerrit S. Miller Jr., a zoologist at the Smithsonian, dropped a bomb on the Piltdown claim in this paper of 1915. Piltdown man, found in Sussex gravel in 1912, was then the pride of British science. Miller worked on the jaw of the famed find, cast and bone side by side.

He showed that the jaw came from an ape, not from a man at all. The teeth wear and the joint shape give the game away to a trained eye. His paper was the first great learned charge on a find now known to be a fraud.
morgan-mendelian-heredity-1915:
Thomas Hunt Morgan led the famous fly room at Columbia, where tiny fruit flies were bred by the thousands. His 1915 book The Mechanism of Mendelian Heredity, written with his team, reports what those flies proved. Genes, the book argues, sit on chromosomes in fixed order.

Morgan shows how traits travel together in linked groups and how those groups sometimes swap parts. Maps of gene order, built from breeding counts, fill the later chapters. The work turned Mendel's rules into physical facts and founded the chromosome theory of heredity. The fly room's small space and huge output became a legend in American science.
nasa-tm-19650012952-saturn-monthly-progr:
Covering August 15 to September 18, 1963, this Marshall report tracks progress on the Saturn I, IB, and V vehicles. One entry notes that the S-1-5 stage, its instrument unit, and payload arrived during the period. The report does not cover engine programs, which were reported separately by the Engine Management Office.

An asterisk marks each item continued from the previous month. That simple device let readers follow long tasks across reports. Taken together, these monthly reports form a detailed diary of the Saturn program. This early volume shows the hardware still in build and checkout, well before the Moon flights.
nasa-tm-19650014322-resume-of-handling-q:
Handling qualities of the X-15 rocket airplane are summed up in this record, marked confidential in its scan. The X-15 flew faster and higher than any other piloted aircraft of its time. Its handling had to be judged across launch, climb, and near-space flight. Reentry and landing placed very different demands on the same aircraft.

A resume of this kind gathers flight experience in one place. Pilots and engineers could see what the aircraft did well and where it was hard to fly. Longitudinal stability and control run through the whole flight path. That record guided both X-15 operations and later high-speed aircraft design.
nasa-tm-19650014323-lateral-directional-:
Commander Forrest S Petersen of the Navy, with Herman A Rediess and Joseph Weil at the Flight Research Center at Edwards, wrote this X-15 report. Their topic is lateral-directional control, meaning how the aircraft rolls and yaws, and how it stays stable in those motions. The document is NASA Memorandum X-726, declassified in 1965.

Sideways behavior is critical in a rocket aircraft. At great height the air is thin and control surfaces lose power. The authors set out the control characteristics found in the program. Their work helped pilots manage an aircraft that flew at the edge of the atmosphere, where small errors grow quickly.

Museum visitors met the same reconstructions in the halls Osborn directed in New York.

plos-pbio-0020015:
Jun R. Huh, Stephanie Y. Vernooy, Hong Yu, and co-workers studied sperm formation in the fruit fly for PLOS Biology in 2004. Caspases are enzymes best known for driving cell death. Yet in fly testes, they help shape sperm in a process that splits a shared mass into single sperm cells.

The surprise is that death enzymes do careful building work here without killing the cell. The team found that more than one caspase chain is needed for sperm to separate properly. That means the system has backup and fine control, not a single switch. The study broadens what caspases are for. It hints that other tissues may also borrow death tools for safe, local tasks.
plos-pone-0000015: A 2006 PLOS ONE paper on stem cell culture. The method avoids colony formation. Pluripotent cells can become any type. The study uses E-cadherin-coated plates. It keeps cells pluripotent. The paper is kept here.
plos-pone-0000115:
Ashraf Yusuf Rangrez, Kannayakanahalli Maheshwarappa Dayananda, Santosh Atanur, and colleagues report this microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2006. They searched the bacterium Aeromonas culicicola for a type four secretion system. This is a molecular machine bacteria use during conjugation, the process of passing DNA to a neighbor cell.

Finding such machinery matters because conjugation spreads genes, including ones for drug resistance, between bacteria. The authors report detecting the parts of this system in this species. The result adds a data point to the map of which bacteria carry the tools for gene swapping, and how those tools are built.
plos-pone-0000215:
Marie-dominique Franco, Jonathan Bohbot, Kenny Fernandez, and colleagues published this insect neuroscience paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. In the moth Manduca sexta, the olfactory epithelium lines the antennae and holds the smell-sensing cells. The authors study how sensory cells proliferate, keep being born, within that tissue as the moth develops into an adult.

A moth's sense of smell guides it to food and mates, and its sensors are renewed over life. Tracking where new sensory cells come from explains how the system stays sharp. The work adds to the study of adult neurogenesis, the birth of new nerve cells in mature animals.
plos-pone-0000315:
Chen Chen, Jiaqi Tang, Wei Dong, and colleagues published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Streptococcus suis is a pig bacterium that can infect people and, rarely, cause streptococcal toxic shock syndrome. The authors compare the genomes of two Chinese isolates of S. suis 2 to get a glimpse of what makes such strains dangerous.

China had seen human outbreaks of this syndrome, so the isolates mattered beyond pig farming. Comparing their genomes with milder strains highlights candidate virulence genes. The study is an early example of using comparative genomics to investigate an emerging zoonotic threat.
plos-pone-0000415:
Frank Powilleit, Tanja Breinig, and Manfred J. Schmitt turned a yeast virus's shell into a building platform, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The L-A virus of yeast wraps itself in a protein capsid. The team used that capsid inside living yeast to assemble chimeric virus-like particles, shells that mix the original protein with foreign pieces.

Virus-like particles are prized in vaccine work because they look like viruses to the immune system but cannot cause infection. A yeast-based assembly line could make them cheaply, and the same platform can display foreign proteins for research. The study is a piece of bioengineering: borrowing a virus's carpentry for human purposes.
plos-pone-0000515:
Liam J. Drew and colleagues identified pain channels that a sea snail toxin can block, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The channels are high-threshold mechanosensitive ion channels, opened by strong pressure, and they mediate pressure-evoked pain. A novel conopeptide, a small toxin from a cone snail, blocked them.

Pressure pain is hard to treat because the channels responsible were poorly defined. A selective blocker is both a research probe and a possible drug lead: cone snail toxins have already yielded one approved pain medicine. Naming the channel and its blocker together moves mechanical pain from a vague complaint toward a molecular target.
plos-pone-0000615:
Sharon J. Sequeira, Aparna C. Ranganathan, Alejandro P. Adam and co-authors studied a stress pathway inside breast cells for PLOS ONE in 2007. When the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell's protein-folding workshop, is under stress, a kinase called PERK switches on. PERK acts on a protein named eIF2α and slows new protein making.

That slowdown can halt the cell cycle or push a cell toward death, limiting growth. The team links this control of cell division to two outcomes. One is how mammary acinar structures, the small sacs of the breast, take shape. The other is how tumors form. Cancer researchers will note the bridge between cell stress and tumor growth.
plos-pone-0000715:
John T. Schousboe, Kevin E. Wilson and Thomas N. Hangartner asked whether one scan can catch two dangers in older women. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study starts from a stark fact: cardiovascular disease is the most common cause of death among post-menopausal women. Their objective was to test lateral spine images taken on a bone densitometer, a machine used to detect vertebral fractures.

Could those same images accurately detect calcification of the abdominal aorta, a warning sign for heart disease? The comparison standard was digital radiography. If fracture-assessment images reveal aortic calcium too, a routine bone check gains heart value at no extra radiation or cost. Screening efficiency matters most in busy clinics.
plos-pone-0000815:
Michelle S. Lewis, Diane J. Pikaard, Mikhail Nasrallah and colleagues pinpointed where one parent's ribosomal genes get silenced in hybrids. In a genetic hybrid, silencing of one parental set of rRNA genes is an epigenetic phenomenon called nucleolar dominance. The team had shown silencing stays within the nucleolus organizer regions. Those are the loci where rRNA genes sit in tandem repeats. Silencing does not spread beyond them.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE study pursues that locus-specific silencing. Ribosomal RNA genes are needed in huge numbers, yet hybrids switch off a whole parental set. How a cell chooses and silences one array, precisely at its locus, is a clean model for epigenetic control of repeated genes.
plos-pone-0000915:
Michael Akhras, Magnus Unemo, Sreedevi Thiyagarajan and colleagues built a one primer system that copies many DNA targets at once, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their method grows out of an older assay called the molecular inversion probe. The team added a complete gap filling step to make it stronger.

They call the result connector inversion probe technology. As a proof of concept, they show it can amplify many chosen sequences in a single reaction. Copying many targets at once, cleanly, is the backbone of genetic testing and pathogen hunting. A flexible system like this can serve labs that need wide screens from small samples.
plos-pone-0001015:
Simone Macri, Paolo Pasquali, Luca Bonsignore and colleagues found that mild stress in newborn mice made adults more alike, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Animal studies of human illness are trusted only if other labs can repeat them. The team note that claim often fails under varied housing and test conditions.

Working under their own lab conditions, they report that moderate neonatal stress decreased variation within groups in behavior, immunity and stress hormone responses. A treatment that tightens results could make mouse studies easier to repeat. It also raises a subtle point: the earliest days of life may set how uniform a lab population stays.
plos-pone-0001115:
Genes are switched on and off by proteins called transcription factors, which bind to short stretches of DNA near their target genes. Stein Aerts and colleagues tackle a basic puzzle in this field in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. From DNA patterns alone, can one predict which genes a given factor will control?

The team works on refining enhancer models, the computer models that score likely binding sites and regulatory regions. Their aim is a method that holds up across several genomes, not just one species. Better predictions would help researchers map the wiring of gene networks without testing every gene in the lab.
plos-pone-0001215:
Arteriosclerosis, the hardening and narrowing of arteries, is a common cause of chronic illness and death. Marcus Mutschelknauss, Marco Kummer, and Juergen Muser took on a diagnostic gap in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Heart attacks and strokes reveal vulnerable patients only after damage is done. Biomarkers to spot them in advance were lacking.

The authors propose scoring each person's arteriosclerosis by empiric clinical profiling, building a risk profile from a patient's clinical features. Finding vulnerable patients before a cardiovascular event is the real prize, since prevention then has time to work. Their approach uses plain clinical data rather than exotic tests.
plos-pone-0001315:
Bacteria of the class 1 integron type shuffle antibiotic resistance genes like cards, catching and using gene cassettes. Véronique Dubois and colleagues present a new lab assay for the enzyme that does the shuffling, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The enzyme, IntI1 integrase, is a tyrosine recombinase.

Recent data had shown that its recombination acts on the bottom strand of the attC site, but the exact mechanism stayed unclear. The authors' in vitro strand transfer assay lets researchers monitor IntI1 activity directly. Such an assay supports work on slowing the spread of antibiotic resistance.
plos-pone-0001415:
Jian Duan and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE review that pools past trials of farm crops and honey bees. Bees are the top pollinators for many crops world wide. They are also a key test species when new pest proof crops are judged for safety. Some feared that such crops could harm bees.

The authors combined data from many prior studies into one pooled analysis. Pooling gives a firmer verdict than any single small trial. Their work weighs the proof on bee harm from crops that make their own pest toxin. The verdict helps regulators and farmers judge real risk as these crops spread.
plos-pone-0001515:
Emma Underwood and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how to spend wild life funds with care. The usual rule favors species hotspots, dense zones packed with species. But dense does not always mean the best value for money spent. The team set cost into the choice in a formal way.

Their method weighs species saved per dollar spent in each region. Some less dense zones win on that scale. The result urges funders to count cost, not just species tallies. With funds tight, return on spend may save more life in the end than hotspot habit alone.
plos-pone-0001615:
Simon Ho, Urmas Saarma, and Ross Barnett wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a pitfall in dating species pasts. Dates drawn from gene data guide much of ecology: they link species splits to past climate and gauge how fast new species form. Those dates rest on calibration points, past facts used to set the clock. The team show what goes wrong when a point is mis set.

Through three case studies, wrong points bend dates by a wide margin. The bends can flip the tale a study tells. Their work is a caution and a check list for the field. Sound dates are the spine of any claim about how life changed over time.
plos-pone-0001715:
Daniel E. Rozen, Michelle G. J. L. Habets, Andreas Handel, and their co-authors tested a textbook claim about small populations in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Small populations are thought to adapt poorly. Harmful mutations hurt them more, and they have limited access to new helpful mutations, above all those with large benefits. Complex fitness landscapes, where many peaks and valleys separate good and bad gene combinations, should make this worse.

The team tracked how small populations actually evolved on such landscapes. Their title promises heterogeneous trajectories: the populations did not all follow one path. The full text gives the evolution experiments and the routes found. Results like these refine when small populations are truly stuck and when they can still climb.
plos-pone-0001815:
Ingrid B. Müller, Julia Knöckel, Matthew R. Groves, and their co-authors studied vitamin B6 production in the malaria parasite in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Plants, fungi, bacteria, and the apicomplexan parasite Plasmodium falciparum can synthesize vitamin B6 themselves, while mammals must take it in from diet. Its active form is pyridoxal 5-phosphate, or PLP.

The team shows the assembly of the plasmodial PLP synthase complex follows a defined course. The full text gives the protein interaction steps and structures. Because humans cannot make B6, the parasite's synthesis machinery is a clean drug target. Blocking it should starve the parasite without touching the host's supply route.
plos-pone-0001915:
Nicholas Funderburg and co-authors studied how germ signals affect the T cells lost in HIV, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. People with chronic HIV show high levels of germ products in the blood, leaked from the gut. That leak has been linked to a fired-up immune system and to loss of CD4 T cells, the cells HIV destroys.

The team exposed human T cells to signals that trip Toll-like receptors, the cell alarms for germ parts. They tracked both activation and death of the cells. Their model may show one way HIV keeps the immune system both overactive and depleted at once, a core riddle of the illness.
plos-pone-0002015:
Beatriz Quinones and co-authors compared the genomes of a gut bacterium's strains from South Africa, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Campylobacter jejuni is a common cause of acute diarrhea and is also tied to later nerve ills, Guillain-Barre and Miller Fisher syndromes. Around Cape Town, strains of one heat-stable serotype, HS:41, have been noted.

The team set clinical strains from South Africa side by side at the genome level. Shared and distinct genes can hint why some strains cause nerve harm after gut infection. Regional genome data also help health labs track which strains circulate near Cape Town.
plos-pone-0002115:
Sokol Todi and co-authors used the fruit fly to study a motor protein vital to hearing, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Myosin VIIA is an unconventional motor protein necessary for hearing in vertebrates. In human ears, sound is caught by sensory hair cells whose tops carry staircase-like bundles of protrusions called stereocilia, and Myosin VIIA maintains those bundles.

As the title states, the protein is necessary for the development of the auditory organ in the fly Drosophila. A fly ear built on the same motor lets labs test hearing genes fast, in an animal that is cheap to breed.
plos-pone-0002215:
Seiko Oda, Tomoyuki Oda, Kenichiro Nishi, and co-authors linked an inflammation protein to a growth signal in low-oxygen cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The protein, macrophage migration inhibitory factor or MIF, acts in inflammation and also has hormone and enzyme roles. It had been tied to tumor growth as well.

Tumors often outgrow their blood supply and turn on a factor called HIF, which helps cells survive with little oxygen. The team reports that MIF switches on HIF, and that this step depends on p53, a famous tumor suppressor. The link ties inflammation, oxygen sensing, and cancer into one chain of events.
plos-pone-0002315:
Chitralekha Bhattacharya, Sita Aggarwal, Madhu Kumar, and co-authors studied a mouse protein family in germ cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The dead-end gene, Dnd1, is essential for keeping germ cells alive; without it, animals become sterile and develop testicular tumors. Its protein binds the tail region of messenger RNAs and can shield them from microRNA attack.

The team examined the mouse APOBEC3 protein, known from antiviral defense, and found it is expressed in germ cells and interacts with DND1. A partnership between an RNA editor and an RNA guardian in germ cells could shape which messages survive to build eggs and sperm.
plos-pone-0002415:
Jelluma joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Nannette Jelluma, Arjan B. Brenkman, Ian McLeod, among others. Its subject is chromosomal Instability by Inefficient Mps1 Auto-Activation Due to a Weakened Mitotic Checkpoint and Lagging Chromosomes. Chromosomal instability (CIN), a feature widely shared by cells from solid tumors, is caused by occasional chromosome missegregations during cell division.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002515:
Bafna led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Pallavi A. Bafna, Prasad G. Purohit, Anthony Auerbach, among others. Its subject is gating at the Mouth of the Acetylcholine Receptor Channel: Energetic Consequences of Mutations in the αM2-Cap.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002615:
Yamaza and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Takayoshi Yamaza, Yasuo Miura, Yanming Bi, among others. Its subject is pharmacologic Stem Cell Based Intervention as a New Approach to Osteoporosis Treatment in Rodents. Osteoporosis is the most prevalent skeletal disorder, characterized by a low bone mineral density (BMD) and bone structural deterioration, leading to bone fragility fractures.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002715:
Teresa Lopardo and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was claudin-1 is a p63 target gene with a crucial role in epithelial development. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Teresa Lopardo, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The epidermis of the skin is a self-renewing, stratified epithelium that functions as the interface between the human body and the outer environment. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002815:
Timothy S. Ham and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was design and construction of a double inversion recombination switch for heritable sequential genetic memory. The catalog record names Timothy S. Ham first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Inversion recombination elements present unique opportunities for computing and information encoding in biological systems. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002915:
Takeshi Hashimoto, Rajaa Hussien, Hyung-Sook Cho and co-authors looked for a lactate-burning system inside rat neurons in 2008. Lactate is often cast as a waste product, yet brain cells may pass it between them as fuel. That passing idea is called a lactate shuttle.

The team checked whether transporter proteins MCT1 and MCT2 and the enzyme LDH sit together in neuron mitochondria. Finding them there would support an intracellular shuttle inside the neuron itself. Published in PLOS ONE, the study backs that complex with direct evidence, reshaping how brain energy use is pictured. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003015:
Scott Fitzpatrick, Greg Nelson and Geoffrey Clark disputed claims of dwarf prehistoric people on Palau in 2008. The western Micronesian islands were settled around 3,000 to 3,300 years ago. Recent claims had suggested the settlers shrank through insular dwarfism, the island trend toward smaller body size.

Biological and archaeological data indicate the inhabitants were normal sized, the authors argue, despite small scattered bone fragments. Published in PLOS ONE, the title makes the verdict plain. The case is a warning about building a dramatic human story on fragmentary remains. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003115:
Joana Borlido, Greg Veltri, Antony Jackson and co-authors tested clathrin's role at the mitotic spindle in 2008. Clathrin is a multi-part protein involved in vesicle coat assembly, the cell's shipping system. Recently its distribution was reported to change during the cell cycle, with clathrin found at the spindle that separates chromosomes.

Recruitment to the spindle might mean an essential mitotic job, or mere association. The title gives the verdict: clathrin is spindle-associated but not essential for mitosis. Published in PLOS ONE, separating presence from necessity is a useful discipline for cell biology claims. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003215:
Yau-Hua Yu, Hsu-Ko Kuo and Kuo-Wei Chang review gene expression work on a head and neck cancer in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Numerous studies were performed to illuminate mechanisms of tumour formation and spread from gene expression profiles of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. The objective of this review is to conduct a network-based meta-analysis to identify the underlying biological themes.

Readers get many single studies combined into one evolving transcriptome picture. A meta-analysis can show which signals repeat across labs and which were local noise. For a cancer with varied courses, shared network themes may point to more reliable markers.
plos-pone-0003315:
Chris Rae and co-authors test virus shells as tiny building blocks in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Cowpea mosaic virus is used more and more as a nanoparticle base: chemists attach many copies of a molecule to its outer shell. Uses range from sensors to drug carriers. Work with live virus, though, raises safety worries for such uses.

The team check whether virus particles killed by ultraviolet light can still be chemically addressed, tagged at set sites on the shell. Readers learn if dead particles keep the useful surface traits. Safe, inert shells are what virus-based nano tools need for real use.
plos-pone-0003415:
Jesper Ryge and colleagues profiled gene activity in rodent spinal cord cells in this 2008 paper. Brain studies often read gene patterns from whole chunks of tissue. That mixes many cell types into one blurred signal. The team instead separated two distinct groups of nerve cells first.

Gene chips then read which genes each group had switched on. The two profiles differed in clear and useful ways. Together they form a molecular fingerprint for each cell group. Such profiles help researchers study how the cord handles movement and feeling. Other teams can reuse the profiles when they study single cell types.
plos-pone-0003515:
Konrad U. Foerstner and co-authors hunted drug-making genes in environmental DNA in this 2008 paper. Polyketides are natural products behind many antibiotics and medicines. Giant enzymes called polyketide synthases build them step by step. The team focused on the type I subgroup of those enzymes.

They screened metagenomic shotgun data with a computational method. The screen estimated how often these synthase genes occur in nature. Finding them in raw habitat DNA skips culturing microbes first. Each hit is a lead toward tomorrow's medicines. Most microbes cannot be grown in labs, so DNA screens are often the only route.
plos-pone-0003615:
Kaisa Silander and co-authors compared heart disease genetics by sex in this 2008 study. Cardiovascular disease rates and burden differ markedly between women and men. Lifestyle factors differ too, but they do not fully explain the gaps. Genetic risk profiles offered another place to look.

The team found those genetic profiles differ between the sexes. Some variants mattered more for women, others for men. Sex-aware risk scoring may predict heart disease better. Prevention plans could likewise be tuned by genetic sex differences. Heart disease is the top killer of both sexes in most rich countries.
plos-pone-0003715:
M. Corrie Schoeman and David S. Jacobs published this bat ecology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Insect-eating bats live long, breed slowly, and face few predators. Forces like competition should therefore shape their communities strongly. So might the defenses of the insects they hunt.

Working in southern Africa, the authors weighed competition against prey defenses as shapers of bat ensembles. They compared the body and wing forms found together at sites with what each force predicts. The study tests which pressure, rivalry or prey armor, does more to decide which bats share a night sky.
plos-pone-0003815:
Jacqueline R. Weissman, Richard I. Kelley, Margaret L. Bauman, and colleagues published this cohort study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Earlier reports linked autism spectrum disorders with faults in mitochondrial energy production. One study claimed children with both diagnoses look just like other autistic children. Careful clinical data were scarce.

The authors analyzed a cohort of patients with autism spectrum disorder for mitochondrial disease. They compared features of those with confirmed mitochondrial problems against the wider group. The overlap suggests energy metabolism deserves a real place in the medical workup of autism.
plos-pone-0003915:
Lijan Lo, Zhenhai Zhang, Ni Hong, and co-authors catalogued gene activity in fish testes in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns the medaka, a small lab fish. Medaka is the first vertebrate whose sperm production was fully run in a dish. Studying that process lacked good molecular markers for each stage.

The team gathered 3,640 distinct gene clusters active in the medaka testis. Such a catalogue lets labs mark stages of sperm formation precisely. Many testis genes are shared across fish and mammals, they note. The list can guide studies of fertility in species far beyond medaka.
plos-pone-0004015:
Jasen Lee Gilge, Michael Fisher, and Yuh-Cherng Chai studied protein changes under oxidant stress in 2008. Cells defend themselves against oxidants in several ways. One protein response attaches glutathione to reactive cysteine sites. That change forms mixed disulfides on many proteins.

Their PLOS ONE article used HEK 293 cells to test what drives the change. Both oxidants and non-oxidant shifts in thiol levels played roles. The work separates causes that earlier studies had mixed together. Clearer chemistry helps explain how cells sense and survive oxidative stress. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004115:
James J. Bull and William R. Harcombe modeled nutrient sharing between microbes in 2009. Cross-feeding means species exchange nutrients with each other. It may start as waste sharing between neighbors. Or it may evolve as cooperation, like reciprocal altruism.

Their PLOS ONE article explores when cooperative cross-feeding can evolve. Population dynamics constrained that evolution in their models. Crowding and mixing decide whether sharers beat cheaters. The result helps explain the stable food webs seen in microbial communities. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004215:
Sophie Lebrecht and colleagues published this psychology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Implicit racial bias means attitudes toward other-race groups that sit outside conscious awareness. Alongside it sits the other-race effect: faces of other races are harder to tell apart than faces of one's own race.

The team asked whether perceptual training, practice at telling other-race faces apart, reduces implicit racial bias. Linking a perceptual skill to a social attitude would offer a new route to easing bias. The study tests whether learning to see faces as individuals changes how the mind judges a group.
plos-pone-0004315:
Isabel Martín Caballero and colleagues published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The molecular changes that occur when a neural stem cell switches from self-renewal to a committed lineage are not well understood. Control of gene expression clearly plays an important role in that switch, and DNA methylation is one of its tools.

The team examined three methyl-CpG binding proteins: Mecp2, Mbd2, and Kaiso. They report that these proteins are dispensable for mouse embryogenesis but play a redundant function in neural differentiation. Backup systems can hide a protein's importance until all the backups are removed.
plos-pone-0004415:
Brain scans in autism care raise an open question. Nathalie Boddaert, Mônica Zilbovicius, Anne Philipe, and co-authors report MRI findings in this 2009 PLOS ONE article. They studied seventy-seven children with non-syndromic autistic disorder.

The clinical relevance of MR scanning in these children is still debated. Past guidance judged MRI of insufficient value for standard clinical evaluation of autism. The authors present their findings against that backdrop and the evolution of the technology. Their catalog helps clinicians decide when a scan adds real value for a child. Seventy-seven children give the catalog weight, since single case reports cannot guide practice.
plos-pone-0004515:
How much exercise postmenopausal women did changed their weight, waist size, and the ways their bodies fought back, report Timothy Church, Corby Martin, Angela Thompson, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. It has been suggested that exercise triggers compensatory responses that eat into weight loss. Until now that idea had only been tested with large exercise doses.

The women in the study were sedentary and overweight. They were assigned different doses of exercise, and the team compared actual weight loss with what the exercise should have predicted. The gap between the two is the compensation. Measuring that gap at modest doses matters for honest advice: many people exercise faithfully and lose less than promised, and this work helps explain why.
plos-pone-0004615:
