One microbe may act as a whole work crew when it breaks down hard organic compounds, suggest Tatiana Karpinets, Dale Pelletier, Chongle Pan, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The microbe is Rhodopseudomonas palustris, known for its flexible way of life. Breaking down such compounds without oxygen is key both for making ethanol fuel and for cleaning up waste in the environment.

In nature, that work is most often done by mixed crews of microbes. The team profiled what this one microbe can eat and do. Their results suggest crews made of a single strain, with cells that share the same genes but split the work between them. If one strain can run the whole job, fuel making and clean-up systems become much simpler to build and run.
plos-pone-0004715:
Daniela Gaglio and colleagues showed that starving cancer like cells of glutamine traps them mid DNA copying, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Genes that drive cancer also rewire how cells use fuel. Cells changed by one such gene lean more on sugar burning and less on oxygen based energy than normal cells.

The team asked what happens when glutamine, a key building block, is removed. The cells stalled in the DNA copying phase, and adding DNA parts rescued them. The work shows a weak point in changed cells. It hints at diets or drugs that stress that weak point.
plos-pone-0004815:
Montse Garcia-Lavandeira and colleagues described a stem cell niche in the pituitary marked by GFRa2, Prop1, and stem markers, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The adult endocrine pituitary hosts several hormone producing cells regulating major physiological processes during life. Some candidates for progenitor and stem cells have been proposed, but pituitary cell renewal throughout life and its homeostasis were not well understood.

The niche description gives renewal a concrete location. Resident stem cells may repair hormone producing groups. Knowledge them could aid pituitary disorders. The niche concept extends to endocrine organs. Follow up work can check whether the same pattern appears in other settings. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0004915:
Shingo Iwami, Takafumi Suzuki, and Yasuhiro Takeuchi modeled the paradox of vaccination against avian flu epidemics, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Although vaccination can control avian influenza epidemics, it might engender emergence of vaccine resistant strains. Field and experimental studies show some strains acquire resistance against vaccination. Mathematical study defines conditions where vaccination paradoxically worsens long term outcomes by selecting escape variants in poultry groups.

Models warn imperfect vaccines need careful deployment. Resistance management parallels antibiotic stewardship. Surveillance must accompany poultry vaccination programs. Short term gains can seed long term risks. Future studies can use these results to refine both methods and theory. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is. Such work helps guide care, field work, and lab work in the years ahead.
plos-pone-0005015:
A rough start in life can leave hidden marks. Zebra finches that went hungry as chicks look fine as adults. Tobias Krause and colleagues tested them under stress. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The focus was early fasting in the first month of life. Adult females were the subjects.

Under stressful conditions, the early differences reappeared. Growth, reproduction and survival had all been touched by early nutrition. Stress exposed what calm conditions hid. Early conditions set a baseline that lasts. The finding links childhood hardship to adult fragility in birds. It echoes patterns seen in many animals, including humans.
plos-pone-0005115:
Spotting the exact T cells that respond to a threat is hard. Common methods use tetramers or surface markers. Nadesan Gajendran and colleagues built a new strategy in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used RAG-deficient mice, which lack their own lymphocytes. The mice were reconstituted with engineered cells. Those cells came from Pax5-deficient pro-B cells, altered by retrovirus.

The strategy identifies T cells that respond to any antigen. It does not need to know the antigen in advance. That is its advantage over tetramers. Immunologists gain a sharper way to find active fighters. The method could reveal responses that standard assays miss. It suits infections and vaccines where the key antigens are unknown.
plos-pone-0005215:
Rare animals and plants often fetch the highest prices, from exotic pets to trophy tourism. Angulo and Courchamp warned in PLOS ONE in 2009 that this love of rarity can itself drive species toward extinction. People will pay the high cost of hunting or trading the last few individuals.

As a species grows rarer, its price can rise, which rewards still harder exploitation. That loop can wipe out a species even while demand stays strong. The argument matters for trade rules, since protecting a species may require breaking the market reward for its rarity.
plos-pone-0005315:
SVOP is a protein found on vesicles that carry neurotransmitters in nerve cells. It resembles transporter proteins, as does its better-known relative SV2. Yao and Bajjalieh reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 that SVOP binds nucleotides.

Nucleotide binding is a concrete clue to what this vesicle protein does. Both SVOP and SV2 share structural similarity with the major facilitator family of small molecule transporters. A binding activity moves SVOP from mystery protein toward a defined role in how vesicles are loaded or controlled. A grip on small energy-rich bits of RNA is a strong hint that this protein may move or sense such bits as part of its day-to-day work in the nerve cell.
plos-pone-0005415:
Ewing's sarcoma family tumors are driven by a chimeric protein, EWS-FLI1, created by a chromosomal rearrangement. That fusion factor is thought to initiate the disease by rewiring gene activity. Kauer and colleagues built a molecular function map of the disease in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Earlier genomic profiling had identified many genes tied to EWS-FLI1. The map organizes those effects into functional networks, showing what the fusion protein actually does to the cell. A function-level roadmap of a childhood cancer can reveal weak points for therapy. Child bone cancer is rare and harsh, and its one driver gene is known. So a map of all that the driver does is the best guide yet for where a new drug might strike it down.
plos-pone-0005515:
Maria Xilouri and co-authors studied a protein linked to Parkinson's disease in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. In the disease, a protein called alpha-synuclein takes a harmful form and nerve cells die. Cells normally clear worn proteins through several clean-up routes.

The team found that the harmful form blocks one clean-up route, in which helper proteins hand targets to the cell's disposal units. With that route jammed, toxic material builds up inside nerve cells. Unblocking the route is one idea for slowing the disease. Other harmful proteins use the same clean-up route, so the block may matter beyond Parkinson's disease alone.
plos-pone-0005615:
Ronald Bonett and co-authors traced giant size in salamanders in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. The amphiuma family holds three species of long, water-dwelling salamanders with tiny limbs. Two of them rank among the largest salamanders on Earth.

The team used gene data to ask how giant size evolved in the family. Comparing the species and their kin shows whether bigness arose once or more than once. Giant, eel-like salamanders are odd enough that their history helps explain how amphibians can change body plan. Their great size comes with slow growth and late breeding, which makes these species easy to harm and slow to recover.
plos-pone-0005715:
Enken Drecoll and colleagues tested in 2009 a way to deliver radiation straight into tumor cells in the belly cavity. Cancers that spread across the peritoneum, the lining of the abdomen, are hard to treat. Alpha-particle radiation kills cells well but must not stray into healthy tissue.

The team attached a radioactive tag to a peptide that homes to tumors. The carrier aims to place the dose inside the tumor cell's nucleus, its control center. A hit there does the most damage to the cancer cell. The study checks whether this aimed delivery works as hoped in practice.
plos-pone-0005815:
Joseph Ivanic and co-authors warned in 2009 that protein abundance can distort maps of protein interactions. Labs chart which proteins bind which, building networks used across biology. But common, abundant proteins can swamp detection methods, faking or hiding links.

The team measured how abundance skews high-throughput interaction data. Some apparent hubs may just be plentiful proteins caught often by chance. Correcting for abundance cleans the networks that drug and systems research rely on. The study is a quality check for a whole data type, of the kind that quietly improves many later papers.
plos-pone-0005915:
Dan Wu, Chao-Yi Li, and De-Zhong Yao explored in 2009 a playful but pointed idea: turning brainwaves into music. Brain rhythms and musical rhythms resemble each other enough to tempt many scientists. Various rules have been tried to convert EEG traces into sound.

The team used the scale-free character of brain activity, a pattern where fluctuations look similar at many time scales, to compose their translation. Music built on that property may sound more natural than earlier attempts. Beyond art, hearing data can reveal patterns the eye misses. The paper sits where neuroscience, math, and music meet.
plos-pone-0006015:
Some protein webs can stretch to several times their length and still hold. Theodor Ackbarow, Dipanjan Sen, Christian Thaulow and colleagues asked in 2009 how they manage that feat. Their PLOS ONE paper studies networks built from alpha-helical proteins, the kind found in the cell's inner skeleton and in the shell around the nucleus.

Even with flaws in the web, the networks protect themselves and tolerate damage, the title reports. Their coiled building blocks unfold under strain instead of snapping, which spreads the load. That design lesson reaches beyond biology: engineers who want tough, forgiving materials can copy a trick that cells have used for ages.
plos-pone-0006115:
The prion protein is famous for a disease, yet its normal job stayed murky for years. Ajay Singh, Qingzhong Kong, Xiu Luo and colleagues found one of its jobs in iron handling in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies mice with the prion protein gene knocked out, building on earlier reports that the protein mediates cellular iron uptake and transport.

The knockout mice show altered iron metabolism, the title reports. A protein that helps cells take in iron, when it clumps in disease, could starve or flood cells of a metal they must hold in balance. The work gives the prion field a normal function to set against the protein's deadly fame.
plos-pone-0006215:
Growth factors that protect brain cells could help in Parkinson's disease, but delivering them into the brain is hard. Fanny Schmidt and colleagues screened small chemicals instead, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. They looked for compounds that act like neurotrophins, the natural protectors, on dopamine neurons grown in dishes.

Dopamine neurons are the cells lost in Parkinson's disease. Chemicals that mimic their natural support might be given as ordinary drugs, avoiding brain surgery. The screening found candidates with the desired protective activity. Early hits like these start the long path toward new Parkinson's treatments. The work shows cell culture can sort promise from noise.
plos-pone-0006315:
Two human proteins that help build new proteins are near twins, yet they favour different tissues. Dinesh Soares and colleagues modelled eEF1A1 and eEF1A2 in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The pair share most of their sequence but have different, overlapping functional profiles across cell types.

Structural models revealed two distinct surface clusters where their sequences vary. The models also suggest differences in where phosphate tags can attach. Surface patches decide which partners each twin can bind. The maps explain how near-identical proteins keep separate jobs. The maps give labs fresh leads for tests on each twin in turn.
plos-pone-0006415:
Stress may be contagious by smell, as alarm substances are in other mammals. Lilianne Mujica-Parodi and colleagues tested whether chemosensory cues to human stress activate the amygdala, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Alarm substances are airborne chemical signals that communicate emotional stress between members of a species.

Sweat samples from stressed donors triggered amygdala activity in others' brains. Humans thus detect conspecific stress by smell, like other mammals. The brain's alarm centre answers before conscious judgement. The finding opens research on unconscious social signalling in people. Scans of this kind show that smell can move the brain with no words at all.
plos-pone-0006515:
Thomas Rolland, Cécile Neuvéglise, Christine Sacerdot, and colleagues traced borrowed genes in yeast genomes for PLOS ONE in 2009. Horizontal gene transfer, genes moving between species, is occasionally mentioned in eukaryotic genomes. Such events appear much less numerous than in prokaryotes, where they play important functional roles. The team studied where transferred genes land in yeast genomes.

They found insertions within conserved syntenic regions, stretches where gene order is preserved between species. Where foreign genes settle may affect whether they survive. The work sharpens ideas about how yeast genomes evolve. It also shows that even mostly vertical inheritance has cross-currents.
plos-pone-0006615:
Bahram Jafar-Mohammadi and co-authors tested rare variants in a diabetes gene in PLOS ONE in 2009. There is considerable interest in the hypothesis that low frequency, intermediate penetrance variants contribute to type 2 diabetes susceptibility not found by common-variant scans. HNF1A is a gene where severe mutations cause a monogenic form of diabetes. The team examined low frequency variants in exons encoding only isoform A of HNF1A.

Their title reports these variants do not contribute to susceptibility to type 2 diabetes. Ruling out a plausible source sharpens the search elsewhere. Careful negative results prevent years of wasted follow-up.
plos-pone-0006715:
Gerhard Rammes and colleagues pinpointed a receptor region that changes how clozapine acts in PLOS ONE in 2009. Clozapine is a widely used drug for schizophrenia. It also strongly blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors. That blocking may contribute to its unusual clinical profile. The drug binds these receptors in several species.

The team searched for the domain that controls two drug properties. One property is kinetics, meaning how fast the drug acts and fades. The other is antagonistic potency, meaning how strongly it blocks. Finding the controlling region explains species differences in clozapine action. It may also guide design of cleaner drugs aimed at the same receptor.
plos-pone-0006815:
Karien E. A. Hack and colleagues followed the development of twins sharing one placenta in PLOS ONE in 2009. Monochorionic twins share a placenta with connecting blood vessels. Those connections raise risks of death and serious illness. Brain injury can follow blood flow disorders during pregnancy. Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome is the best-known danger.

The study matched monochorionic twins with dichorionic twins for comparison. It measured long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes in both groups. Long-term data matter more than birth outcomes for families. They show whether early risks leave lasting effects on learning and movement. The comparison gives doctors firmer ground for counseling parents.
plos-pone-0006915:
Joshua T. Herbeck and colleagues checked DNA typing accuracy in virus-transformed cell lines in PLOS ONE in 2009. Primary human cells are often limited for genetic studies. Lymphoblastoid cell lines supply DNA instead. They are made by infecting B cells with Epstein-Barr virus. Genome-wide studies rely on these lines heavily.

The team assessed fidelity of SNP array genotyping in such lines. Transformation could, in principle, distort the genome being typed. Any distortion would infect association study results. Their assessment tells researchers how far the lines can be trusted. Trustworthy DNA sources underpin the whole genome-wide association enterprise.
plos-pone-0007015:
E. Ray Dorsey, Joel Thompson, Melisa Carrasco, and colleagues audited research spending in PLOS ONE in 2009. They estimated United States biomedical research funding by disease area. Then they set that funding against the burden each disease causes. Finally, they counted the new drug approvals that followed from the investment.

Their window ran from 1995 to 2005. Approval counts came from the Food and Drug Administration. The comparison tests whether money follows need. Misalignment between funding and burden is a policy question, not just a budget one. Their tallies give reformers concrete numbers to argue from.
plos-pone-0007115:
Nitika Pant Pai, Milton Estes, Erica Moodie, and colleagues followed HIV patients through jail in PLOS ONE in 2009. Jails are key sites for HIV care, testing, and referral. In San Francisco County jail, infected inmates are offered antiretroviral treatment. Many take it only while inside. The team evaluated what that stop-start pattern does.

They tracked patients going in and out of the jail. Treatment given during custody had effects that carried beyond release, or faded. Their results argue for linking jail care with outside clinics. Interrupted therapy risks resistance, so continuity is a public health issue.
plos-pone-0007215:
Laurent Verkoczy, M. Anthony Moody, T. Matt Holl, and colleagues studied antibody targets on HIV-1 in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their focus is a region of the viral protein gp41 called the membrane proximal external region. That region attracts vaccine designers because antibodies can reach it.

Yet raising a protective antibody response against that region has proved very hard. The authors examine interactions with a restricted set of IgM B cell receptors. They ask whether basic recognition problems help explain past failures. Their work informs efforts to design a vaccine that finally uses this target.
plos-pone-0007315:
Astrid Rohrbeck and Jürgen Borlak used cancer genomics to track lung tumor progression in transgenic mice in 2009. Lung cancer is a leading cause of cancer illness and death. The authors study a mouse model where the signaling protein c-Raf is targeted to respiratory lining cells in the lungs.

Targeted c-Raf first produces dysplasia, abnormal but non-cancerous growth. Later it produces advanced lung adenocarcinomas. The authors identify regulatory gene networks tied to that transition. Their PLOS ONE networks may reveal which early lung lesions are most likely to become dangerous cancers in humans.
plos-pone-0007415:
Zhenfeng Duan, Edwin Choy, and Francis J. Hornicek identified a compound that reverses drug resistance in cancer in 2009. Multidrug resistance is a major factor in chemotherapy failure. Numerous efforts to overcome it had not yielded a tolerable and effective therapy when this study appeared in PLOS ONE.

The authors use a high-throughput cell-based screen. They identify a compound called NSC23925. They report it reverses multidrug resistance in their tests. A safe resistance reverser could restore the power of standard chemotherapy drugs. Their hit gives medicinal chemists a starting point for that long-sought therapy.
plos-pone-0007515:
Tara Kashav and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the DNA-copying machinery of Helicobacter pylori, the bacterium behind most stomach ulcers. Copying begins with DnaB helicase, a ring-shaped motor that unwinds the double helix. Its front section, the N-terminal domain, was poorly characterized. The team solved that domain's three-dimensional structure. They also mapped how the helicase interacts with its partner enzyme, the primase.

The structure shows the shape of the motor's front end in atomic detail. The interaction map shows where primase grips the helicase during replication. Together they expose the joint between two essential machines. A joint that the bacterium cannot live without is a candidate drug target. New antibiotics are badly needed as this bacterium grows drug-resistant. Structural work like this tells chemists exactly where to aim.
plos-pone-0007615:
Krishan Kumar and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a new angle against tuberculosis. The tuberculosis bacterium secretes proteins that help it cause disease. One, ESAT6, is a known virulence determinant involved from the start of infection. The team designed short peptides rich in the amino acid phenylalanine. They tested whether those peptides would bind ESAT6 tightly, and what binding would do to the pathogen.

The peptides latched onto ESAT6 and, at the same time, slowed the bacterium's growth. Blocking a secreted weapon outside the cell is a different tactic from classic antibiotics. It may also sidestep some resistance routes. Tuberculosis still kills over a million people a year, so fresh angles are needed. The study offers a candidate class of binders aimed at a single, important target.
plos-pone-0007715:
Bogdan Paun and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns colon tumors whose DNA repair is faulty, a state called microsatellite instability. In such tumors, short repeated DNA stretches gain or lose units. Those shifts can knock out genes and drive cancer growth.

Most screens look for shifts in the coding parts of genes. This team also searched the tail ends, the untranslated regions that tune gene use. They found frequent mutations in one gene, RIC1, in colon tumors. The result widens the search for cancer-driving changes beyond the usual coding regions.
plos-pone-0007815:
Inaki Comas and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It warns about the limits of typing methods for the TB bacterium. Mycobacterium tuberculosis varies very little in its DNA from strain to strain. Such monomorphic bacteria give standard genotyping tools little to grip.

Most current methods track mobile or repeated DNA elements instead. The authors used direct DNA sequencing to test those markers. Their data highlight where current methodologies fall short. The warning matters for epidemiology, since tracing outbreaks depends on telling strains apart. Better markers would sharpen TB control worldwide.
plos-pone-0007915:
Keith Hobson and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It uses chemical fingerprints to trace where declining ducks come from. Finding where migratory birds join breeding populations is a core goal of conservation. It is hardest for species breeding in remote northern areas.

The test case is the lesser scaup, a diving duck in North America. Stable isotopes in feathers record the waters where they grew. By reading those isotopes in harvested birds, the team inferred their origins. The method gives managers a map of which breeding grounds supply which hunting areas.
plos-pone-0008015:
Brian Fischer and colleagues modeled how owls place sounds in space, in PLOS ONE in 2009. An owl judges where a sound comes from by comparing the two ears: which ear hears it first, and which hears it louder. Brain cells combine those two cues.

The team showed the combination works by multiplying the cues, layer upon layer, across groups of cells. That layered math yields cells tuned to one spot in space. A clear model of the owl's trick may help engineers build hearing aids and robots that locate sound as sharply as the bird does.
plos-pone-0008115:
Jolanta Skalska and colleagues proposed a surface chemistry trick behind a plant compound's effects in PLOS ONE in 2009. The compound, parthenolide, comes from the feverfew plant and draws interest as a cancer fighter. It tunes the cell's redox balance, the push and pull of oxidation.

The team pointed to free thiols, sulfur groups sitting on cell surface proteins, as a key site of action. Changing those groups can change how a cell behaves and what it lets in. The surface site is a fresh angle on a compound long studied for inside-cell effects.
plos-pone-0008215:
Borna Müller and colleagues evaluated tests for bovine tuberculosis in Chad in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. The disease now mainly affects developing countries. In Africa it is present across nearly the whole continent. Yet accurate data on its spread remain scarce. Tests for the disease in cattle also lack solid evaluation.

The team used Bayesian methods to estimate how well several tests perform together. Receiver operating characteristic analysis compares tests without assuming a perfect standard. Better test estimates help veterinary services target control efforts. The work gives Chad rare, grounded numbers on cattle tuberculosis.
plos-pone-0008315:
Paula L. Diaz-Sylvester and Julio A. Copello studied heart calcium channels in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Ryanodine receptors release calcium that drives heart muscle contraction. Protamine, a small protein, was known to block the skeletal muscle version. It also inhibits calcium release in skeletal muscle preparations. The team extended those studies to the cardiac receptor, RyR2.

They placed RyR2 channels into artificial lipid bilayers to measure them. Protamine modulated the channels in a voltage-dependent way. Such detail matters because protamine is used in heart surgery. Knowing its channel effects helps predict its actions in patients.
plos-pone-0008415:
Paul A. Baldock and colleagues used knockout mice to study bone and body weight in PLOS ONE in 2009. Changes in body energy levels are closely linked to body weight and bone mass. Hypothalamic signals in the brain help regulate bone mass. They do so in line with the brain's perception of energy status. Mice lacking neuropeptide Y, or NPY, were the test case.

Without NPY, the coordination of bone mass to body weight broke down. NPY thus plays a central role in matching skeleton to body size. The brain, not just local forces, sets bone mass. That insight may inform osteoporosis treatments.
plos-pone-0008515:
Tao Sun and co-authors model wound healing in skin in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They focus on TGF-beta1, a key factor in epidermal wound repair. Lab and animal studies give it a paradoxical picture. It stimulates migration of keratinocytes, the main skin cells. Yet it also inhibits their proliferation, or growth in number. Both effects seem needed, but how they fit together was unclear. The team build a 3D multiscale computer model.

The model of the human epidermis lets them visualize both effects at once. Migration and growth inhibition play out in different zones and times. That spatial split reconciles the paradox. The model can test healing strategies in silico.
plos-pone-0008615:
Satyendra Kumar and co-authors test RNA therapy against a brain virus in mice in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Chandipura virus causes encephalitis in parts of India. It strikes children in epidemic and sporadic forms. The disease follows a rapid course with very high mortality. No specific treatment exists for it. The team test RNA interference, using small RNA to silence a viral gene. They target the P gene of the virus and deliver siRNA into the brain.

Intracranial administration protects mice from lethal Chandipura encephalitis. Silencing one viral gene is enough to save the animals. That proof of principle offers hope where no drugs exist. RNA therapy might serve other rapid viral brain infections too.
plos-pone-0008715:
Sarah Coleman, Chunlin Cai, Nisse Kalkkinen, and colleagues examined the tail end of a brain receptor part. Their study came out in PLOS ONE in 2010. AMPA receptors carry much of the fast talk between nerve cells. Placing the right receptor parts at a synapse strengthens that talk. A part called GluA4 has a long tail that may dock with helper proteins.

PDZ proteins are common docking helpers at synapses. The team tested whether the GluA4 tail truly binds them. Their assays weigh a small detail with large effects on learning circuits. Knowing the docking rules helps explain how synapses adjust strength.
plos-pone-0008815:
Rong-Yong Man, Taishi Onodera, Emi Komatsu, and colleagues studied a revved-up antibody response in engineered mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Memory B cells mostly carry IgG-type receptors. Naive B cells normally carry IgM or IgD types. The IgG receptor signals differently from its naive cousins. Mice engineered to carry IgG early let the team isolate that signal's role.

Their B cells answered antigen more strongly than normal naive cells. Oddly, the boost came without the usual antigen-triggered signaling step. A shortcut pathway may explain memory cells' speed. Understanding it helps explain why booster shots work so fast.
plos-pone-0008915:
Mark Little, Wolfgang Heidenreich, and Guangquan Li laid out theory for when model parameters can actually be known. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Models of complex biology can carry dozens of parameters. Some cannot be pinned down from data, no matter how much is gathered. Such parameters are called unidentifiable. Redundant parameters can also be merged without changing predictions. Modelers often discover these traps only after wasted effort.

Their theoretical treatment gives tests to spot trouble early. Checking identifiability before fitting saves time and false confidence. Any field leaning on big fitted models benefits, from epidemiology to cell biology. The paper serves as a rulebook for honest modeling.
plos-pone-0009015:
Richard Koup and co-authors tested a two-step vaccine plan against HIV, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A vaccine must raise both antibodies and T cells tuned to HIV-1. Prime-boost plans use two different vaccine types in sequence. Earlier animal work showed such mixes can raise strong, broad T-cell responses.

The team primed with a DNA vaccine, then boosted with an adenoviral vector vaccine. The DNA first step made the boost work harder. Both antibody levels and T-cell responses against HIV-1 grew stronger. Better priming could stretch the power of vaccines that are weak alone.
plos-pone-0009115:
Jessica Yorzinski and Michael Platt tracked people's eyes to see how watching others shapes desire, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mate-choice copying means judging possible partners by the choices others make. Animals from fish to humans show this copying behaviour. The mental machinery behind the copying in humans was unknown.

Men and women viewed a series of photographs while their gaze was recorded. A face that viewers of the same sex gazed at longer grew more attractive. Attention, it seems, is the channel through which the copying flows. We borrow not just each other's choices but the focus of each other's eyes.
plos-pone-0009215:
Antoine Nougairede and co-authors published this diagnostics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. When the 2009 swine flu pandemic spread, large-scale screening was soon dropped in France. Hospitals still needed fast answers for the patients in front of them. The team set up a different approach for the public hospitals of Marseille.

Starting at the end of June 2009, they ran a point of care strategy for the new virus. Samples were tested rapidly where patients were treated, instead of being shipped to central labs. Fast results let doctors isolate and treat cases without long waits. The study describes how the system worked as a model for pandemic testing.
plos-pone-0009315:
Mauro D'Amato and co-authors published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A gene called NPSR1, for the neuropeptide S receptor, had been tied to asthma and bowel inflammation. The receptor also works in the brain, shaping anxiety and stress responses. It appears in immune cells and lungs as well.

The team tested whether variants in NPSR1 also play a role in rheumatoid arthritis. That disease is another long-running inflammation, this time of the joints. A gene shared across several inflammatory diseases would point to common wiring. Their analysis checks arthritis against this candidate, adding one more piece to the genetics of inflammation.
plos-pone-0009415:
Li-Fong Seet and co-authors published this glaucoma surgery study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Glaucoma raises pressure inside the eye and slowly steals sight. Filtration surgery drains fluid to lower that pressure. The surgery often fails because the body scars over the new drain.

The team used mice lacking SPARC, a protein involved in tissue repair and scarring. In their new mouse model of the surgery, SPARC deficiency improved surgical survival. Less scarring kept the drain working longer. The result marks a target: calming SPARC after surgery might keep human glaucoma operations working too.
plos-pone-0009515:
Anna Sawka and colleagues reviewed trials on hip fracture prevention in nursing homes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Older residents of long term care face a high risk of breaking a hip. A break can lead to death or lasting loss of independence. Many prevention ideas exist, from vitamin D to hip pads. It was unclear which had solid proof in this setting.

The review gathered the randomized trials done in long term care homes. It mapped what has been tested and how strong the proof is. Gaps stood out where popular practices rest on thin evidence. The map can guide carers and policy makers toward steps that truly help frail residents.
plos-pone-0009615:
Kosuke Yoshihara and co-authors built a survival forecast for ovarian cancer in PLOS ONE in 2010. Serous ovarian cancer found at an advanced stage is hard to treat. Doctors lack strong tools to tell who will do well and who will not. The team read gene activity in tumors from patients. From those patterns they built a profile meant to predict survival.

They then tested the profile on a second, independent set of patients. It held up across both data sets, which is the real test of such a tool. A sound gene based forecast could guide how hard to treat each patient. It could also spare some patients treatment that is unlikely to help.
plos-pone-0009715:
Breast cancer cells cut off from growth factors must survive without their usual fuel signals. Yan Cheng and colleagues studied how such starved cells protect themselves. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The cells relied on autophagy, a process where a cell eats parts of itself for fuel. A protein called elongation factor-2 kinase helped drive that self-eating. The process shielded the cancer cells and kept them alive under stress. Blocking it could make growth-blocking therapies hit harder. The finding names a possible weak point in stubborn tumors.
plos-pone-0009815:
Cyclosporine is a drug best known for calming the immune system after transplants. Fiona Fernandes and colleagues found another action for it against hepatitis C. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hepatitis C is a virus that attacks the liver.

The drug blocked a direct interaction between cyclophilins and NS5A, a hepatitis C virus protein. Cyclophilins are helper proteins found in human cells. Blocking that contact points to a route for stopping the virus. The finding supports drug ideas that target host proteins the virus needs. Hepatitis C still lacks a vaccine.
plos-pone-0009915:
Immune cells called thymocytes mature in the thymus before joining the body's defenses. Li-Ying Liou and colleagues studied a sugar coating those young cells cannot develop without. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The coating is the functional glycosylation of dystroglycan, sugars attached to a surface protein. Glycosylation means adding sugar chains that change how a protein works. Thymocytes become T cells, central players in immunity. Without that sugar work, thymocyte development faltered. The result links a surface detail to the making of immune cells. The thymus sits just above the heart.
plos-pone-0010015:
The authors were Xixi Zhou, Peiwei Han, Jiangmei Li, and others. In 2010 they presented a lab method for measuring a subtle protein change. The change is S-nitrosation, where a nitric oxide based group attaches to a protein. It is a key route for nitric oxide signaling, yet measuring the body's own levels has been hard.

Their method, named ESNOQ, aims to count these modified proteins as they occur in real samples. A reliable count lets researchers link the change to health and disease with far less guesswork. The paper's value lies in the tool itself and in the studies it makes possible.
plos-pone-0010215:
The authors were Saroj Mohapatra, Amir Guri, Montse Climent, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used mice with experimental bowel inflammation. A receptor called PPAR gamma sits in gut lining cells and immune cells of the colon. Such receptors are thought to modulate inflammation and immune responses in the gut, which fail in inflammatory bowel disease.

The team focused on PPAR gamma in epithelial cells, the colon's surface layer. They tested how that receptor in those cells alone regulates nearby immune activity. A lining-specific effect would point to drugs that act at the gut surface, limiting wider side effects.
plos-pone-0010315:
Deborah Pain, Ruth Cromie, Julia Newth and others published a health study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject was lead left inside game animals shot with lead bullets or lead shot. People who eat wild game were long thought to face little risk from this source. Most eaters, after all, spit out or avoid whole pellets.

Newer evidence, the authors explain, shows that bullets often break apart when they hit. Tiny lead bits can spread through the meat, far from the wound. Those bits are small enough to be swallowed without notice. Because lead harms both animals and people, even small extra doses matter. The study frames game meat as a route of exposure worth measuring with care.
plos-pone-0010415:
Michelle Berny and colleagues mapped clotting factors on blood clots formed under flow, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Making thrombin, the enzyme that builds clots, is central to vein clot formation. In still plasma, platelets that expose a certain surface lipid support that process. Blood in veins, though, moves and shears. The team asked where key factors sit on clots formed under such flow.

They tracked factor Xa, thrombin, and fibrin, the clot's mesh protein. Their locations under flow may differ from textbook still-plasma pictures. Drugs that prevent vein clots must work in flowing blood, not test tubes. Maps like this help aim those drugs. The study brings clot science closer to real circulation.
plos-pone-0010515:
Elena Kondratieva and colleagues used special mice to study lung lumps that form in TB-like infections, for PLOS ONE in 2010. Those lumps, called granulomas, are balls of immune cells. They wall off germs, yet they also harm lung tissue. How host genes shape them was not well known. The team crossed mouse strains with opposite traits. One strain resisted one germ but not the other, and the cross flipped that pattern.

That neat setup helps isolate the genes that matter for each germ. The lung disease in these mice looked much like human disease. Good animal mirrors of human lung illness are rare and prized. They let researchers test how the lumps both help and harm. The study provides such a mirror, plus the gene tools to probe it.
plos-pone-0010615:
Lakshmanane Boominathan reported a wider job for famous tumor suppressor proteins, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The proteins p53, p63, and p73 guard cells against cancer. They were known to switch genes on and off directly.

The study found they also control the machinery that builds microRNAs. MicroRNAs are tiny molecules that fine-tune hundreds of other genes. When the suppressors fail, that fine-tuning breaks down too. The wider role helps explain why losing p53 has such sweeping effects. It also suggests new paths for drugs that might restore lost control in tumors.
plos-pone-0010715:
Bernard Paule and colleagues looked for blood signs that predict kidney cancer drug response, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sunitinib blocks blood vessel growth and can shrink kidney cancers that have spread. Only some patients gain from it, while all face its side effects.

Soluble forms of the vessel growth factor VEGF were measured in patients' blood. Certain forms and levels lined up with better response to the drug. A blood test given before treatment could steer patients toward or away from months of hard therapy. Trials that sort patients first also read out faster and more fairly.
plos-pone-0010815:
Dardo Tomasi and colleagues mapped brain connections in people addicted to cocaine, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cocaine is known to disturb dopamine signaling, the brain's reward currency. How that disturbance ripples into wider brain function was less clear. The midbrain, where dopamine cells sit, talks to nearly every major brain region.

Brain scans showed the midbrain's functional links were weakened in cocaine users. Regions for attention, control, and memory were among those less in step. Addiction thus looks like a network disorder, not just a reward disorder. Treatments that retrain whole networks, not only craving, gain support from maps like these.
plos-pone-0010915:
Laurent-Herve Perez, Matt Butler, Tammy Creasey and co-authors published this gut immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Nod2 is a protein that senses bacteria inside cells, and mutations in its sensing region are tied to Crohn's disease, a chronic bowel inflammation. The authors asked what those mutations actually break, beyond sensing itself.

Working with purified pieces of the protein, they found that healthy Nod2 directly attacks bacteria: it binds them, disrupts their membranes, and disturbs their metabolism. Versions carrying Crohn's-linked mutations were generally poor at this killing. Related sensing proteins showed the same direct antibiotic activity. Perez and colleagues reframe Nod2 from a passive alarm into a weapon, suggesting Crohn's may begin when the gut loses a layer of direct bacterial control.
plos-pone-0011015:
Leslie Kozak, Susan Newman, Pei-Min Chao and co-authors published this nutrition study in PLOS ONE in 2010. What a mammal eats in its first days can set lifelong disease risk, a phenomenon called nutritional programming. The authors proposed that early feeding fixes a pattern of gene activity in fat tissue that later waxes and wanes with adult energy balance.

They overfed and underfed newborn mice, then tracked body fat and gene expression in fat at several ages, including after a high-fat diet in adulthood. Undernutrition sharply suppressed insulin and reshaped expression in gene networks tied to caveolae, tiny flask-shaped structures in cell membranes. Kozak and colleagues identify a structural gene network in fat that remembers early nutrition. That memory may explain why early deprivation raises later obesity risk when food becomes plentiful.
plos-pone-0011115:
Chen, Gracheva, Yu and colleagues studied fruit fly embryos in PLOS ONE in 2010. They looked at a protein called neurexin where nerves meet muscles. In a growing embryo, those junctions must form in the right place and shape for movement to work.

The team traced what neurexin does as these junctions are built. Their results show part of the blueprint that wires nerve to muscle early in life. Fruit flies share many wiring genes with humans, so the lessons apply broadly. The work aids science on how brains and bodies connect during development.
plos-pone-0011215:
Nachman, Gish, Virag and colleagues mapped peptide shapes in PLOS ONE in 2010. A domain in the Src protein reads phosphate tagged pieces of other proteins, passing growth signals in cells. To block that reading in cancer, designers must know the exact shapes those pieces take when bound.

The team mapped which shapes the bound peptides prefer. Those structural rules guide the design of blockers that fit the domain precisely. Src signaling drives several cancers, so better blockers have wide value. The study turns loose chemical pieces into a shape based blueprint for drug design.
plos-pone-0011315:
Delogu, De Marco, Di Trani and colleagues asked how wild birds catch flu in PLOS ONE in 2010. Waterbirds are the natural home of influenza A viruses. Preening, when birds clean and oil their feathers with their bills, was tested as a possible route by which virus on feathers or water reaches the bird.

If preening contributes to infection, surveillance should account for it alongside drinking contaminated water. Understanding every spread route sharpens bird flu watch programs. Wild bird monitoring warns farms and health agencies of coming outbreaks. The study adds a plausible, everyday behavior to the list of transmission paths to check.
plos-pone-0011415:
Ross Vanderwert and co-authors measured brain activity in 2010 in children who had suffered severe neglect early in life. Children raised in deprived institutions show lasting changes in how the brain handles emotion and attention. A foster care program moved some children into families, and the team asked whether the age at which a child was rescued still showed in the brain years later.

Brain wave measures differed with the timing of the move: children placed in family care earlier showed patterns closer to typical development. That timing effect is strong evidence that the young brain has a window when rescue helps most. The finding supports policies that place neglected children in families as early as possible. It also gives science a rare, ethical window into how early experience sculpts the human brain.
plos-pone-0011515:
Flavia Autore and co-authors reconciled in 2010 two conflicting portraits of a human anti-HIV protein. APOBEC3G attacks HIV by damaging its genetic code, and drug designers want its true shape. Crystallography, which freezes the protein in a crystal, and NMR, which watches it in solution, had given structures that disagreed in worrying places.

Running molecular dynamics simulations, computer movies of the protein's motion, the team showed how the two views can both be honest snapshots of a flexible molecule. The merged picture explains the clash instead of declaring one method wrong. A truer shape matters because blockers and boosters are designed against it. The study also models a healthy habit for structural biology: when two trusted methods disagree, motion, not error, is often the missing term.
plos-pone-0011615:
Joseph Forbi and co-authors reconstructed the history of hepatitis B in two rural Nigerian communities, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Infection with this liver virus is extremely common in Nigeria, but where it came from and how it spread there had remained a puzzle. The two communities studied are remote and partly isolated.

By sequencing virus samples and building their family tree, the team traced the outbreak history and how the virus changed over time. Their reconstruction shows separate local patterns shaped by isolation. Such histories help health planners understand long-standing infections and design control efforts that fit local conditions.
plos-pone-0011715:
Gregor Ilc and co-authors solved the structure of a disease-linked human prion protein, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Prion diseases are fatal brain disorders caused when the normal prion protein misfolds and piles up. Inherited forms arise from mutations in the protein's gene, including one called Q212P that swaps a single building block.

Using nuclear magnetic resonance, the team determined the mutant protein's three-dimensional shape. The structure shows unique features not seen in the normal form. Seeing how one small change reshapes the protein helps explain why it turns harmful and may guide future treatments.
plos-pone-0011815:
Qiana Matthews and co-authors built a new kind of HIV vaccine carrier, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Adenovirus shells are used to carry vaccine cargo for cancer and for germ diseases. The standard design makes the body build the target antigen from an added gene, but in some cases that route falls short.

This team set HIV antigen straight into a loose loop of the shell protein hexon. A carrier that shows the antigen on its face from the start may train immunity in a new way. The hope is to teach the body to spot HIV before infection can take hold.
plos-pone-0011915:
Chanyarat Paungfoo-Lonhienne and colleagues reported in 2010 that plants can take in microbes as food, reversing the usual picture of who eats whom in soil. Soil microbes and plant roots compete hard for nutrients, and that contest sets how much plant growth an ecosystem can support. Textbooks cast plants as producers and microbes as decomposers on opposite sides.

The experiments show plant roots consuming microbes and drawing nutrients from them. That direct route helps explain how plants in poor soils still get fed when free nutrients are scarce. It also reframes the root zone as a hunting ground, with consequences for how fertilizers and soil life are managed on farms.
plos-pone-0012015:
Silverio Perrotta and colleagues told in 2010 of a family whose blood runs too thick with red cells. The cause is a hormone switch stuck in the on pose. The switch hears the call of erythropoietin, the hormone that orders new red cells to be made. Stuck-on forms of the switch are the chief cause of a rare inborn ill in which the blood grows far too rich in red cells.

In this family the stuck switch did more than flood the blood. It bent the path of young blood stem cells as they chose their fate. It also raised the count of cells that go on to line the walls of veins and arteries. One fault thus speaks to both the blood and the tubes it flows through. Such families are gifts to science: a single gene fault that lays bare a switch's whole job.
plos-pone-0012115:
Robert Kirmse, Zhao Qin, Carl Weinert, and colleagues examined the building blocks of cell fibers in PLOS ONE in 2010. These fibers, called intermediate filaments, form part of the inner frame that gives cells their shape. In a test tube they grow from small protein units into threads thinner than a hair yet several micrometers long, and the team watched how those units bend and flex.

The units proved able to change shape far more than a rigid building block would. That flexibility may explain how the fibers stay tough while being stretched and squeezed inside living cells. Knowing how the parts move helps scientists model whole fibers and the diseases that strike when they fail.
plos-pone-0012215:
Robert Robinson, Becki Lawson, Mike Toms, and co-authors documented bird declines caused by a new disease in Britain, in PLOS ONE in 2010. New infections are often blamed when wildlife falls, yet hard proof that a disease, rather than food or habitat loss, emptied a region is rare. Garden bird counts and post-mortem records gave this team an unusual chance to test the claim for common British birds.

Their evidence shows an emerging infectious disease driving rapid falls in once-common species. Proving disease can do this to abundant birds, not just rare island ones, changes the risk picture for wildlife everywhere. It also argues for monitoring backyard birds as an early alarm for new infections.
plos-pone-0012315:
Lev Prasov, Nadean Brown, and Tom Glaser scrutinized a retinal gene's message processing in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene, called Math5 or Atoh7, switches on briefly as retinal cells leave division, and it is essential for making ganglion cells, the eye's output neurons to the brain. Its message is made from a single exon, a simple design, and mice without the gene grow retinas almost entirely missing those output cells.

Their critical analysis checks claims about how that message is spliced in the developing mouse retina. In a field where one gene decides an entire cell type's existence, the exact form of its message matters. Settling the record prevents other labs from building on a splicing pattern that may not be real.
plos-pone-0012415:
Maria Motta, Carolina Catta-Preta, Sergio Schenkman and colleagues filmed a bacterium that lives inside another cell dividing in step, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The host, Crithidia deanei, is a single-celled parasite relative that carries a bacterial tenant it cannot live without. In such hosts, division must copy the nucleus, the DNA granule, and the tenant in the right order.

The team showed that the tenant bacterium divides in tight coordination with the host nucleus. That sync keeps each daughter cell supplied with its tenant. Studying this partnership helps explain how lasting cell tenants evolve, the same road that long ago produced mitochondria, the energy parts of our own cells.
plos-pone-0012515:
Ofra Benny, Kei Nakai, Takeru Yoshimura and colleagues tested a broad vessel-blocking treatment for eye diseases, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Wet age-related macular degeneration blinds older adults when abnormal vessels grow and leak under the retina. Current drugs target one growth factor, VEGF, and need repeated eye injections, so broader blockers are sought.

Their treatment hit neovascularization across models, aiming wider than single-factor drugs. A broad antiangiogenic agent could help patients who respond poorly to VEGF blockers alone. Eye disease is a proving ground for vessel drugs, since success can be photographed directly in the living retina.
plos-pone-0012615:
Liao, Gock, Michie and co-authors asked whether a tiny worm can smell the chemicals given off by explosives. Finding hidden explosives from a distance is a hard safety problem. The roundworm C elegans carries a huge family of smell receptor genes, far more than its simple body suggests.

Their 2010 tests gave both behaviour and genetic evidence that the worm detects those vapours. A living sensor of that kind could one day be built into cheap detection tools. The study also shows how much sensing power sits in a worm with only a small set of nerve cells.
plos-pone-0012715:
Mayorek, Naftali-Shani and Grunewald tested an old pain drug against pancreatic cancer in mice. Diclofenac has been in pharmacy use for decades as an anti-inflammatory. Besides its known targets, it blocks other enzymes tied to inflammation and growth signals.

Their 2010 mouse study found the drug slowed tumour growth, partly by changing VEGF levels and arginase activity in the tumour setting. Pancreatic cancer has few working treatments, so any cheap, known drug with an effect earns attention. The work supports trials of drug reuse in this disease.  The authors link both shifts to the slower growth they measured in treated mice.
plos-pone-0012815:
Halton, Cook, Paterson and co-authors priced a bundle of care steps meant to stop infections from central vein lines. A central venous catheter feeds drugs and fluids into a large vein, but the line can also carry germs into the blood. Hospitals were being urged to use a fixed bundle of hygiene steps every time.

Their 2010 analysis weighed the bundle's costs, including its consumables, against the infections it prevents. Bundle steps are cheap beside the cost of one blood infection, yet hospitals still need proof before adopting them widely. Their figures make the economic case concrete.
plos-pone-0330015:
Maxwell Ateni Assibi and his team set out a plan for a study in Ghana. The site is the University for Development Studies. There, health trainees learn by work in the towns they will serve. Such town-based work is a fine place to teach mixed crews to act as one team. Yet few have asked how the trainees and staff feel about it.

The plan calls for one-on-one talks with last-year trainees and staff of two town schemes. The team will sort the talks by theme and check the themes back with those who spoke. They hope to learn what helps, what blocks, and how team drills could be built in with more care.
plos-pone-0343915:
Karambu Kiende Gatimbu and Paul Njiru Nthakanio study Kenya's housing drive. Can the national programme last? Their work covers Meru and Embu counties. It appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Two hundred and fifteen people rated the programme. They were residents, academics, and builders. They scored its economic, social, and green performance. The drive was launched to close a severe housing shortage. That shortage hits low- and middle-income families hardest.

Respondents praised better affordability and social safety. But green design lagged behind. So did use of local materials and real public input. Older respondents prized safety and sound basic services. Postgraduates prized green features. The authors urge stronger public involvement. They also want green building standards. Both should come before the programme grows further.
plos-pone-0344615:
Anna M Knochel, Mark V Erdmann, and co-authors attached satellite tags to reef manta rays in Papua New Guinea's Samarai Islands, the first tracking of this population. Reef mantas roam tropical Indo-Pacific waters, yet their local habits decide whether tourism and protection plans can work. Their 2026 study followed ten adults for up to six months across two monsoon seasons, recording horizontal travel and dive depth.

The rays proved homebodies: three quarters of their positions fell within ten kilometers of the tagging site, and none wandered beyond about eighty-seven kilometers. Shallow water rich in plankton pigment drew them most. They adjusted their diving to the ocean's mixed surface layer, going deeper when that layer thinned. The authors say such loyalty to place supports site-based tourism and local management.
plos-pone-0344915:
Tayyaba Shehzad and colleagues built the first paired sentence collection for simplifying Punjabi written in the Shahmukhi script. Shahmukhi is one of the two main scripts for Punjabi, yet computer tools have largely ignored it. Each hard sentence in the new collection sits beside a plainer version that keeps the meaning with clearer words and form.

An automatic system trained and tested on the pairs rewrote hard sentences with strong scores on a standard quality measure for simplification. Human aims stayed central: keep the sense, drop needless difficulty, and help readers who struggle with formal text. The collection opens a path for reading aids, school tools, and wider access to written Punjabi in daily life.
plos-pone-0346515:
Roshan Puri, Lucia R Levers, and Amit K Pradhananga valued the control of invasive species in fresh water, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Invaders choke lakes and rivers, harming native life and recreation, and removing them costs real money. The team used a survey method that asks people what such management is worth to them.

Puri's contingent valuation turns those answers into estimates of economic benefit. Policymakers can set those benefits beside program costs when arguing budgets. Invasive species work is often funded after damage is obvious and control is dear. A hard cost-benefit case for acting early helps agencies move sooner, when prevention is still cheap and ecosystems can still recover.
plos-pone-0347415:
Zhongqun Guo and co-workers use helpful bacteria to harden and clean up waste piles left by rare earth mining. The tailings are weak as soil and laced with heavy metals that can wash away. Their 2026 study treats samples with a microbe that forms a chalky mineral, varying the feeding solution and metal load to see what works best.

Strength rose with the amount of mineral formed, reaching its peak at the strongest feeding mix. Leaching of heavy metals dropped sharply after treatment. Under the microscope, lumps of mineral had trapped metals inside, locking them in place. The method could turn loose, polluted waste into firmer, safer ground, though scaling it up needs more work.
plos-pone-0348015:
Juliet Furaha Karisa and co-workers take stock of coral reef repair efforts across the Western Indian Ocean. Reefs there are badly degraded, and local repair projects remain small and scattered. Their 2026 review draws on published studies, online sources, a survey of practitioners, and a regional workshop to gather lessons and judge current practice.

Twenty-two active projects ran across eight countries, most involving local communities closely. Nearly all grew coral by fragments, a cheap method, while breeding from eggs stayed rare. Watching results varied a lot, and few projects tracked social or economic gains. The review fed into a new regional network meant to help projects share methods and grow.
plos-pone-0348115:
Sheila Timp, Nicky van Foreest, and Willem van Rhenen asked whether the professional guiding a sick employee back to work changes how long the absence lasts. They analysed more than thirty thousand mental health related absence cases in the Netherlands, where occupational health professionals coach workers through recovery and return. A multilevel statistical model separated the professional's influence from that of the worker, the employer, and the sector.

The professional mattered a lot. Under the most effective professionals, typical absences lasted eighteen weeks or less; under the least effective, twenty-eight weeks or more. Employers mattered too. The authors urge professionals and organisations to coordinate, and call for research into which habits make the difference.
plos-pone-0348215:
Jeyalakshmi Kandhavelu, Clement Penny, and co-authors tested two old drugs, used together, against colon cancer cells grown in the lab. One drug, valproic acid, loosens how DNA is packed, and the other, zebularine, blocks a process that silences genes. Their 2026 study treated an early-stage and a late-stage colon cancer cell line and tracked two genes that help control cell growth.

Together the drugs slowed cancer cell growth more than either drug alone. They raised levels of a protective gene, strongly in the late-stage cells, while lowering a growth-driving gene in a dose-linked way. Treated cells also showed signs of orderly self-destruction. The authors say the pairing deserves further study as a possible low-cost way to fight colon cancer, though all tests so far are in dishes, not patients.
plos-pone-0348315:
Zhaohua Chai and Na Yang asked how art founders dare to try bold new work with so little cash. Most studies of this kind look at big tech firms. Their survey reached two hundred three art founders in China. It used tools that hunt for mixes of traits, not lone causes.

No one trait proved a must. Three mixes led to bold work. One lined up skills inside the firm. One seized a chance from outside. One sensed a tech shift and moved fast. The team says there is more than one road to the same peak, which should cheer small art firms.
plos-pone-0348515:
Hao Tang and his team hunted for genes that weak bone and bad kidneys share. The two ills often strike the same people. The team mined large gene data sets with smart tools. Four hub genes rose to the top of the list. They then checked these genes in mice bred with each ill.

All four genes split sick from well with high marks. One gene did best of all. In the mouse checks, all four genes dimmed in weak bone. In bad kidneys, three of the four rose. The genes also tied to immune cells in the blood. The team sees drug targets and test marks here.
plos-pone-0348615:
Shinhaeng Cho and colleagues compared two ways of checking radiotherapy plans on a modern ring-shaped treatment machine. One method uses the machine's own built-in imaging panel to verify each beam separately; the other uses an external phantom device to verify the combined dose. Both were run on prostate, throat, and breast cases, then stressed by deliberately shifting the treatment centre to see which check caught the error.

Both methods agreed excellently under standard scoring rules. The phantom check reacted more sharply to shifts, while the panel check scored consistently higher and steadier, so steady that its natural pass rates sat far above the conventional alarm thresholds. The authors conclude the panel method is a dependable clinical alternative, provided departments set their own tighter limits for it.
plos-pone-0348715:
Ryan SangBaek Kim studies how people writing about relationships online balance story detail against raw feeling. The 2026 study draws on more than three hundred fifty thousand English posts from support communities. Each story is scored for how built out it is. Each is also scored for how intense its expressed emotion sounds. The gap between the two scores is the focus.

Most posts kept story and feeling fairly matched, but three smaller patterns appeared often enough to count as real styles. Some writers poured out feeling with little story, some built detailed stories with muted feeling, and some showed feeling with almost no story support. A chatbot tested the same way covered a narrower range and hugged the matched middle. Human telling, it seems, keeps room to pull back or lean in.
plos-pone-0349015:
Isac Davidson Santiago Fernandes Pimenta and Grasiela Piuvezam set out a plan to audit safety gauges in intensive care. Such gauges track harm to patients. Yet many were never built or checked in a sound way. Bad gauges make fair contrast between hospitals moot. This 2026 paper is a protocol. It fixes the method in print before the work starts.

The team will search seven databases plus grey sources. They seek studies that build or test care safety gauges. Two staff will screen each study on their own. Set tools will judge study and gauge quality. Gauges will be sorted by type and by unit, from newborn to heart care. The aim is a sound, shared set for the field.
plos-pone-0349115:
Ingunn Fride Tvete and Marianne Klemp followed more than thirty-six thousand Norwegian women with breast cancer to show how the meaning of a risk factor changes with time since diagnosis. Standard survival models assume each factor's effect stays constant, which may mislead over long horizons. Their 2026 registry study compared cancer deaths against other deaths across tumor subtypes, body weight, and treatments, letting effects vary over time.

The most aggressive subtypes carried over triple the cancer death hazard of the reference group in the first three years, but that excess largely faded or shrank in later years. Radiation's protective effect likewise peaked early and then dwindled. Body weight groups showed no difference in cancer mortality. The authors warn that fixed-effect models can badly misstate long-term prognosis.
plos-pone-0349215:
Anna Tubek-Krokosz, Jarek Baran, and co-authors tracked the daily movement of one hundred forty-one healthy young women to see how moderate activity relates to immune cells that patrol for cancer. Natural killer cells and killer T cells are central to that surveillance, and exercise is thought to tune them. Activity was recorded with wrist trackers across two menstrual cycles while blood samples measured the cell populations.

Women who walked more and spent more minutes active carried higher shares of certain bright natural killer cell subtypes. More very active minutes went with stronger natural killing power in lab tests, though the cells then responded less to a stimulating signal. Total killer cell counts and T cell measures showed no clear links. The authors say moderate daily activity may quietly sharpen parts of immune surveillance.
plos-pone-0349315:
Wenxin Zhu and Huanxing Zhu developed a single lab test that detects two major causes of deadly calf diarrhoea at once: a cattle virus and a toxin-making strain of E. coli. Young calves die quickly from scours, and testing for each germ separately wastes time farmers do not have. Their combined test uses fluorescent probes that light up only when the matching germ's DNA is present.

The test proved extremely sensitive, picking up tiny amounts of either target, and it stayed silent for other cattle germs, avoiding false alarms. Repeated runs gave steady results, and trials on real clinical samples confirmed it works outside the development bench. The authors present the assay as a faster way for vets to pin down outbreaks and limit losses on cattle farms.
plos-pone-0349415:
Anna Savio and colleagues updated a systematic review of surgery's carbon footprint, gathering studies from 2023 to 2025. Operating rooms burn far more energy than any other hospital department, three to six times as much by some counts, and lean heavily on single-use materials and anesthetic gases. Twenty-six studies met the review's criteria, and each was checked for scope, boundaries, and quality.

Reported footprints varied enormously, from under five kilograms of carbon equivalent for minor procedures to over four hundred for a complex operation, and around a thousand for a whole multi-stage patient pathway. The spread reflects both real differences and inconsistent accounting. Standardizing how surgical emissions are counted is the review's central plea, because hospitals cannot cut what each study measures differently.
plos-pone-0349515:
Yolanda María de la Fuente-Robles and colleagues surveyed two hundred and nine women aged sixty and over living at home in eastern Andalusia, Spain, about abuse suffered in the past year. Using a standard mistreatment scale, they counted overall abuse and its forms, from psychological harm to neglect, and looked for the circumstances that raise the risk.

Nearly half the women reported some form of abuse. Psychological abuse was most common, reported by more than a third, followed by physical harm, financial abuse, sexual abuse, and neglect. Age, marital status, poor self-rated health, and loneliness all tracked with higher risk. The authors urge health and social services, especially frontline social workers, to get better at spotting quiet forms of abuse inside the home.
plos-pone-0349615:
Mohammadreza Eslami and colleagues looked back at ninety-four stem cell transplant patients in western Iran to see how donor and recipient blood traits jointly affected survival. Transplant doctors still struggle to predict who will do poorly years later. The team focused on two simple measures: the donor's hemoglobin level and whether the recipient had very low infection-fighting white cells before transplant.

Higher donor hemoglobin alone showed only a weak trend toward worse survival. The striking result was the interaction: the effect of donor hemoglobin depended on the recipient's white cell state before transplant. Because the study is small and exploratory, the authors treat it as a lead for larger studies, not a rule for choosing donors today.
plos-pone-0349715:
Nickson Severian Kahigi and three colleagues audit the environmental cost of a plant based building material across its whole early life, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their product pairs sisal yarn, grown and spun in Tanzania, with a corn derived plastic, and is pressed into plates in Denmark. Marketed as a green alternative, it first has to survive an honest accounting that includes shipping fiber between continents.

The audit found air freight responsible for nearly two thirds of the product's warming impact. Switching to ocean shipping, wind power, and a higher fiber share cut the footprint by about forty-four percent. Judged per unit of stiffness, the improved version then beat common plastic and aluminium window frame materials on warming. But some harms, notably certain toxic effects on people, grew worse, a burden shifting trade off the authors say designers must face openly.
plos-pone-0349815:
Tamer Abdelrehim and colleagues validated a high frequency ultrasound method for measuring jaw bone loss around teeth, with detail finer than a millimetre. Tracking tiny bone changes helps judge gum disease treatment. In lab bone models, controlled bone cuts were measured by hand and by automated ultrasound, against photo based truth.

System error stayed near a tenth of a millimetre, and the smallest reliably seen change was about one hundred and forty micrometres. Detection hit rates ranged from about eighty to one hundred percent by method and step size. Automated reads tracked change with tiny bias and excellent consistency. Radiation free ultrasound could let dentists follow bone healing visit by visit.
plos-pone-0350015:
Xitong Yang and colleagues hunted for genes tied to the immune system in pulmonary arterial hypertension, a disease where lung arteries narrow and strain the heart. They merged three public gene datasets from patient lungs and layered several analysis methods, including network mapping and machine learning, to find genes that sit at the center of the disease's activity.

Eight hub genes survived the screening and held up in separate datasets, with one gene, BCLAF1, best at telling patients from healthy tissue. Immune cell patterns in the lungs also shifted with the disease. A mouse model was used to confirm key genes in living tissue. The shortlist offers starting points for diagnostic tests and immune-focused treatments.
plos-pone-0350115:
Javier Urban-Olivares and colleagues mapped the small second genome found in copepods, tiny crustaceans that fill seas and lakes. Despite huge diversity, copepod genetic tools stay thin. The team compared nineteen full copies from public records with five fresh ones from a Mexican genus, checking size, gene order, and stretches that do not code for proteins.

New copies were the largest yet seen in copepods, swollen by long non coding stretches full of repeats and odd structures. Gene order shifts a lot, even breaking blocks that stay fixed in most animals. Some groups kept near ancestral layouts while others expanded greatly. Most genes also bear marks of active change, hinting at fast, ongoing evolution.
plos-pone-0350515:
Hongmin Wang, Zhiyong Lei, and Xing Liu proposed a joint method in 2026 for passive radar, which listens to broadcast signals instead of sending its own. Quiet radar suits covert watching, but weak signals and slow targets make both naming and locating targets unreliable.

Their framework couples a learning encoder, which judges whether a target moves, with a physics based position solver, each feeding corrections to the other in a loop. Broadcast television signals supplied the test case. Enforcing the true signal geometry at every step kept the two answers consistent. The loop design aims to stop the common failure where class and position contradict each other.
plos-pone-0350615:
Lena Jelinek and co-authors followed German patients one year after a very short, intense treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder. The Bergen four-day treatment packs standard exposure therapy into four days instead of many weeks. Earlier outcome reports came mostly from Norway, so the team tested whether the gains hold in a German day clinic.

Fifty-eight adults were checked a year after treatment. Symptom scores stayed far below where they began, and about seven in ten people still met the standard for a good response, with about half in remission. Mood, daily functioning, and quality of life also stayed better. The findings support the brief format as a real option where long therapy waits block care.
plos-pone-0350815:
Qinhui Lu, Yanli Yang, and Biao Ruan investigated why cell power units falter in allergic rhinitis, the long term nose inflammation behind endless sneezing and blockage. Gene data pointed to two linked genes that were raised in diseased nose cells. Dish tests used human nose lining cells stirred into an allergy like state with a signal protein.

Raised genes went with lower levels of two proteins that start cleanup of worn out power units, plus more cell stress and weaker power unit charge. Quieting the first gene lowered the second, restored cleanup proteins, and eased stress. Blocking that gene pair, the team proposes, might restore healthy cell cleanup in allergic noses.
plos-pone-0350915:
Jason Johnson-Peretz led a team of eight authors on this 2026 interview study of home-based blood pressure care in rural Kenya and Uganda. Inside a pilot trial, community health workers visited adults with serious hypertension and linked them by telehealth to clinicians, instead of relying on clinic trips. Forty patients and fifteen providers described the experience.

Both groups welcomed the model, praising saved travel and steady contact, and suggested adding services like medicines delivery. Johnson-Peretz presents worker-led telehealth as a patient-centered route to better hypertension control where clinics are far.
plos-pone-0351115:
Lili Sun, Chenwen Wei, and Heliang Huang ran an online experiment on how shoppers come to feel a natural food will taste good before any bite exists. Three hundred twenty volunteers saw food pages that varied by platform style, by whether the photo showed a lifestyle scene or raw nature, and by whether the text stressed eating or producing. The team modeled the chain from seeing naturalness to trusting the seller to imagining taste to thinking hard about the product.

Perceived naturalness fed engagement through several routes: directly, through credibility, through taste imagination, and through a chain where trust unlocks taste imagination, which keeps people thinking. Platform type changed which routes carried the effect. Sellers of natural foods online are really selling a simulation, and this study maps the wiring between a rustic photo and a shopper's willingness to linger, compare, and believe.
plos-pone-0351215:
Tamar Klaiman and seven colleagues explore how underrepresented Americans view taking part in clinical research. Their 2026 study covers Black, Hispanic or Latinx, women, and rural participants. These groups join studies at low rates, which weakens the science and deepens health gaps. The team worked across the Philadelphia, Atlanta, and Washington, DC areas.

Instead of standard survey questions, they used freelisting. Participants simply listed words that came to mind about research participation. Shared word patterns reveal what each group values, fears, or expects. Comparing lists across groups shows where concerns overlap and where they differ. Recruiters can then design outreach that answers each community's real concerns, rather than relying on one generic message for everyone.
plos-pone-0351315:
Gerald Agyapong-Opoku and colleagues set out a plan for mapping non-drug approaches to anxiety and depression in young people aged ten to twenty-four. Talk therapies, school programs, digital tools, and exercise schemes have multiplied, but they vary so widely that nobody can see the whole field at once. This protocol describes a scoping review that will chart what exists rather than judge what works best.

Searches across six databases will gather studies of any design, screened by two reviewers working independently and reported against a standard checklist. As a protocol, the paper reports no findings. Its contribution is the map's design: by sorting interventions by format, setting, and who they target, the finished review should show busy areas, blank spots, and the questions trialists should tackle next.
plos-pone-0352015:
Marijane Luistro Jonsson and four colleagues publish a protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026 for a wide-ranging review linking symptoms people report to proteins measured in their blood. Earlier reviews usually stayed inside one disease. This team wants a diagnosis-free map, hoping shared biology behind common symptoms will show up across conditions.

The protocol describes searching four large databases and screening the huge yield with an artificial intelligence tool, after a pilot run showed it saved real time.
