Five reviewers will extract each reported symptom-and-protein pairing and chart the patterns. The finished map is meant to guide clinicians and point symptom research toward the most promising leads.
plos-pone-0352115:
Yujie Yan, Yanling Wang, and Na An published this 2026 simulation study of acid treatment in carbonate oil reservoirs. Pumping acid into the rock dissolves winding channels called wormholes, which let oil flow more freely. Using a coupled flow-and-etching model, they tested how uneven rock, directional layering, and natural cracks shape those channels.

More uneven porosity produced bushier wormholes and slower acid breakthrough. Strong directional layering instead grew one main channel across the grain, and cracks steered growth strongly. Yan's results give field engineers a clearer picture of where injected acid will actually travel underground.
plos-pone-0352315:
Gloria Anderson and seven colleagues publish the protocol for a Rome trial, in 2026. The trial tests whether women can learn to push more effectively in labor by watching ultrasound images of their own bodies. Pushing works best when abdominal effort pairs with relaxation of the pelvic floor, yet a sizable minority of first-time mothers do the opposite, narrowing the passage and prolonging labor. The trial will enroll just under two hundred seventy women having their first baby, before labor begins.

Half receive standard midwife-led pushing training, and half add a session using real-time perineal ultrasound as biofeedback. The main measure is how long the active pushing stage lasts, with secondary measures covering muscle co-activation, type of birth, perineal injury, bleeding, continence months later, and the birth experience. The authors frame the study as a test of whether seeing changes doing in one of childbirth's hardest skills.
plos-pone-0352515:
Shrawan Patel and four colleagues redesign a basic microwave component for modern antenna arrays. Their 2026 paper presents a Wilkinson power divider that splits one signal into any number of equal outputs. Conventional designs need awkward crossovers or impossible wiring for odd counts. Their topology stacks simple one-to-two and one-to-three units, mixing equal and unequal stages. Tapered transmission lines keep every impedance inside factory-friendly limits. A two-stage triple divider was built and measured as the proof.

The prototype performed broadly and evenly. It worked across most of its target band around a common wireless frequency. Output balance stayed tight in both loudness and timing. The layout shrank by well over half against conventional equivalents. Beamforming networks, which steer 5G and radar signals, need dozens of exactly such splitters. A compact, scalable, crossover-free design removes a quiet bottleneck in building them.
plos-pone-0352815:
Zhang and Yu examined an underground ring road in a future technology district of Hangzhou in a 2026 study. The loop was built to move cars below ground and free the surface, but few drivers use it. The team gathered traffic counts on site and asked drivers about their experience with the loop.

Only about one in ten cars used the loop for arriving or leaving the district. Drivers cited low awareness, weak guidance signs, uneven access rules at each plot, and little flexibility in how the loop runs. Gains in cutting carbon also fell short of hopes. Drawing on similar projects in other Chinese districts, the authors propose clearer guidance, shared access rules, and smarter traffic control.
plos-pone-0353115:
Shelly Loewenstein and eight colleagues show that the cells lining the belly cavity send out tiny parcels that encourage new blood vessels to grow, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. That lining, the mesothelium, sits where gut and ovarian cancers spread, and the vessels they grow help tumours settle. The team harvested the parcels — extracellular vesicles — from mesothelial cell cultures and tested them on vessel-lining cells in dishes and in living tissue.

The parcels made vessel cells multiply, migrate, and form tubes, in dishes and in implanted plugs alike. A cargo protein that drives vessel growth proved to be the key messenger. Blocking that pathway, the authors propose, might starve peritoneal metastases of their blood supply.
plos-pone-0353215:
Donough, Mthimunye, and Daniels explored how exams are designed at a South African nursing school in a 2026 study. Written tests should match what students were taught and mix easy and hard thinking fairly. Interviews with nine nurse educators and reviews of moderator reports supplied the evidence.

The authors recommend training in test design, tighter matching of questions to learning goals, and stronger moderation routines. Weak tests misjudge students and can pass nurses who are not ready for clinical reasoning. Nursing programs under resource pressure still need valid exams, since patient safety later depends on the judgment those exams certify.
plos-pone-0353615:
Charlotte Lee and three colleagues test whether remembering a good or bad doctor's visit changes what patients later remember, in this 2026 PLOS ONE experiment. Two hundred and forty-five adults living with chronic pain recalled either a consultation where they felt believed and respected, or one where they felt dismissed. Afterwards everyone listened to twenty health messages and was tested on recall.

Those who had recalled feeling validated remembered more of the messages — roughly a fifth better odds for each one — than the dismissed-memory group. The boost was not explained by changes in fear of pain. The authors suggest that feeling taken seriously may free up mental room for medical advice to stick.
plos-pone-0354015:
Marloes Oomen, Lyke Esselink, and Floris Roelofsen published this 2026 experiment on yes-no questions in Dutch Sign Language. Signers acted out conversations while the researchers varied what the asker likely expected and what evidence sat in view. The team catalogued the question forms produced and what extra elements contribute.

Contrary to earlier claims, raised eyebrows were not the steady marker of a yes-no question; lowered brows appeared often too. A forward lean of head or body looked like the real signal. Oomen suggests eyebrows instead carry a range of side meanings in nonstandard questions.
plos-pone-0354115:
This 2026 notice from the PLOS One editors is a formal correction to an earlier cancer study, and it should be read before anyone relies on that study's figures. The original article claimed that a small RNA molecule slows triple-negative breast cancer by targeting a gene called KLF5. After publication, readers flagged problems in a key figure and in the statistics described in the methods.

One panel in the figure duplicated another, and a protein signal appeared in a cell line known to lack that protein entirely — raising contamination worries. The corresponding author supplied a corrected figure and conceded the signal should not be read as genuine protein. The correction leaves the paper's conclusions in a clouded state.
plos-pone-0354515:
Sugjit Singh Padda and Bradley Cardinale carried a famous farming debate into streams: share land with nature, or spare it by farming intensively elsewhere. The sharing-versus-sparing question had barely been tested in fresh water. Their 2026 study paired Pennsylvania streams flowing through shared and spared farm landscapes, matched for habitat and water quality.

Water invertebrate communities looked much the same in both stream types. Richness, evenness, total numbers, and overall composition showed no meaningful differences. Only a small shift appeared in one feeding group, which the authors judge biologically minor. Padda and Cardinale caution that land strategy lessons from forests and fields may not transfer to streams.
plos-pone-0354715:
Alice Vinet and Denis Guilbeau published this 2026 archaeology study of obsidian arrowheads deliberately cut with marks in Neolithic central Anatolia. Eleven newly identified pieces from a Cappadocian settlement joined a known set of only a few dozen, all dating to roughly nine thousand years ago. The team examined the stone sources, making sequence, wear, and the cuts themselves.

The marks varied widely and matched nothing about material, shape, or use, and they were cut at different stages of manufacture. Earlier guesses called them hunters' identity marks. Vinet urges caution, while noting the odd custom persisted through cultural change.
plos-pone-0354915:
Monica Emendi and co-authors model a lung support machine in 2026. The machine takes over when lungs fail badly. It drains blood, adds oxygen, and returns the blood. The study asks what a second drainage tube changes. Computer fluid models were built in an average heart chamber. Layouts, tube types, and tube positions were compared.

One standard layout wasted the most flow in a short loop. It also gave the lowest blood oxygen level. A dual layout did far better on both counts. It used a multi hole tube placed in the neck. Pressures and wall stress differed sharply by layout. Stagnant blood volume also varied a lot. The best choice should fit each patient, the authors say.
plos-pone-0355315:
Ameerah Ibrahim and co-authors interview in 2026 community pharmacists in Amman, Jordan, about offering services that promote health and prevent disease. Such services could ease pressure from long term diseases, and pharmacists are easy for the public to reach. Themes from the talks were mapped onto a framework covering capability, opportunity, and motivation.

Pharmacists described wide and growing roles, but heavy workload, weak patient engagement, no pay for the extra work, and little owner support held them back. Training, better undergraduate teaching, and closer work with doctors were seen as needs. Fixing those blocks could let pharmacists prevent more illness, the authors say.
plos-pone-0355415:
Matthew J Hardy and a team of wildlife and poultry researchers track wintering geese with GPS collars on the Delmarva Peninsula, a hotspot for both wild waterfowl and chicken farming. Bird flu carried by wild geese threatens flocks, and response teams cannot guard every farm equally. Across four winters, the team followed several dozen snow geese and Canada geese and scored thousands of poultry sites by goose traffic nearby.

The scoring separated risk well: farms that later saw outbreaks sat high in the ranking, one among the very top of thousands. A third of all farms had collared geese nearby at some point. Timing mattered, with each goose species peaking in a different part of winter. Hardy and colleagues offer the ranking to aim scarce biosecurity effort where birds actually gather.
plos-pone-0355515:
Correction notice. Asuka Tanno and co-authors correct three figures in their published study of a four-celled green alga and its response to light. The original paper reported weak swimming behaviour toward light and strong protection against light damage. This 2026 notice replaces faulty panels and data traces.

In one figure, the control panels had duplicated the treated panels at three time points; corrected panels from the original experiments now replace them. A supplementary legend carried a wrong sample number for swimming speed. A third figure's model traces came from an earlier paper by the same group and should not have been included. The authors supply the underlying images so readers can verify the corrected record.
plos-pone-0355715:
Violeta Carrillo and colleagues describe in 2026 how they tagged two fungi that attack pyrethrum, a crop grown for natural insecticide. Using a bacterium based method, they inserted glowing markers into each fungus. One strain glowed green and the other red, letting infection be watched under a microscope.

Genome checks showed mostly single insertions, and tagged strains grew and infected leaves much like wild ones. In one fungus, spores sprouted within a day and hyphae entered leaf skin by three days. These tools give the first clear view of early infection for that species and support later work on how the disease spreads.
plos-pone-0356815:
Jianxing Liu and colleagues studied how freezing changes the grip of a railway track bed, the crushed stone that keeps rails from sliding sideways. Their 2026 study combined full-scale track bed tests, compression tests on stone and ice mixtures, and computer simulations of individual stones, varying ice content, temperature, and freezing depth in a systematic design.

Ice content and freezing depth dominated: both pushed sideways resistance upward as they grew, while temperature mattered only weakly and indirectly. The simulations showed the microscopic reason, ice bonding stones into a stiffer mass. Their predictive model helps engineers in cold regions judge how track strength swings through freeze and thaw, information that feeds into winter safety margins and maintenance planning.
plos-pone-0356915:
Md Golam Kibria and colleagues surveyed 660 tobacco-using patients with chronic diseases at government hospitals in Bangladesh. They asked what the patients knew about services that help people quit. They also asked whether the patients would use them. Their 2026 cross-sectional study is, the authors note, among the first to measure this. In Bangladesh, tobacco use remains heavy and quit support is thin.

Knowledge was strikingly low: only about one patient in ten knew the services moderately well. Yet two thirds said they would use them. Schooling drove knowledge. Knowledge in turn tripled the odds of willingness, alongside frequent hospital contact. The practical conclusion writes itself. Tell patients the help exists, every visit, and most are already willing.
plos-pone-0357015:
Si Yang leads a team of five examining how sex shapes the gut and metabolism story of aging, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their subjects were mice: young and older animals of both sexes, with and without a gene called Nrf2 that defends cells against oxidative stress. The team ran glucose tolerance tests, measured fats and sex hormones, examined liver and fat tissue, and sequenced gut bacteria from droppings.

Aging male mice lacking the gene showed clearly impaired glucose handling, a combination that spared the other groups. Fat piled up in liver and body fat stores with age across genotypes and sexes. Blood fat patterns diverged by group rather than marching together. One striking gut result: older females without the gene carried notably less diverse gut bacteria than both their male counterparts and normal females. The study argues that aging research ignoring sex will keep averaging away real effects.
plos-pone-0357115:
Moritz Unnerstall led a team of six authors improving a lab separation method, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Porphyrins are pigments in blood whose levels signal certain diseases, but separating them cleanly from serum is hard. The team analyzed serum porphyrins and tested a special column type for liquid chromatography.

Unnerstall's group showed that inert biphenyl columns give cleaner, sharper separations. Better separation means more reliable readings for labs that test these pigments. Small method gains like this rarely get attention, yet diagnosis depends on them: a muddy separation can hide or fake a result. Labs adopting the column advice can cut fuss and repeat tests in porphyrin work.
plos-pone-0357215:
Jasmine S Turner and colleagues build, together with refugee communities in Uganda, a program to keep refugee children attending school consistently. Attendance falters for reasons that outsiders often misread. In settlements across Uganda, caregivers and teachers joined workshops to map what drives attendance. The maps were checked in validation meetings. The resulting program, called SchoolLinks, was then tried in one school. Its pupils were young children and catch-up learners.

The maps showed caregiver attitudes and encouragement at the center, shaped by how well caregivers and teachers communicate across language barriers. The program therefore works on that relationship as much as on the child. Turner and colleagues collected feedback from staff, families, and children during the trial run to refine the design before any wider rollout.
plos-pone-0357315:
Nabasmita Malakar, Ravikanth Gudasalamani, and Ganesan Rengaian published a 2026 taxonomy study in PLOS ONE untangling two Asian trees in the laurel family that botanists have confused for two centuries. The two names have been mixed in herbaria and books, blurring where each species actually grows. The team combined twenty-eight physical traits, family trees from two nuclear gene markers, and ecological niche modeling.

Every line of evidence agreed: the two are distinct species with separate homelands. One is confined to the Indo-Burma biodiversity hotspot, the other to India's Eastern Ghats and the Western Ghats–Sri Lanka hotspot. Physical trait clustering matched the genetic split, and their modeled ranges barely overlap. Sorting out such confusion matters: conservation plans protect species, and a species wrongly merged with another can quietly vanish. The laurel family in India, they say, needs more of this integrative attention.
plos-pone-0357815:
Yael Rozman and Miri Tal-Saban compared inner strengths in teenagers with attention and movement disorders, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Adolescents with ADHD, developmental coordination disorder, or both face daily friction at school and in sport. Yet some thrive. The team measured resilience, feelings of hope, and a sense of coherence across these groups and typically developing peers.

Rozman and Tal-Saban's comparisons reveal which inner resources differ, and which protect struggling teens most. That matters because support often focuses only on deficits. Building on strengths that a group already has can be more effective than generic help. The study gives therapists, teachers, and parents a map of where each group's reserves lie, and where they run thin.
plos-pone-0357915:
Jun Lin published a 2026 engineering study in PLOS ONE on tightening bolts evenly in curvic couplings, the toothed metal joints used in aircraft engines. If the ten bolts in such a coupling end up with uneven grip, the joint loses precision and loads spread unevenly. Using computer simulations plus an elastic-interaction model, Lin compared ways of tightening the bolts in stages and in different orders, with a flat disk joint as a reference.

The toothed surface made grip differences between bolts much larger than in the flat reference, and the outcome became more sensitive to the tightening path. Tightening one bolt after another in sequence performed worst, while a crisscross pattern across two axes gave the most even result. A three-stage version of that pattern, rising gradually to full tightness, worked best overall. The findings warn engineers not to carry flat-joint rules over to toothed couplings.
plos-pone-0359015:
Xiangcai Luo and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on lithium-ion batteries. It estimates state of health, how much capacity a battery has left, using data-driven methods with feature sifting, selecting the most telling signals. The model joins KPCA with a transformer-LSTM hybrid whose tuning is optimized by an algorithm called NRBO.

Accurate health estimates decide when electric vehicle and storage batteries are safe, tired, or ready for a second life. Hybrid models that both compress signals and read their sequence aim for accuracy without huge computing cost. Battery engineers and energy storage researchers are the readers for this estimation recipe.
plos-pone-0359215:
Carver and co-authors reported in 2026 on genomic surveillance of ticks collected from farm animals living in communities in Eastern Ontario, Canada. The work follows the One Health idea, that human, animal, and environmental health are one connected system. Ticks picked off animals such as horses, cattle, and goats can carry the microbes that cause tick borne illness in people.

By reading the DNA in those ticks, the team identified which microbes are circulating in the area before they show up as human cases. Surveillance of this kind gives public health officials an early map of risk by place and season. It also shows how much can be learned from animals that share fields and trails with their owners.
plos-pone-0359415:
Dong Hun Lee and five colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on breast surgery. It addresses red breast syndrome, a complication that can follow reconstruction using ADM, a processed tissue material that supports the rebuilt breast. The authors build an exploratory scoring model to predict which patients face this problem.

The model uses routine hematologic markers, ordinary blood test values already collected before surgery. A score built from cheap, standard tests could flag high-risk patients early without extra procedures. Reconstructive surgeons are the audience, since forewarning lets them watch or treat the patients most likely to develop the syndrome.
plos-pone-0359515:
Daniel Wright published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies survey scales, the multi-question measures used across social research. The question is whether adding follow-up probes to selected responses, extra questions attached to some answers, changes how people respond to those very items.

Probes are meant to clarify answers, but any change to a question can shift the answers it collects. If probing some responses alters later ones, surveys using the technique may not match surveys without it. Survey methodologists, who design questionnaires for governments and researchers, are the readers for this cautionary test.

Blin and co-authors describe version seven of antiSMASH, a software tool for finding useful chemistry in microbes. Small living things make special compounds as part of their normal growth. Many of these compounds can kill germs or fungi, fight viruses, or attack cancer cells, so they matter for drugs and farming.

Version seven improves how the tool spots the gene groups that make these compounds. It also improves guesses about how those groups are switched on, what the compounds look like, and how results are shown. Better maps of hidden chemistry help teams choose which microbes deserve costly lab work.

Kumar, Stecher, Suleski, and co-authors introduce MEGA12, the twelfth version of a widely used program for studying evolution from DNA. MEGA stands for Molecular Evolutionary Genetic Analysis. Researchers use it to build family trees and test how species changed over time.

The new version cuts the computing time for key steps, such as picking the best model of change and running repeat tests of tree support. It also aims at leaner, greener computing that uses less energy. Faster analysis lets teams handle larger datasets on ordinary computers, widening who can do this work.

Shafiei, Latorre, and Shimmin ask whether offset liners in hip replacements raise the risk of the socket working loose. Restoring a hip's natural geometry is key to a replacement that lasts. Offset, or lateralised, liners push the joint outward, raising total offset and tightening soft tissues, which can steady the new hip.

Whether that gain costs fixation was unknown. The team studied the question in Australia's national joint replacement registry, following real-world implants at scale. Registry data answer questions trials are too small to settle. Their findings help surgeons weigh a steadier hip today against the chance of a loosening, and a revision operation, years later.

Mustafa and colleagues test elastic bands that double as body sensors. Their bands are crocheted textiles threaded with yarn coated in silver, which carries electric signals. Soft, stretchy sensors could track movement or breathing without hard cases, but keeping their signals steady through repeated stretching and wear is the hard part.

The team measured the bands' strength, stretch, look, and electrical behaviour under use-like conditions. They ask how the signal drifts as the band is pulled again and again, as real clothing is. Results like these decide whether smart garments can leave the lab bench and survive daily life on a moving body.

Rai and an international team based largely at Baylor College of Medicine challenge a basic assumption behind a class of cancer drugs. Histone deacetylase inhibitors are approved for blood cancers and tested in hundreds of trials. The drugs are assumed to work by blocking the enzymes they are named for. The team checked that assumption with genetics, cell screens, and animal models.

Across most cancers, enzyme levels and variants failed to track with tumor growth, survival, or drug response. Genome-wide CRISPR screens likewise never flagged the enzymes as decisive. Crippled versions of the enzymes mimicked the drugs' chemical marks but not their killing effect. Removing a drug's enzyme-blocking power chemically left its anticancer action intact in mice, suggesting other targets drive the benefit.

Copper and zinc moved with iron and manganese oxides in the soil. Transfer into food stayed modest, with intakes below European food safety limits.

Karan Patil and colleagues reviewed a new direction in biological pest control: insect-killing fungi that live inside plants. Their article appeared in the World Journal of Microbiology and Biotechnology in 2026. Sprayed fungi often fail in the field because of cost, short shelf life, and weather sensitivity. As endophytes, genera such as Metarhizium, Beauveria, and Lecanicillium persist within plant tissue instead of sitting on the surface.

Inside the plant, these fungi still attack insect pests, and they can shift plant scents to draw in the pests' own predators. They also promote plant growth and help crops tolerate drought and other stress. Gene transfer from plant hosts may explain how they gained these mixed skills. Colonization in real fields remains uneven, though, and host range, ecological risk, and scale-up are open problems. The review maps what must improve before farmers can rely on them.

Mohamed Hemdan and colleagues designed a filter membrane that separates oil from wastewater and then cleans itself with light. Their paper appeared in Scientific Reports in 2026. The membrane starts from a common polymer and mixes in a metal-organic framework plus sheets of graphitic carbon nitride. Together the additives make the surface love water and repel oil, while light activates a photocatalytic cleaning action.

Performance held up across changes in pressure, dose, and oil concentration, and fouling built up more slowly than in the plain polymer. Repeated cycles showed the membrane could be reused without losing its edge. The authors present the design as a low-energy answer to oily industrial wastewater. Its mix of filtering, adsorption, and self-cleaning in one sheet is the central claim.

Renate Reisenegger and Frank Bremmer asked whether letting the eyes roam helps people judge how far they have traveled through a virtual scene. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports in 2026. Volume one, Mary, contains the Protevangelion of James, an early account of Mary's birth and childhood and of Jesus's infancy. Suppressed is Wake's provocative word; most of these texts were simply never canonized, though churches debated some for centuries. Their stories, including an aged Joseph, Mary's parents Joachim and Anna, and midwives at the nativity, shaped medieval art and devotion deeply. Readers meet the New Testament's cast-offs in stately English.
tob-0115:
Priests and thinkers of late Roman Egypt wrote dialogues in which Hermes Trismegistus, the thrice-great, teaches chosen pupils. Eight of those tractates form this selection of the Corpus Hermeticum. Hermes speaks of God, the making of the cosmos, and the soul's climb back toward light.

The teachings blend Greek philosophy with Egyptian religion, and Renaissance readers took them for wisdom older than Moses. Magicians, theologians, and artists all drank from this spring. Modern scholars place the texts in the first centuries of the common era. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry.
tob-10415:
James Legge's classic English version of the Analects presents twenty books of brief sayings and dialogues preserving Confucius's teaching. Disciples compiled the record after his death from remembered conversations. Short exchanges, sometimes only a sentence or two, carry nearly all of it, often opening with the Master said.

Honor your parents, keep your word, study constantly, and govern by virtue rather than force: these counsels recur in many settings. Rulers, students, and family members all receive instruction fitted to the moment. The Analects became the moral backbone of Chinese civilization for two thousand years, and Legge's translation remains a standard way in for English readers.
tob-10815:
Three Initiates compressed Hermetic wisdom into seven working principles in The Kybalion, first published in 1908. The plain Gutenberg text of that classic is what stands here. Principles include mentalism, summed up as the All is Mind, correspondence in as above, so below, and vibration: everything moves, nothing rests.

Unlike a scripture to be admired, the principles are presented as tools meant to be used on oneself and one's circumstances. Each receives a short chapter with axioms and explanation. Brief enough to read in an evening, the book has been quoted for a century wherever modern Hermetic and New Thought teaching circulates, and argued over just as long.
tob-4015:
Giorgio Vasari, painter, architect, and tireless gossip, effectively invented art history in his Lives of the Most Eminent Painters, Sculptors and Architects. Volume one begins with Cimabue and Giotto, the pioneers who, in Vasari's story, pulled painting out of the Byzantine dark toward natural life. Anecdote, judgment, and hero-worship fill every life.

Vasari knew workshops, patrons, and surviving works at first hand, though he never let a missing fact spoil a good story. The Renaissance here tells its own story, arranging masters as a rising line toward perfection. Later research corrects him often, yet his framework, progress through great individuals, still shapes how art is taught.
tob-4115:
Reynold A. Nicholson, the great Cambridge scholar of Persian, translated Rumi's Mathnawi with a full commentary. Volume one opens the vast poem Jalal al-Din Rumi composed in thirteenth-century Konya. The song of the reed flute sounds first: cut from its bed, it cries for home, like the soul exiled from God.

Tales of kings, fools, lovers, and parrots carry the teaching from story to story. Nicholson's version, begun in 1925, became the definitive English Mathnawi, praised for accuracy and grace alike. Verified from the 1919 edition record, volume one starts Sufism's supreme poem on its long, winding road.
tob-4214-10715:
Counsels and Maxims gathers Schopenhauer's rules for daily life, in Saunders's crisp English translation. The thinker who called existence a mistake still wanted to help readers suffer less. His counsel is worldly and dry-eyed: guard your privacy, expect little from others, and enjoy solitude.

He advises readers to keep money matters quiet, to bear fools with patience, and to rest happiness only on what lies in their own power. Some maxims sting; many prove wise with age. The short pieces read well in sittings of a few pages. Few self-help books since have matched its candor or its style.
tob-4215:
Rudolf Steiner's Philosophy of Spiritual Activity, also known as The Philosophy of Freedom, appeared in Hoernlé's translation under its alternate English title. Written before Steiner's esoteric period, it argues that free will is real and that thinking itself is a spiritual activity the thinker can observe. Steiner considered this book the foundation of everything he later built.

Knowledge, freedom, and moral individualism are worked out philosophically, without appeal to revelation or clairvoyance. Action is free, he claims, when it flows from ideas the individual has made fully conscious. His most philosophical and most accessible book, it lets readers judge Steiner the thinker separately from Steiner the occult teacher.
un-ga-res-15: Two money panels of the United Nations owe their shape to Resolution 15, passed on 13 February 1946. Rule changes fix the Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions at nine members, with at least two finance experts of known standing. A second panel, the Committee on Contributions, gets ten members. The same rules set out how the first panels would draw lots for one, two, and three year terms.
un-ga-res-a-69-15:
Small island states won a plan of their own at a world meet in Samoa, and Resolution A/69/15 adopts its text. The third world meeting on Small Island Developing States sat at Apia from 1 to 4 September 2014, at the highest level. The Assembly thanks the state and people of Samoa for hosting the meet and for all their support of it.

The outcome text bears a long name: the SIDS Accelerated Modalities of Action, or SAMOA Pathway. It is annexed to the vote in full. Heads of state and chiefs at Apia restated their pledge to the lasting growth of small island lands. Such lands face sharp risks, from rising seas to far markets, and the plan sets swift paths for aid and joint work.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 15, adopted on 13 February 1946, amended the Assembly's provisional rules of procedure to fix the makeup of two budget bodies. The Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions was set at nine members, at least two of them noted finance experts, and the Committee on Contributions at ten. Added rules set staggered first terms, so part of each body would be chosen for three years and part for two.

General Assembly resolution 69/15 was adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014. It endorses the outcome of the third International Conference on Small Island Developing States. The conference was held in Apia, Samoa, from 1 to 4 September 2014. The resolution itself is short; its substance is the long annexed document it adopts.

That annex, the SIDS Accelerated Modalities of Action (SAMOA) Pathway, sets out how small island states and their partners should pursue sustainable development. It takes account of the islands' special vulnerability to sea-level rise and climate change. It reaffirms the earlier Barbados Programme of Action and Mauritius Strategy. It calls for genuine, durable partnerships across economic growth, oceans, and food security. It also calls for them across water, energy, and disaster risk. Endorsement by the Assembly turned a conference outcome into the United Nations framework for island development for the following decade.
un-sc-res-1315:
Sierra Leone's war crimes were set on the road to a court on 14 August 2000. The Council voiced deep concern at the very serious crimes committed against Sierra Leone's people and at United Nations staff. Impunity reigned in the country. The Lomé amnesty, the Council recalled, could not cover genocide, crimes against humanity, or war crimes. Sierra Leone's president had written on 12 June asking for help.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to negotiate an agreement with Sierra Leone's government to create an independent special court. He was to recommend its reach. The court should cover crimes against humanity, war crimes, and other grave breaches of humanitarian law, plus set crimes under Sierra Leonean law. It should be able to try those who bear the greatest responsibility. The court's fairness and independence had to be secured, and a report on the plan was due to the Council.
un-sc-res-1415:
The Golan Heights observer force came up for renewal in May 2002. On 30 May 2002 the Security Council renewed UNDOF for seven months. The new term ran until 31 December 2002. The Secretary-General had reported on the force two weeks earlier. The Council also restated its rule on protecting peacekeepers from disease. Little else in the text changes the mission's shape.

As usual, the parties had to carry out resolution 338 at once. That 1973 text demanded a ceasefire and a move toward peace. The Secretary-General owed a report at the end of the term. UNDOF's soldiers kept their posts between Israeli and Syrian lines. The routine renewal masked a border that stayed tense beneath the calm.
un-sc-res-15:
Claims of border raids in the north of Greece led the Security Council to send its own team to look, under Resolution 15, passed on 19 December 1946. Greece, Yugoslavia, Albania, and Bulgaria had each laid claims and charges before the Council. The charges dealt with a state of unrest along the Greek border with the three states to its north. In the Council's view, the facts must be found before any firm word can be given.

A Commission of Investigation is set up under Article 34 of the Charter. One member from each state on the Council, as it will stand in 1947, forms the team. It must reach the ground by 15 January 1947 and report back at the soonest date. The probe was the young Council's first field test of its peace powers.
un-sc-res-1515:
A step-by-step plan toward two states in the Middle East won the Council's backing on 19 November 2003. The plan was called the Road Map. It had been drawn up by the Quartet, a group of four: the United Nations, the United States, the European Union, and Russia. Tragic and violent events in the region were still going on. Resolution 1515 was adopted unanimously.

The Council endorsed the Quartet's performance-based Road Map to a permanent two-state solution of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. The parties were called on to meet their obligations under the plan. They had to work with the Quartet to reach its goal. The Council restated its vision of the region. Two states, Israel and Palestine, would live side by side within secure and recognized borders. It also repeated its demand for an immediate end to all acts of violence, including terrorism, provocation, incitement, and destruction.
un-sc-res-1615:
Georgia and Abkhazia are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1615, adopted on 29 July 2005. The Abkhaz side still refused to discuss the paper on sharing powers between Tbilisi and Sukhumi. Talks on Abkhazia's status had not even begun. Whoever shot down a United Nations helicopter in 2001, killing nine, was still unknown.

The text extends the United Nations Observer Mission in Georgia, called UNOMIG, until 31 January 2006. It urges the Abkhaz side to take up the powers paper at last. Both sides must drop warlike talk and restart the peace work in earnest. A letter of intent on refugee returns should be signed fast. The remaining police officers for the Gali sector must be let in.
un-sc-res-1815: Security Council Resolution 1815 is held here as a transcription of the official record, sourced from English Wikisource. Its paragraphs demonstrate the Council's way of turning politics into text: agree on a description of events, then agree on what follows from it. The entry preserves that agreed text whole, exactly as the members left it.
un-sc-res-1915: Resolution 1915 is a Security Council act preserved here in its official-record wording, sourced from English Wikisource. The text's life in the record is permanent, unlike the meeting that produced it. Readers get the permanent part complete: the situation as the fifteen members stated it and the decision they collectively imposed on it.
un-sc-res-2015:
Piracy trials are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 2015, adopted on 24 October 2011. Navies caught many Somali pirate suspects but few faced trial anywhere. A United Nations report had set out how special anti-piracy courts might work in Somalia and nearby states. Kenya and the Seychelles were already trying suspects with outside help.

The Council decides to keep studying the plan for specialized courts backed by international support. The Secretary-General must consult Somalia and regional states, with the United Nations drugs and development agencies. He should report what help the courts need, how suspects and proof would be transferred, and what the courts would cost. The text also stresses that Somalia itself bears the main duty to end piracy.
un-sc-res-215: Official record keeping at the United Nations preserves Resolution 215, a Security Council text the catalog dates to 1965. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-315: The decision entered as Resolution 315 forms part of the Council record catalogued for 1964. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-415: A formal decision of the United Nations Security Council, Resolution 415 is catalogued here under 1977. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Morocco regained independence from France in March 1956. The kingdom moved fast to claim its place among states. Its UN application reached the Council that summer. Resolution 115 was adopted unanimously on 20 June 1956 at the 731st meeting.

Members recommended that the General Assembly admit Morocco. The Assembly did so that November, in a landmark admissions round. Many new states entered the UN the same season. For Morocco, the seat crowned its return to sovereignty. It also began the kingdom's long UN involvement with the Western Sahara question. That file would return to the Council again and again in later decades.

Crimes in Sierra Leone's war demand a court, and Resolution 1315, adopted on 14 August 2000, starts building one. The Council voiced deep alarm at grave crimes against Sierra Leoneans and UN staff, and at the impunity that prevailed. Sierra Leone's government and West African leaders were both working to end the war for good.

The Council asked the UN chief to work out a pact with Sierra Leone for a stand-alone special court. Its job would be to prosecute those bearing the greatest responsibility for crimes against humanity, war crimes, and other grave breaches of the laws of war on Sierra Leonean territory since 1996. Negotiations produced the Special Court for Sierra Leone.

A seven-month term, not six, marks this Golan renewal of 2002. On 30 May, the Council adopted Resolution 1415 without dissent. The Secretary-General's May report on the observer force lay before it. That force, UNDOF, had watched the Israel-Syria split zone since 1974.

The text calls on the parties to carry out Resolution 338 at once. That 1973 order pairs a truce with peace talks. The mandate then runs seven months, to 31 December 2002. The extra month lined the renewal cycle up with the calendar year. A report from the Secretary-General is due at the end. It must cover events and steps taken toward Resolution 338.

Greece and its northern neighbours had traded charges over disturbed conditions and border violations in northern Greece, and on 19 December 1946 the Council decided the facts had to come first. Albania, Bulgaria, and Yugoslavia were the neighbours named. Before drawing conclusions, the Council wanted evidence gathered on the ground.

Acting under Article 34 of the Charter, it set up a Commission of Investigation with one member from each Council state as constituted in 1947. The commission was to reach the area by 15 January 1947 and report its findings as soon as possible. It could work across northern Greece and other relevant places, call on officials and citizens for information, and send early reports if needed.

Resolution 1515 is a UN Security Council endorsement of the Middle East Roadmap, adopted unanimously on 19 November 2003, amid continuing Israeli-Palestinian violence. It recalls the Council's core texts, including Resolutions 242, 338, and 1397, and repeats the demand for an immediate end to violence, terror, and incitement.

The resolution endorses the Quartet's phased Roadmap, drawn up by the United States, Russia, the European Union, and the United Nations to end in two states living side by side. It calls on both parties to fulfill their Roadmap obligations in cooperation with the Quartet. By adopting the plan itself, the Council gave the Roadmap the standing of a UN-endorsed framework.

Georgia's observer mission is extended amid a stalled peace process in Resolution 1615, adopted on 29 July 2005. The Abkhaz side still refused to discuss the 'Basic Principles' paper on dividing competences between Tbilisi and Sukhumi. A security-guarantees meeting had been cancelled. The 2001 shooting down of a UNOMIG helicopter, which killed nine people, remained unsolved. Geneva meetings of the Group of Friends had kept momentum.

The Council extends the UN Observer Mission in Georgia, UNOMIG, to 31 January 2006. It insists Abkhazia's status must be settled within the Georgian state. It urges the Abkhaz side to accept the principles paper and negotiate. It demands progress on refugee and displaced-person returns, which it calls a special responsibility of the Abkhaz side. It presses for the UNOMIG civilian police to deploy fully in the Gali sector and for those behind the helicopter attack to be identified and brought to justice.

The race to lead the UN ended behind closed doors in 2006. Kofi Annan's two terms were nearly done. The Council met in private on 9 October 2006 to pick its choice. Resolution 1715 came out of that closed 5547th meeting. No vote count was made public in the text.

The members put one name to the General Assembly: Ban Ki-moon. He was South Korea's foreign minister. His term would run from 1 January 2007 to 31 December 2011. The Assembly backed the choice days later. Ban became the eighth person to hold the post. He led the UN through the Haiti quake and the Arab Spring's first years. This one-line text set that decade in motion.

The Beirut bombing investigation commission is extended until 31 December 2008 on 2 June 2008. Its March report described steady progress in the inquiry into the February 2005 attack and other attacks in Lebanon since October 2004. Its head had asked for more time to keep the investigation stable and continuous.

The commission's outstanding professional work in hard conditions is praised, and the extension is granted. The commission is to keep helping the Lebanese authorities and report on progress as asked. The step also bridged toward the start of the Special Tribunal for Lebanon, which the Council had decided in 2007 to establish to try those accused in the case.

One large trial at the war crimes court for the former Yugoslavia ran into delays in early 2010. Resolution 1915, adopted on 18 March 2010, makes a narrow change to help that trial finish. An earlier decision had let two temporary judges stay past the end of their terms. They were finishing the Popović case, and judgment had been expected by the end of March.

Unforeseen problems pushed the judgment back. The Council therefore extended the same arrangement for a few more months. The court could keep up to thirteen temporary judges at once, one above its normal maximum. The arrangement would end on 30 June 2010, or when the Popović case ended, whichever came first. Nothing else about the court changed. One case simply needed more time to reach its judgment.

Prosecuting Somali pirates is the focus of Resolution 2015, adopted on 24 October 2011. Many captured suspects were still being released without trial. Hostage-taking continued in inhuman conditions. A Secretary-General's report had set out how specialized anti-piracy courts could work. It said courts in Somaliland and Puntland might reach international standards in about three years given enough help.

The Council demands a complete set of Somali counter-piracy laws, covering financiers and organizers as well as attackers, with a report from the Somali authorities by 31 December 2011. It urges all states to criminalize piracy at home and to report their measures by the same date. It decides to keep considering, urgently, specialized anti-piracy courts in Somalia and the region with substantial international support. Their reach must extend to the criminal networks' key figures. It asks for detailed implementation proposals within 90 days.

Two months after its first cease-fire demands in the India-Pakistan war, the Council spoke again on 5 November 1965. Resolution 215 regrets the delay in reaching a full cease-fire. Troops had still not pulled back to the lines held before 5 August 1965.

The Council reaffirmed Resolution 211 in all its parts. India and Pakistan were told to order their forces to cooperate with the United Nations and stop all military activity. The two governments had to work out an agreed plan with an envoy of the Secretary-General. Their representatives would meet the envoy to set a timetable for the withdrawals. A progress report was due within three weeks.

Half a year more for the Cyprus peacekeeping force was granted on 15 June 1972, as had happened many times before. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 6 May, found the force still needed to preserve peace. The government of Cyprus agreed it should continue beyond 15 June. Resolution 315 records that decision.

The Council reaffirmed its Cyprus resolutions, from Resolution 186 of 1964 onward. The parties were urged to show the utmost restraint. They were also told to speed up their joint efforts toward the Council's goals. The calmer climate on the island was to be used in a constructive way. The extension runs to 15 December 1972. The Council expected that progress toward a final solution might then allow the force to leave or to shrink.

Britain wrote to the Council in September 1977 with fresh proposals for ending the Rhodesia rebellion by negotiation. Britain, the ruling power, invited the Secretary-General to take part. The proposals pointed toward majority rule in place of the white minority regime. Resolution 415 was adopted on 29 September 1977.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to appoint a representative. The choice would be made in consultation with the members of the Council. The representative would open discussions with the British resident commissioner designate. All the parties involved were included as well. The talks had to cover the military and related arrangements needed for a move to majority rule. The Secretary-General had to report on the talks as soon as possible. All parties were called on to cooperate with the representative.
us-amendment-15:
Ratified in 1870, the Fifteenth Amendment closed the Reconstruction era with a promise about the ballot. Congress wrote it to stop states from keeping Black men from voting because of race. Its words also cover color and a past state of being held in slavery.

The text is short, but its meaning is large: the right to vote cannot be denied on those grounds. For decades after 1870, many states still blocked Black voters through tricks, tests, and fear. Only with the Voting Rights Act of 1965 did the promise gain real force. The amendment remains a core guard for voting rights.
vaux-de-cernay-latin-1615:
Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay marched with the crusade against the Cathars and wrote its history in Latin. Historia Albigensium, in the Latin edition of 1615, is his eyewitness account of the Albigensian Crusade. He wrote from the crusaders' side, as a monk in their camp.

His chronicle follows the war from its launch in 1209 through sieges, battles, and burnings in the south of France. He names towns, lords, and churchmen as the conquest rolls on. No source stands closer to the crusaders' own view of the war. Later study of the Cathars still starts with his hard, bright pages.
veblen-imperial-germany-1915:
Veblen applied his institutional method to a nation in Imperial Germany and the Industrial Revolution, from 1915. Germany had taken up machine industry late and fast. Its dynastic state, with an emperor and a military caste, ruled over that new industry. The mix of old power and new plant is Veblen's subject.

He asks what such a mix means for war, trade, and social change. Germany borrowed technology whole, skipping the slow habits England grew through. That borrowed edge, plus dynastic aims, made a dangerous compound in his analysis. The book appeared while Europe was already at war. It reads as institutional study turned on national growth.
woolf-voyage-out-1915:
Virginia Woolf published The Voyage Out in 1915, her first novel, after years of drafting and illness. Woolf was thirty-three and had already seen early versions rejected. The book carries a young woman from sheltered London into the wider world.

Rachel Vinrace, a shy pianist of twenty-four, sails to South America on her father's ship. At a small resort she meets young English tourists and falls into a first serious love with the writer Terence Hewet. Books, talk, and a trip upriver open her mind to adult life. Then fever strikes, and the voyage toward self-knowledge ends in death. The novel already shows Woolf's gift for inner life.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol15:
Volume XV of the Journal of Discourses, issued at Liverpool in 1873, gathers sermons from a church deep into its Utah era. Brigham Young, his counsellors, and the Twelve Apostles preach across its many pages in turn. Their words went from shorthand notebooks to print abroad, then back to readers across the world.

Faith, conduct, and community fill the talks in the Journal's usual close mixture of high and daily things. Because nothing was smoothed for later tastes, the record stays a primary source of the first rank. Volume XV carries the doctrinal story forward by one more year of the movement's own voice.
